en: The *Lengqie abatuo luo bao fa jing jing jie ping lin* (A Critical Commentary on the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*).
Regarding the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, Luo Zhen’ang’s *Yinzhi ji* states:
"When Bodhidharma transmitted the Dharma to the Second Patriarch, he said that the four-fascicle *Laṅkā* could [serve as the basis for transmission]."
The *Lankavatara Sutra* has been translated four times in total. The version in four fascicles is the translation from the Liu Song period;
its prose is quite profound and difficult to read, yet it undoubtedly originated from the Buddha. (Xing Jianzi said: "The great purport of the *Lankavatara Sutra* consists of four points.")
[The text] says: "The five dharmas; the three self-natures; the eight consciousnesses; and the two kinds of non-self. (Master Daoyi addressed the assembly, saying:
"You all should each believe that your own mind is Buddha; this mind is itself the Buddha-mind.
Master Bodhidharma transmitted the Dharma of the Supreme Vehicle’s single mind to cause you to attain awakening. Furthermore, he cited the text of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*. )

This serves to seal the minds of sentient beings. Fearing that you might fall into inversion and fail to have confidence in this Dharma of the single mind—which each and every one possesses—the *Laṅkāvatāra* takes the Buddha’s words on the mind as its core principle (*amala-dharmaparyāya*).
The commentary states: Laṅkā is the name of a city; in the language of China, it means "unapproachable. This city is situated atop Mount Malaya in the Southern Sea;
those who lack supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) cannot go there. It was at this place that the Buddha preached the Dharma; it is, therefore, the realm of the Buddha.
The location indicates the Dharma. *Abhuttara* (阿跋多羅) means "unsurpassed" in the language of the Flower [China], and it is also translated as "entry.

"Jewel" (*ratna*) refers to an object of supreme value; it is used as a metaphor for the venerable and noble nature of this sutra. Thus, the title is formed by combining the Dharma with the metaphor. "Sutra" (*sūtra*) means "to string together," signifying that it strings together and penetrates all meanings.
Regarding its essence being the "mind of the primary meaning" (*paramārtha-citta*), this refers to the Tathāgatagarbha itself.

"Nature is pure" refers to the mind of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). "Taking the realization of delusion to reveal nature as its essence" means that by penetrating delusion, one reveals the true, thereby departing from attachment to a fixed nature.
"Using the refutation of the Lesser Vehicle and the discernment of the heterodox as its function" means that it destroys the biased attachments of the Hīnayāna.

It destroys the heterodox views of non-Buddhists. As for the "Vaipulya Mahāyāna" as a characteristic of the teaching, it means that while the sutra is common to the three vehicles, its meaning follows the perfect and sudden [teaching].
"Laṅkā" is the name of a mountain. When Bodhidharma entrusted [the Dharma] to Huike, he said:
"I have observed all the scriptural teachings existing in China; only the four-fascicle *Laṅkāvatāra* can serve as a seal for the mind."
Su Dongpo’s postscript to the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "This sūtra is called the 'Chapter on the Essence of the Buddha's Words.
It has been traditionally regarded as the Dharma of the Mind, much like the *Nan jing* (Difficult Classic) among medical texts. In recent years, scholars have sought only the simple and convenient;
having grasped a single phrase or a single verse, they claim to have realized and attained enlightenment. This has led even women and girls to clap their hands in laughter and vyingly discuss it."
Regarding the discourse on Chan: those of superior caliber seek fame; those of inferior caliber seek profit.

It is like knowing a secular physician who, without relying on medical treatises, directly receives prescriptions to treat illnesses—though his treatments are not necessarily incorrect, when it comes to encountering a disease and reaching its root, or prognosticating life and death with certainty, he cannot be compared in the same breath to one who knows the classics and has studied antiquity.
Without studying the *Nan jing*, how could one possibly [attain such mastery]?
How unerring!
Zhao Wen-yuan’s preface to the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states that Shi Yan-shou claimed this sūtra takes "the Buddha’s words on the mind" as its core tenet,
whereas Li Tongxuan took "the five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two forms of selflessness" as its core tenet.
What Yan-shou says refers to its principle; what Tong-xuan says refers to its phenomena.
○ Thus have I heard: at one time the Buddha was dwelling on the peak of Mount Laṅkā by the shore of the southern sea, adorned with various kinds of precious flowers.
To adorn [the assembly], he was accompanied by a great community of bhikṣus and a multitude of great bodhisattvas who had come from various and diverse buddha-fields.
These bodhisattva-mahāsattvas possessed mastery over immeasurable samādhis and sported with supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).
The bodhisattva-mahāsattva Mahāmati was their leader; all the Buddhas had personally poured water upon his crown in the consecration of sovereignty.

They thoroughly understand the meaning of the objective realm as a manifestation of their own minds. They universally manifest in accordance with the various types of sentient beings through diverse mental forms and immeasurable gates of liberation.
They have attained ultimate penetration into the five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness.

[The phrase] "dwelling on the peak of Mount Laṅkā by the shore of the Southern Sea" indicates the place where the Dharma is taught. [The phrase] "adorned with precious flowers" describes the excellence of that location.
[The phrase] "a great assembly of bhikṣus and bodhisattvas" enumerates the multitude of those who heard the teaching together.

[The phrase] "having come from various other buddha-fields" cites the distant to illustrate the near, thereby manifesting the vastness of the assembly. [The phrase] "immeasurable samādhis, etc. is a praise...
This is the virtue of a bodhisattva; it is the entry into one's own mental state, wherein the characteristics of objective practice are abandoned and the true meaning is realized.

(The five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness constitute the fundamental framework of this sutra. As for the five dharmas, they are: name, appearance, conceptualization, correct wisdom, and suchness. Name refers to—

They are called: appearance (*lakṣaṇa*), false discrimination (*parikalpita*), correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*), and suchness (*tathatā*). As for the three natures (*trisvabhāva*): they are called false discrimination (*parikalpita*), dependent origination (*paratantra*), and perfected reality (*pariniṣpanna*).

Consciousness refers to the eight consciousnesses. The two kinds of selflessness (*dvividha-nairātmya*) are the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).
The commentary states: "Thus" refers to the Dharma that was heard. "I heard" means that Ānanda heard and upheld this Dharma from the Buddha.
"At one time" refers to the occasion when the Teacher and his assembly gathered in auspicious conclave. "Buddha" means awakening.
This means that once the path of awakening has been perfected, one preaches the Dharma according to the capacities of beings to guide and benefit all living creatures.

From the passage "Great Wisdom" (*mahāmati*) downward, the virtues of Great Wisdom are praised individually. Regarding the phrase "the Buddhas pour water upon his head," this clarifies that his rank is that of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), and as he is about to receive the position of a Buddha, he is thus consecrated.
Regarding the phrase "objects manifested by one's own mind," these refer to all objects of experience, whether wholesome or unwholesome.
All arise from the manifestation of one's own mind; Mahāmati understands this well, for his wisdom is transcendent and supreme. Regarding the various forms of the mind:

this refers to the diverse differences among the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) of all sentient beings. Mahāmati universally responds to them through immeasurable gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*);
thus, the Dharma-gates are profound and vast. Mahāmati is able to investigate all these aforementioned phenomena to their ultimate conclusion.
[The discourse] concludes. These five dharmas, self-nature, consciousness, and the two kinds of selflessness—these are the subjects for which he acts as the initiator among the assembly;
this is why the Buddha praises him so deeply.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati, together with the Bodhisattva Maitreya, traveled throughout all the buddha-fields, receiving [their teachings].
By the Buddha’s spiritual power, he rose from his seat and praised the Buddha in verse, saying: “The world is free from arising and ceasing, like flowers in the sky.
Wisdom finds neither existence nor non-existence, yet you give rise to great compassion. All phenomena are like illusions, far removed from mind and consciousness.
Wisdom finds neither existence nor non-existence, yet you give rise to great compassion. Free from the extremes of annihilation and permanence, the world is eternally...”
Like a dream, wisdom finds neither existence nor non-existence, yet it gives rise to great compassion.
(All beings in the world turn their backs on awakening and unite with the sensory dust;

they wander through birth and death, giving rise to deluded thoughts and consciousness, and further calculating the two views of annihilationism and eternalism, having no means of escape. Therefore, the Tathāgata desires to deliver and liberate them.)

The commentary states: The Tathāgata, through his wondrous wisdom, observes and thoroughly penetrates all phenomena, such as arising and ceasing, as being like flowers in the sky, like illusions, and like dreams—neither existent nor non-existent. Therefore, he gives rise to great compassion and delivers sentient beings across [suffering].
May they all attain complete detachment.
Knowing that persons and phenomena lack selfhood, and that afflictions and their latent tendencies are eternally pure and signless, they give rise to the mind of great compassion.

(This refers to being free from the two obstacles: the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the obstacle of knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). "Affliction" is the Chinese term for *kleśa*; "er yan" is the Sanskrit term for *jñeyāvaraṇa*).
The commentary states: Wisdom fundamentally destroys delusion. Delusion consists of the two attachments to a self and to phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-grāha*).

To be "without self" means to be free from these two attachments. If one generates attachment toward wisdom itself, wisdom also becomes an obstacle. The Tathāgata fully understands that both persons and phenomena, as well as afflictions and wisdom, are fundamentally [empty].
Because it is empty, it is said to be eternally pure and signless. Because sentient beings are deluded and undergo suffering, he gives rise to a heart of compassion to deliver them.
There is no nirvana in anything; there is no Buddha who attains nirvana, nor is there nirvana within a Buddha. It is far removed from both the awakening and that which is awakened.
Whether existence or non-existence, both are entirely transcended.
(The Buddha and sentient beings equally possess this principle; since there is not even birth-and-death to be severed, how could there be nirvana to be realized?)
However, it is not through proof that one proves; one proves this *nirvāṇa*. Thus, the Buddha is the person who realizes, and *nirvāṇa* is the dharma that is realized.
Apart from the dharma there is no person, and apart from the person there is no dharma; therefore, it is said that [neither] exists.
The commentary states: "All" refers to all sentient beings. "Nirvana" is the principle of non-arising and non-ceasing.
Awakening is itself the Buddha; that which is awakened to is Nirvana. Since both person and phenomena have been extinguished, it is called "far removed.
Person and phenomenon are two items; when these two are both extinguished, they exist yet have never existed, and are non-existent.
Yet it has never been non-existent; this is what is called being entirely free from both [extremes].
The Sage’s tranquil contemplation is thus a departure from arising; this is called non-grasping. It is peaceful in this life and in future lives.
(*Muni* is a Sanskrit term meaning "silent sage," a name for the Buddha. (The verses of praise to the Buddha end here.
The commentary states: These words mean that if a person can contemplate the Buddha’s tranquil essence in this way, it arises from detachment.
Thus, one does not give rise to grasping or attachment toward the Buddha; therefore, one attains purity in both this life and future lives.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how many kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing are there for the various consciousnesses?
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "The various consciousnesses have two kinds of arising, abiding, and ceasing, which cannot be known through discursive reasoning."
The various consciousnesses have two kinds of arising: namely, arising as a continuous flow (*pravāha-utpāda*) and arising as a manifestation (*nimitta-utpāda*). They have two kinds of abiding:

namely, abiding as a continuous flow (*pravāha-sthiti*) and abiding as a manifestation (*nimitta-sthiti*). They have two kinds of cessation: namely, cessation as a continuous flow (*pravāha-nirodha*) and cessation as a manifestation (*nimitta-nirodha*).
(This is a dialogue concerning the five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness.
The commentary states: "Arising" refers to that which is produced by causes and conditions; "abiding" refers to remaining; "changing" refers to transformation; and "ceasing" refers to extinction.

The term "changing" was not explicitly mentioned here because the text is abbreviated. However, as for these characteristics of the arising and ceasing of the various consciousnesses, only the Buddha—

Because it is the clarity of wisdom, it is said to be "not known through discursive thought. Regarding the phrase "flowing forth, arising, abiding, and ceasing," this refers to the aggregate of consciousness within;
moment by moment it continues in succession like the flow of water, never for a moment pausing.

Regarding the phrase "characteristics arising, abiding, and ceasing," this refers to characteristics manifesting externally; as the sense organs and their objects encounter one another, there arise arising, abiding, and ceasing.

Mahāmati, all consciousnesses have three characteristics: namely, the characteristic of transformation (*pariṇāma-lakṣaṇa*), the characteristic of activity (*karma-lakṣaṇa*), and the characteristic of reality (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*).
(As for the characteristic of transformation: it is the beginningless perfuming and transformation whereby awakening becomes non-awakening. As for the characteristic of activity:
because of non-awakening, movement constitutes activity. As for the characteristic of reality: it remains unchanging amidst conditions, its essential nature being truly pure.)

The commentary states: Regarding the "characteristic of karma," the "characteristic of transformation," and the "characteristic of manifestation," these refer to the arising of delusion from the True [Nature].
Through the movement of delusion, karma is formed; because of this movement, there is a transformation whereby objects appear, manifesting in succession.
Although this does not explicitly say "manifestation" but rather "True," it is called "True" because its essential nature remains unchanging while following conditions.
Mahāmati, briefly stated there are three kinds of consciousness; in detail, there are eight aspects. What are the three?

They are the true consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*), the manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*), and the consciousness that discriminates phenomena (*vastu-vikalpa-vijñāna*). Mahāmati, just as a bright mirror reflects all forms and images, the manifestation within the locus of the manifesting consciousness is likewise so.

Regarding the "three kinds": the True Consciousness (*tathatā-vijñāna*) is the *tathāgatagarbha-vijñāna*. The Manifesting Consciousness (*khyāti-vijñāna*) is that which evolves from the *tathāgatagarbha*;

it is also called the "consciousness-store" (*vijñānagarbha*), for while its name evolves, its essence does not evolve. The Discriminative Consciousness of Phenomena (*vastu-vikalpa-vijñāna*) refers to the mental faculty (*manas*), the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and the five bodies of sensory consciousness (*pañca-vijñānakāya*).

This [classification] opens the store-consciousness into two and combines the consciousnesses of phenomena into one. Regarding the "eight aspects," these are the aforementioned True... [text truncated].

The manifesting consciousness (*vijñapti-vijñāna*) is taken as the one storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), while the aforementioned discriminative object-consciousness (*viṣaya-vijñapti-vijñāna*) is opened up into seven consciousnesses, namely:
the mental faculty (*manas*), the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*), and the visual, auditory, olfactory, gustatory, and tactile consciousnesses.

The commentary states: These various consciousnesses differ in their extensive or concise presentation and their opening or closing because the *tathāgatagarbha* is the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome;
it undergoes different transformations through perfuming according to defiled or pure conditions. Since beginningless time, sentient beings have been perfumed by the cessation of evil.
Because it follows defiled conditions, the Tathāgatagarbha is renamed the "consciousness-store" (vijñānagarbha) and sequentially gives rise to the various consciousnesses;

this is the transformation of the absolute truth into delusion, and the transformation of principle into phenomena. If one can follow pure conditions and realize that all consciousnesses are identical to true wisdom, the Tathāgatagarbha no longer undergoes this renaming;
thus, phenomena are immediately principle, and one returns from delusion to the source.

Truly so. The analogy of the mirror refers to the manifesting consciousness (*ādarśa-vijñāna*), which is the source capable of producing all phenomena. The creation of causes and the summoning of results are like a mirror reflecting objects;
its representation of beauty and ugliness is never mistaken.

Mahāmati, the manifesting consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*) and the discriminating consciousness of objects (*vastu-vikalpa-vijñāna*)—these two have the characteristics of being perishable and imperishable, and they serve as mutual causes for one another.

(Whether facing an object or detached from it, dwelling in the dust of the senses or emerging from them, though one is perishable and the other imperishable, they are neither different nor not different.
These two consciousnesses differ only in being perishable and imperishable, yet they are mutually dependent causes; they are neither different nor not different.)
The commentary states: The manifesting consciousness (xiànshí) contains and stores the seeds of good and evil without loss; therefore, it is called "indestructible" (bùhuài).

The objective consciousness (shìshí), however, encounters objects through the sense organs and gives rise to feelings of aversion and attachment, arising and ceasing from moment to moment; therefore, it is called "destructible" (huài).
Mahāmati, the inconceivable perfuming and the inconceivable transformation are the causes of the manifesting consciousness (*ābhāsava-jñāna*).
(To speak of "inconceivable perfuming" means that the entirety of the Real becomes delusion; to speak of "inconceivable transformation" means that the entirety of Principle becomes phenomena.)
The commentary states: "Infusion" (vāsanā) means to permeate; "transformation" (pariṇāma) means to undergo change. Truth and falsehood are non-dual; phenomena and principle are of one essence.

There is infusion without being infused, and transformation without changing. This cannot be conceived by the mind nor discussed by the mouth. Such infusion and transformation constitute the cause for the manifestation of consciousness.
Mahāmati, the grasping of various objects and the perfuming of beginningless false discrimination are the causes of the *vijñapti-mati-vijñāna* (the consciousness that discriminates phenomena).
(Regarding "various objects": these are the six sense-objects. Regarding "grasping": it refers to the six sense-faculties grasping the six sense-objects, thereby giving rise to craving and views.)

The commentary states: "That which is perfumed by beginningless false conceptualization" means that from time immemorial, this conceptualization of craving and views has arisen, perfuming and forming the *kṣaṇavijñāna* (empirical consciousness); this constitutes the cause.
Mahāmati, if that true consciousness is covered and the various unreal, false delusions are extinguished, then all sense-faculties and consciousnesses are extinguished;
this is called the extinction of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-nirodha*).
(When the sensory faculties and their objects cease, then the illusion also ceases).
The commentary states: "To 'cover' means to turn back. This means that if one can reflect back upon true consciousness, then all delusions of craving and views will naturally be extinguished.
Once the delusions that act as perfumers have ceased, the sense-faculties and consciousness that are perfumed by them will also vanish.
This is the cessation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇanirodha*).
Mahāmati, as for the cessation of the continuity (*saṃtatinirodha*): when the cause of the continuity ceases, then the continuity ceases;
when that from which it proceeds and its objective support (*ālambana*) cease, then the continuity ceases. Why is this so, Mahāmati? Because it is that upon which it depends. "Dependence" means...

"Perfumed by beginningless false conceptualization; as for 'conditions,' this refers to the false conceptualization of the objects of the consciousnesses, such as the 'seeing' aspect of one's own mind.

'The cessation of continuity' refers to the cessation of the underlying flow (*āsrava*). The continuity of consciousness has causes and conditions; if these causes and conditions cease, then the continuity ceases.
The 'cause' refers to beginningless false conceptualization; the 'condition' refers to the objects of discrimination perceived by one's own mind."
The realms (dhātus) are beginningless false conceptualizations; that is, they are fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*).
Mahāmati, it is like a lump of clay and its atoms: they are neither different nor not different. The ornamentation of gold is also like this.
Mahāmati, if the lump of clay were different from the atoms, it would not be produced by them; yet in reality, it is produced by them. Therefore...
They are not different. If they were not different, then there would be no distinction between a lump of clay and its constituent atoms.
(This metaphor illustrates how delusion arises from the Truth, and when delusion ceases, the Truth is revealed; the case of gold being fashioned into ornaments is likewise an illustration.
This metaphor is the essential core of this sutra—what is called the "Heart of the Buddha's Words").
The commentary states: The lump of clay is a metaphor for the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*); the fine dust is a metaphor for the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*).

The storehouse consciousness is real, while the evolving consciousnesses are delusory. Because the lump of clay is formed from the fine dust, their substance is one; therefore, they cannot be said to be different.
Yet, if the lump of clay and the fine dust were definitively one, there would be no differentiation between them; therefore, they cannot be said not to be different.
In this way, Mahāmati, if the evolving consciousnesses were different from the true nature of the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), the storehouse consciousness would not be their cause.

If they were not different, then when the evolving consciousnesses cease, the storehouse consciousness should also cease; yet its own true nature does not actually cease. Therefore, Mahāmati, [it is as I have said].

It is not that the consciousness of the self-characteristic is extinguished; rather, it is only the aspect of karma that is extinguished. Mahāmati, if the consciousness of the self-characteristic were extinguished, then the ālayavijñāna would be extinguished.
Mahāmati, if the ālayavijñāna were extinguished, that would be no different from the doctrine of the nihilistic view held by the non-Buddhists.

If the various evolving consciousnesses were different from the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), then when they are stirred by the winds of ignorance, the essence of the storehouse consciousness would not follow along with conditions;

this would lead to the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*). However, since the storehouse consciousness is the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome, it does not fail to follow along with conditions.

If, on the other hand, they were not different, then when the evolving consciousnesses ceased, the storehouse consciousness would also have to cease; this would lead to the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*). However...
"The true nature of the ālayavijñāna can never be extinguished.

The commentary states: The passage beginning with "In this way" explains that while the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) are extinguished, the ālayavijñāna is not extinguished; this already demonstrates that they are neither different nor non-different.
Fearing, however, that Mahāmati might not yet have grasped the profound meaning, [the Buddha] further declares: "The true nature is not extinguished; it is merely..."
The characteristic of karma ceases. Indeed, the true nature is immutable and fundamentally free from arising and ceasing. Karma is a mark of ignorance and delusion;
therefore, it possesses arising and ceasing. Once one turns away from delusion and returns to the truth, the delusion ceases while the truth does not cease.
If the truth were subject to cessation, how would it differ from the non-Buddhist paths?
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are seven kinds of self-nature (*svabhāva*). They are:

the self-nature of accumulation, the self-nature of essence, the self-nature of characteristics, the self-nature of the great elements, the self-nature of cause, the self-nature of conditions, and the self-nature of accomplishment.

(This explains the names and meanings of the seven kinds of self-nature. While the great elements fundamentally apply to both ordinary beings and sages, here they refer specifically to the retribution of sages—namely, that form is eternal, and so forth.
"Eternal" refers to true eternity; this is precisely the five aggregates of the dharma-nature.)

The commentary states: "The nature of the collection" (*saṃbhāra-svabhāva*) refers to the cause that gathers all virtues. Because it is a cause of collection, it possesses both essence (*svabhāva*) and appearance (*lakṣaṇa*);
essence is internal while appearance is external. "The nature of the great elements" (*mahābhūta-svabhāva*) refers to the fruit of the four great elements.

Because it is a fruit, it possesses both causes and conditions; the cause is proximate while the condition is remote. That which is accomplished by cause and fruit constitutes the nature of the collection.
It is the nature [of things].
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are seven kinds of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*):

namely, the realm of the mind (*citta*), the realm of wisdom (*prajñā*), the realm of knowledge (*jñāna*), the realm of vision (*darśana*), the realm that transcends the two views, the realm that transcends the stages of the sons [of the Buddha], and the realm of the Tathāgata’s own self-attainment.
(Regarding "object-sphere" (*viṣaya*): it refers to the sphere of activity, which has both general and specific distinctions. Regarding "mental object-sphere" (*citta-viṣaya*):
it refers to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) realized by the mind.)
The commentary states: The mind is able to give rise to wisdom (*prajñā*). Once the power of wisdom is preeminent, it constitutes the function of knowledge (*jñāna*).

Once the function of knowledge is established, right view (*samyag-dṛṣṭi*) manifests before one. When right view manifests, one transcends the two views of annihilationism and eternalism, and even surpasses the stages of the bodhisattvas to reach the realm of the Tathāgata’s own arrival.
Mahāmati, this is the mind of the ultimate reality of the intrinsic nature of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, future, and present.
By means of this mind of the ultimate reality of the intrinsic nature, they accomplish the worldly, the transcendental,
and the supreme dharma of the Tathāgatas.
(From this point onward, it clarifies how the Tathāgata, relying upon the ultimate truth of self-nature, accomplishes the virtuous functions of his own practice and the transformation of others.
The commentary states:
"Accomplishing the mundane" means demonstrating that he conforms to human laws in order to transform others. "The supramundane" refers to...
It penetrates the three vehicles. As for the supreme supramundane dharma, only Buddhas and Buddhas can realize it to its ultimate conclusion.
Mahāmati, whether it be continuity, entities, birth, existence, nirvāṇa, the path, karma, fruits, or truths—these are the doctrines of nihilism and annihilationism.
Why is this? Because these cannot be apprehended even in the present moment.
[This is] seen, because it is not part of the beginning.

(If "continuity" refers to the continuity of cause and effect; if "thing" refers to material entities; if "arising" refers to the arising of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*);
if "existence" refers to these aforementioned phenomena being substantially real—then [this would contradict] the four truths such as *nirvāṇa*).
"All phenomena are non-existent" (thus they establish a doctrine of destruction and nihilism).
The commentary states: "Nirvāṇa and the Path are supramundane phenomena; whether it be karmic conditions or the fruits of suffering, these are mundane phenomena.
These are called the Four Noble Truths, the gates of the Dharma of the ultimate and conventional truths as taught by the Buddha. They [the opponents] regard them as...
[If one were to hold that] there is nothing, one would fall into the doctrine of annihilationism. Therefore, the meaning is further investigated and explained as follows:

regarding these presently manifest dharmas of the Four Noble Truths, they [the nihilists] all consider them to be truly non-existent. To reckon either existence or non-existence at the very point where the view of self first arises is both a false view;
for it does not constitute a portion of the true cause for liberation.
"Mahāmati, it is like a broken jar that no longer performs the function of a jar, or like a scorched seed that no longer produces a sprout.
(These two metaphors are set forth to clarify the nihilistic view of the non-Buddhists.)"

The commentary states: The first analogy refers to the absence of fruit; where there is no fruit, there is no cause. The second analogy refers to the absence of cause; where there is no cause, there is no fruit. Thus it is, Mahāmati:
if the nature of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases has already ceased, is now ceasing, or will cease, these are merely the perceptions of one's own mind’s false imaginings.
Because they lack a cause, they do not arise in succession.
(Master Xingjian said: "Skandhas" refers to the five skandhas; "dhātus" refers to the eighteen dhātus; and "āyatanas" refers to the twelve āyatanas.)
The commentary states: If one were to claim that the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas) have already ceased, then this would be causeless;

yet their present cessation would likewise be without effect, and their impending cessation would again be without cause. When examined in this way, all are seen as the delusive imaginings of one's own mind.
Since those causes do not exist, there can be no sequential continuity of arising.

Mahāmati, if there are other śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who perceive that all things are devoid of self-nature—like floating clouds, a whirling firebrand, a city of the gandharvas, the unborn, a magical illusion, a mirage, the moon reflected in water, and a dream;
and who realize that the internal and external world is a manifestation of the mind’s own false discrimination, arising from beginningless falsity and not separate from one's own mind;

and who, through the cessation of the causes and conditions of such false discrimination, transcend false discrimination and speak of neither the speaker nor the spoken, nor the observer nor the observed.
The ālayavijñāna, which establishes the body for experience, is dissociated from the grasping and the grasper within the objective sphere of consciousness.
It is devoid of the objective sphere of non-existence and is free from arising, abiding, and ceasing; it enters into the conceptualization that arises from one's own mind.

"Seeing the absence of intrinsic nature" means seeing that all phenomena are entirely free from the attachment to an inherent nature arising from self, as well as being free from the attachment to an inherent nature arising from another, from both, or without cause.
"Objects" refers to the six sense-fields (*ṣaḍviṣaya*); "appropriation" refers to the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*);
and that which is called "appropriation" [in this context] refers to the six consciousnesses (*ṣadvijñāna*).
The commentary states: Because its intrinsic nature is free from attachment to a self-nature, it is unarisen.

It is, for example, like clouds in the sky, like a whirling firebrand, like a city of Gandharvas, like a magical illusion, like a mirage, like the moon reflected in water, and like what is seen in a dream.

It is identical to illusory phenomena. If one realizes that these illusory phenomena are fundamentally without interior or exterior, yet perceives them as having interior and exterior, this is because they are formed by beginningless false thoughts and delusions;
thus, they do not depart from one's own mind. When the nature of one's own mind is detached [from delusion], the causes and conditions of false thoughts are extinguished.
This is precisely the extinction of the bitter fruits of the three realms of existence produced by false thoughts. This is the capacity... [to attain liberation].
Regarding the speaker and the spoken, the observer and the observed, and even the ālayavijñāna which establishes the body for experience—all these are transcended.
To say they are "incompatible" means that because one realizes the emptiness and quiescence of the objects of consciousness, there is no longer any duality or opposition;
how then could there be arising, abiding, or ceasing? Only then does the ālayavijñāna arise from its own mind and enter into all realms of experience. By means of this—
Through the discernment of correct wisdom, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished.
By understanding the three realms to be like an illusion and by discerning them through observation, one shall attain the Illusion-like Samādhi.
Having transcended the manifestations of one’s own mind as being non-existent, one abides in the Prajñāpāramitā. One abandons the skillful means generated therein; this is the Vajra-like [Samādhi].
Through samādhi, they enter into the body of the Tathāgata and enter into the transformations of suchness (tathatā).

Endowed with the adornments of sovereign supernormal powers, compassion, and skillful means, they equally enter all buddha-fields and the abodes of non-Buddhists, transcending mind, thought, and consciousness.
This bodhisattva gradually transforms his body and attains the body of a Tathāgata.

(Regarding the "diamond-like" [samādhi]: this refers to the bodhisattva of equal enlightenment who, by means of Buddha-wisdom, severs the final thought-moment and thereby attains the meditative concentration.)
From this meditative concentration, one transitions into the Buddha-ground).
The commentary states: This is the realization that the three realms are like an illusion, whereby one attains the Illusion-like Samādhi.

Having transcended the objects manifested by one's own mind, there are no longer various appearances, and one thus attains abiding on the further shore of wisdom. This is what is meant by "abandoning and leaving behind."
That which arises is the skillful means of what is to be accomplished. Suchness is the principle of original enlightenment (*mūla-avabodha*).

Abiding eternally in this principle, one gives rise to various transformations; therefore, one is able to exercise mastery over supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), adorning oneself with compassion and skillful means.
To speak of "entering all Buddha-fields" means entering the realm of the Buddhas. To speak of "the entry-points of non-Buddhists" means entering the realm of Māra.

This is because one is able to ultimately transcend mind, intellect, and consciousness, thereby attaining non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) and the Samādhi of the Universal Manifestation of the Form Body (*vairocana-rūpakāya-samādhi*).
To speak of "transforming the body to personally attain the state of a Tathāgata" is the summary of the Bodhisattva.
This is the fruit of realization.

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, regarding what has been taught concerning mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), the five dharmas, the self-natures, and the characteristics—the sphere of activity of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, consisting of the objects of perception such as the manifestations of one's own mind—"
Harmony. This reveals the true nature established by all teachings, the heart of all Buddha-words.

For the sake of the great Bodhisattvas dwelling on Mount Malaya in the land of Laṅkā, the Tathāgata spoke of the Dharma-body, the realm of the ocean-like storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) praised by the Tathāgatas.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāmati, saying: "By four causes and conditions, the eye..."

The transformation of consciousness. What are the four? They are: the failure to realize that what is grasped is the manifestation of one’s own mind; attachment to the habitual tendencies of false appearances from beginningless time;
the intrinsic nature of consciousness itself; and the desire to see various forms and characteristics. Mahāmati, these are called the four causes and conditions.
Just as waves arise upon flowing water, the waves of the evolving consciousnesses arise from the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna).

Regarding "conditions": the faculty is the eye-faculty; the object confronted by the eye manifests from one's own mind. Due to a lack of awakening, one falsely gives rise to grasping. Regarding the condition of form:
the dust of form is fundamentally empty, yet from time immemorial it has been clung to as form;

this is caused by the habitual perfuming of deluded thoughts. Regarding the condition of consciousness: consciousness takes discrimination as its nature and arises when the faculty and the object confront one another.

Regarding attachment: as for those who wish to see conditions, even though the three conditions have converged, if they do not give rise to the thought of wishing to see, then the various forms and appearances will still not be seen.

The commentary states: As for the four conditions, they are the condition of the sense organ (*indriya*), the condition of the object (*rūpa*), the condition of consciousness (*vijñāna*), and the condition of the desire to see.
Based on these four conditions, visual consciousness arises. If one traces its origin, it arises from the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*); hence it is said, "in the place where water flows.
From the storehouse consciousness, the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) arise, just as waves arise from water.
Mahāmati, just as the visual consciousness arises simultaneously with all the sense organs, atoms, and pores, so too does it arise in accordance with its respective objects.
It is like a bright mirror manifesting various forms and images, or like a violent wind blowing across the waters of the great ocean.
(The essence of the mind is like the ocean; the eight consciousnesses are like flowing water. The seventh consciousness is like a violent current; the sixth consciousness is like waves.

(The metaphors of the bright mirror and the ocean water signify that there is a distinction between those who have attained awakening and those who are still in the realm of devas and humans. As for the mirror manifesting images:)
There is no sequence of before and after. When the wind blows upon the ocean waters, the preceding wave rises and the subsequent wave follows.
The commentary states: As the eight consciousnesses flow and move, the waves of the evolving consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, arise.
From the five sense organs down to a single atom or a single pore, all are co-arisen with consciousness; there is nothing that is not perceived. This occurs in accordance with...
"Next, the arising of objects is also like this" means that external objective realms also arise gradually along with consciousness.
That "the myriad dharmas are but consciousness" is seen herein. However, the manner in which consciousness arises is both sudden and gradual.
The analogy of a bright mirror manifesting various forms and images illustrates sudden arising; the analogy of a fierce wind blowing upon the waters of the great ocean illustrates gradual arising.
This is a metaphor for gradual arising.

The winds of external objects toss the ocean of the mind, so that the waves of consciousness flow without interruption. Due to the characteristics produced by causes—whether distinct or non-distinct—the signs of karmic birth arise;
one becomes deeply attached to them and is unable to comprehend the intrinsic nature of form and the other sense-objects. Consequently, the five bodies of consciousness evolve.
Mahāmati, you should know that the cause for the differentiation and sequential cognition of those very five groups of consciousness is the cause of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

When the mind is moved by external objects— like the wind blowing upon the ocean, giving rise to waves of the various consciousnesses— they arise in an uninterrupted succession from the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
It acts as a cause for the successive arising of causes; thus, one enters into false conceptualization and attachment, failing to realize that the intrinsic nature of form and so forth is empty.
Therefore, the five consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, arise in succession.

The commentary states: The term "body" (*kāya*) has the meaning of "aggregation. This refers to the aggregation of various objects of perception (*viṣaya*) to form a single visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*), and so forth.

Once the five consciousnesses have arisen, there is a mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that arises simultaneously with them as their common object; therefore, it is said to be "simultaneous with those five bodies of consciousness.
Furthermore, those five consciousnesses give rise to cognition based on the differentiated and segmented characteristics of the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*). The mind...
Regarding the cause of consciousness: it is said that the five consciousnesses are the causes of the sixth consciousness.
As that body evolves, it does not form the thought, "We evolve through mutual causality. Rather, it evolves as a conceptual attachment to the manifestations of one's own mind;
yet these various evolving forms proceed simultaneously, discriminating objects and distinguishing their respective divisions. This is what is meant by "evolution."

(As for that transformation of the body: it refers to those five consciousnesses transforming to give rise to the six consciousnesses, yet these consciousnesses do not themselves claim to arise through mutual causation.)
The commentary states: That body transforms, yet it does not give rise to this thought: "I am successively dependent upon one another;
all is manifested by my own mind through false conceptualization of external objects. While objects undergo arising and ceasing, the transformation follows them accordingly.

Alternatively, because those objects possess the characteristic of change and decay, consciousness also transforms simultaneously with them. Furthermore, because that consciousness discriminates various objects, consciousness [is so named].
It transforms; therefore, it is said that "it is that which transforms.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "The sun and moon and their radiance are neither different nor not different.
The waves arise from the ocean; the seven consciousnesses are likewise. They arise in conjunction with the mind, in harmonious union."
(Commentary by Master Xingjian: From this point onward, all are in verse form. The sun, moon, ocean, and water serve as metaphors for the root;
light, radiance, waves, and ripples serve as metaphors for the branches.)
The commentary states: These two metaphors refer precisely to the eight consciousnesses of mind, which arise simultaneously in conjunction with the six consciousnesses;

they are neither different nor not different. As for the mention of "the seventh consciousness," this refers to the mental faculty (*manas*), the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and the five groups of sensory consciousnesses taken together.
Just as the waters of the ocean transform and various waves arise, so too do the seven consciousnesses arise in conjunction with the mind.

That is to say, within the locus of the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), various consciousnesses evolve; specifically, it is by means of that mental consciousness (manovijñāna) that one contemplates the meanings of various signs.
There are eight non-disintegrating characteristics; even the signless is itself signless. Just as with the waves of the ocean, there is no distinction between them;
so it is with the various consciousnesses and the mind—no difference can be found.
(To continue with the metaphor of the waves of the Yangtze River. The preceding section speaks of difference; the following section speaks of non-difference.
(When water freezes into ice and ice melts back into water, what distinction can there be?)
The commentary states: The eight consciousnesses transform to give rise to various cognitions, just as the waters of the ocean transform to produce various waves.

Regarding the statement that "the mental consciousness contemplates various characteristics," it means that the mental consciousness contemplates the characteristics of the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) and so forth; therefore, it is called "different."
The eight non-disintegrating characteristics refer to the fact that the eight consciousnesses possess no characteristic of disintegration.

"Non-characteristic and yet no characteristic" means that the eight consciousnesses are fundamentally without any visible characteristic; likewise, all consciousnesses, which equally rely upon the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), are also without any visible characteristic.
All the consciousnesses rely equally upon the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), and thus no distinct characteristics can be perceived among them.

Just as the waves of the ocean differ from one another yet share the same nature of moisture and are therefore without distinction, so too all consciousnesses are but mind; since the storehouse consciousness is what is apprehended, it is said that even their difference cannot be found.

The mind (*citta*) is called that which accumulates karma; the intellect (*manas*) is called that which extensively accumulates. The various consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) cognize their respective objects; these five are said to be those that manifest before one’s face.

(The triad of *citta*, *manas*, and *vijñāna* are synonyms for a single dharma: it is called "mind" in relation to enumeration, "intellect" when it acts as the producer, and "consciousness" when it performs discrimination.)
Furthermore, that which arises first is called *citta* (mind); that which arises next is called *manas* (intellect); and that which subsequently discerns is called *vijñāna* (consciousness).

The commentary states: Regarding the statement that *citta* is named the "gathering agent," when the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) encounter one another, a single moment of mind arises, giving rise to grasping and attachment, thereby forming wholesome or unwholesome karma.
*Manas* is named the "extensive gathering" because it proceeds from the preceding *citta* and enters the faculty of intellect (*manas-indriya*).
They give rise to greed, hatred, and delusion, and extensively create various karmas. Regarding that which is "cognized by the various consciousnesses," this refers to the sixth consciousness;

it discriminates the five sensory objects previously received by the first five consciousnesses. Therefore, it is said that the five [objects] appear before it; these "five" refer to the five consciousnesses.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva asked in verse: "Blue, red, and all other forms and images cause sentient beings to give rise to various cognitions.
Like waves, there are manifold phenomena; how is this so? I pray you, speak of it. Then the World-Honored One replied in verse: "Blue, red, and all various colors—waves do not exist at all.
It is the mind that gathers and accumulates karma; this is taught to awaken the deluded common people. That karma..."
There is nothing at all. It is free from what is grasped by one's own mind; that which is grasped has no grasper. This is identical to those waves.
(This clarifies that both the karma produced and the mind that produces it are entirely empty and quiescent, likewise identical to waves;
"grasping" means to take up.)
The body is established through experience; this is the manifest consciousness of sentient beings. Within it, all karmas appear, just like waves upon water.
(To realize delusion as truth is like realizing waves as water; they share the same moisture in their arising—how could there be any mark of distinction?)

The commentary states: This clarifies that the two types of retribution—of sentient beings and their environment—as well as the karma they perform, are all illusory manifestations of one’s own mind, like waves arising from water.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva spoke again in verse: "The rising sun shines equally upon sentient beings of inferior, middling, and superior capacity."
"The Tathāgata illuminates the world and speaks the truth for the sake of the ignorant; having already categorized all phenomena, why does he not speak of reality?
At that time, he replied with a verse: "If one speaks of reality, that mind itself lacks reality.
Just as the waves of the ocean, reflections in a mirror, and dreams—all appear simultaneously—so too are the objects of the mind."
(The Tathāgata’s intention was precisely to speak the truth, yet he has not spoken it because the capacity [of the audience] is not yet mature;
therefore, it is said that "that mind lacks reality.")

The commentary states: Because that mind lacks true reality, the Tathāgata taught that the ālayavijñāna transforms to give rise to the various consciousnesses, like waves arising from the sea or images within a mirror, or events in a dream. Although these appear simultaneously, none are real;
therefore it is said that the objects of the mind are likewise unreal.
Because the objective spheres are not complete, the karmic process evolves in succession. That which cognizes is consciousness (*vijñāna*); that which intends is the mind (*manas*).
As for the five [sensory consciousnesses], they manifest; there is no fixed order.
(Distinguishing the external objects apprehended by the five consciousnesses, it is said that "they are what is cognized by consciousness.
The commentary states: This clarifies that external objective realms are not inherently possessed by the mind, but arise only through the turning of karma.

It is likewise with the sixth consciousness and the mental faculty (*manas*), which give rise to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) in relation to the dharma-objects; the five consciousnesses also follow their respective five objects.
They manifest. Must they necessarily arise in a fixed sequence?
It is like a master painter and his apprentice spreading colors to depict various forms; my teaching is also like this.
Colors originally possess no patterns; they are neither brush nor silk. Yet, for the sake of pleasing the patron, various images are painted in intricate detail.

(This metaphor refers to words and letters, which lack substantial meaning. [When] one clearly and thoroughly illuminates [reality], being self-awakened and free from both the perceiving subject and the perceived object—why then would one not speak?
The commentary states: The Tathāgata preaches the Dharma according to the capacities of sentient beings, just as a painter produces images according to their forms.

Although these are accomplished through pigments, brushes, and canvases, in reality they are not the pigments, brushes, or canvases themselves; they exist merely to please the sentiments of the multitude.

Just as one uses colors to depict various images, so too does the Great Physician prescribe remedies according to each patient's condition; likewise, the Tathāgata teaches sentient beings according to their mental dispositions and capacities.
It is not the realm of false conceptualization, nor is it the portion of the śrāvakas. This is the realm of self-realization taught by the Compassionate One.
(Just as a skilled physician prescribes different medicines according to the specific ailment, so too does the Tathāgata teach the Dharma differently according to the minds [of his disciples]).
The commentary states: "That which the Tathāgata has taught is the realm of self-realization; it is not the realm of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) or the Hīnayāna.
False appearances constitute the domain of the non-Buddhists.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, knowing the thoughts in the minds of the assembly of great Bodhisattvas, addressed them as "Sages."
In the first section of the *Jñeyāśraya-vibhāga*, the *Svabhāva-sūtra*, empowered by the majestic spiritual authority of all Buddhas, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, we pray that you will expound for us the *Āryajñeyāśraya-vibhāga-svabhāva-sūtra* in eight hundred phrases, which analyzes the basis of what is known."

The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, based on this discrimination, explains how Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas enter into the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) of both specific and common characteristics.
Because he explains the imagined nature through such discrimination, they are able to thoroughly know and universally observe the selflessness of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharmanairātmya*),
purify their conceptual constructions, illuminate the various stages (*bhūmi*), and transcend all sounds.
Having heard of the joy of the meditative concentrations of the pratyekabuddhas and various non-Buddhists, and having observed the inconceivable sphere of activity of the Tathāgatas,
they definitively abandon the five dharmas and the self-nature (*svabhāva*). Adorned by the wisdom of the *dharmakāya* of the Buddhas,
the Tathāgatas give rise to illusory realms and ascend to the Tuṣita palaces of all Buddha-fields, up to the limit of the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*).
Reaching as far as the celestial palaces, they attain the Tathāgata’s eternally abiding Dharma-body.

(The Tathāgata, hearing that the various bodhisattvas give rise to attachments to the self-characteristics and common characteristics of phenomena, explains for them the gateways of meaning regarding the distinctions of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Once they have understood this meaning and observed it thoroughly, they become free from the attachments to the two selves of person and phenomena. Once these attachments [are abandoned]...)

Having detached [from these], one enters the various stages (*bhūmi*). Thus, one transcends the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna-samādhi*) of ordinary beings and those of the Lesser Vehicle, and enters with ease into the inconceivable realm of the Tathāgata.
Regarding the false attachments to the five dharmas and the three natures (*trisvabhāva*): they are detached even while not being detached.

As for the adornment of the *dharmakāya* and wisdom, this is the perfection of the fruit of one's own practice (*svayaṃ-pratipatti*). As for the arising of illusory realms, this is the manifestation of lands to transform others. Up to...
In all Buddha-fields and celestial palaces, there are no sentient beings capable of being transformed whom he does not manifest within by taking birth and attaining perfect enlightenment.
Tuṣita means "Contentment" (in Chinese), signifying that one knows contentment with respect to the five desires.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "It is not because of non-perception that one says a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) does not arise, nor that it is non-existent.

Why is this? Because a conceptual construction arises dependent upon that [object]. When one says 'a conceptual construction arises dependent upon those horns,' it means the conceptual construction arises based on the horns; therefore, it is said to be dependent upon its cause.

Since it is neither different nor non-different [from its cause], it is not the case that one says 'the horns do not exist' simply because the conceptual construction does not arise through non-perception."

(Regarding "horns": because one previously perceived that a rabbit has no horns, one forms the notion that an ox has horns; this arises from the dualistic views of existence and non-existence held since birth).
The commentary states: This statement regarding "not observing" and so forth is because one realizes that deluded thoughts lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); it is not [that they do not exist].

Regarding the distinction between identity and difference: where there is existence, one speaks of non-existence. This is because they take discriminative conceptualization to be the cause for the arising of phenomena.
Just as one gives rise to discrimination based on whether a horn exists or not, it is said that "conceptualization arises in dependence upon the horn."
Regarding the statement "departing from difference and non-difference": "difference" refers to arising based on the horns while remaining without conceptual differentiation;
"non-difference" refers to the horns themselves being without conceptual differentiation. It is because one departs from these views that it is so stated.
"Mahāmati, if further, false discrimination were different from the horns, it would not arise dependent upon the horns.

If it were not different, then because it is dependent upon them, even when analyzed and sought down to the level of atoms, it cannot be found; for it is not different from the horns, it too lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Since both are without intrinsic nature, what dharma and for what reason could one say 'non-existent'? Mahāmati, if it is because of non-existence..."
"There are no horns. To observe that they exist and then say 'the rabbit has no horns'—one should not form such a conception.
Mahāmati, because it is based on an incorrect cause, the assertion of both existence and non-existence fails to be established."
(This explains the meaning of how conceptual construction differs from a horn.
The commentary states: If conceptual construction were different from the horn, then the horn would not be its appropriate cause.

If they were not different, then one would have to analyze the horn down to its subtlest atoms (*paramāṇu*) in order to find it as the basis from which that conceptual construction arises; yet, upon such analysis, nothing at all can be found.
Thus, both views—that it has horns and that it lacks horns—are extinguished. Therefore, it is said: "Because it is not different from having horns, that [lack of horns] is also not a nature.
"Not a nature" means it is not a real nature. If both dharmas—existence and non-existence—lacked a nature, then of what dharma would one point to when speaking of "non-existence"?
To say "it lacks horns because it does not exist" means to speak of "lacking horns" as being distinct from "having horns."
This is absolutely irrational; therefore, it is said that one should not form such a conception. As for the term "incorrect cause," it means that a correct cause is not obtained.
Regarding the discussion of existence and non-existence, both lack any real meaning; hence it is said that neither is established.
Mahāmati, space is form; it enters into the categories of form. Mahāmati, form is space; it is established by way of the nature of the container and the contained.
One should understand the distinction between the phenomena of form and space. Mahāmati, when the four great elements arise, their own characteristics are each distinct;
they do not abide in space, yet it is not that space does not exist therein.
(Above it was said that one does not improperly discriminate between form and emptiness; here it is said that emptiness is itself form, and form is itself emptiness.
(When these four great elements arise, their respective characteristics—solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion—are each distinct.
Although they have never been separate from space, it is therefore said that there is no space apart from them, yet they do not abide within space.)
The commentary states: Regarding "that which sustains and that which is sustained," it means that form is sustained by space.
Since all forms are established within the locus of what is sustained, there is no form outside of space. How, then, can one speak of arising from space while maintaining a perception of boundaries?
As for the phrase "the nature of form is emptiness," this refers to the fact that the nature of form is the nature of emptiness; one should make such a distinction.
Furthermore, the four great elements are earth, water, fire, and wind.
In this way, Mahāmati, one observes that because the ox has horns, the rabbit has no horns.

Moreover, Mahāmati, if the horn of an ox is analyzed down to its subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*), and those subtle atoms are further analyzed as not abiding for even a single moment (*kṣaṇa*), then what is there to observe such that one says [the rabbit] has no [horns]?
If one says that other things are observed, those phenomena are likewise so (this view of existence and non-existence is entirely attachment). (A "moment" refers to a subtle thought-instant.)
The commentary states: "Observing that the ox has horns" refers to the existence of the ox's horn, in contrast to which one speaks of the non-existence of the rabbit's horn.

If this ox's horn is analyzed into atoms (*paramāṇu*) and further analyzed down to the level of the *aṇu* (the infinitesimal), then no characteristic of cognition (*buddhi*) or the absence of cognition can be perceived;
even a momentary state of abiding (*kṣaṇasthiti-lakṣaṇa*) cannot be found. Such is the view of those non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who calculate [existence] as non-existent.
Regarding the existence of a cow's horn, since not even a single atom can be found when searching for it, one does not know with respect to what it is said to be non-existent.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, saying: "One should abandon [discriminations regarding] the horns of a rabbit and the horns of a cow."
The perception of differences in forms and colors is a false imagination. You, all you bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, should contemplate that these are manifestations of your own minds;
entering accordingly as the most excellent sons of all buddha-fields, you should instruct them through the skillful means of the manifestations of your own minds.
(This concludes the exhortation regarding two kinds of views. Furthermore, it says: "One should contemplate that these are the false imaginings manifested from one's own mind.
[The term] "Sujāta" means "Son of the Buddha.")
The commentary states: If one wishes to know the reality of whether deluded thoughts exist or not, one should simply turn back and observe one's own mind.
Is it that they exist? Or do they not exist? Are they both existent and non-existent? Or are they neither existent nor non-existent?
By contemplating this, one will realize it for oneself. One should also use this to instruct others; therefore, it is said that one "enters all lands accordingly."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "Form and so forth, as well as mind, do not exist; yet form and so forth nourish the mind.

The body, experience, and false establishments arise from the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which manifests as sentient beings. Mind, thought, and consciousness—these five factors constitute the nature of phenomena.
The two kinds of selflessness and purity are what the Great Teacher has proclaimed. Length, shortness, existence, non-existence, and so forth, arise through mutual dependence."

They arise from one another; through non-existence they become existence, and through existence they become non-existence. The analysis of atoms into discrete entities does not give rise to the false imagination of form.
This is the domain established by the measure of mind (*cittamātra*), which is not favored by those with evil views. It is not the sphere of discursive thought, nor is it for the Śrāvakas;
it is the realm of self-realization taught by the Savior of the World.

"The non-existence of form and so forth, as well as the mind" refers to the verse on the nature of false discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), which does not posit external objects such as form nor internal consciousness.

"The detailed explanation and so forth" refers to the verse on the false discrimination of existence and non-existence, as well as the principle of relativity (*apekṣā*) and others; these are all not the correct cause.

Regarding "the analysis of atoms and the conceptualization of things": one does not give rise to the false discrimination of form. This refers to the verse on the erroneous attachment that there is no horn when a horn is analyzed.

This is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Regarding "the locus where the measure of mind is established": this refers to the preceding verse’s contemplation that one's own mind is free from the reckoning of existence and non-existence (i.e., the ultimate truth).

The commentary states: "Form and so forth, as well as the mind—when spoken of according to principle—have fundamentally no existence. This single word "non-" (*wu*) cuts off [all conceptual proliferation].
There is no delusive blade more sharp than this. If one can accept it as it is, what thought would not be eliminated? Yet ordinary beings do not understand this;
they give rise to false imaginings and, conversely, take them to nourish their own minds. Thus, the body, sensory enjoyments, and other things are established by means of this.
Speaking from its fundamental source, these are what the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) perceives; therefore, mind, intellect, and consciousness arise in succession.

Regarding the five phenomena of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-dharma*): based on the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), one establishes the five factors—name, characteristic, and so forth—as well as the two kinds of selflessness (*nairātmya*).
The locus of their establishment is not a realm of experience sought after by the false views or dream-like imaginings of non-Buddhists or those of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*).
This is the realm of self-realization taught by the Buddha.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva, in order to purify the stream of manifestations within his own mind, again requested the Tathāgata, saying to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One, how does one purify the stream of manifestations within the minds of all sentient beings? Is it sudden or gradual?"
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "The Dharma-teaching Buddha explains that all dharmas enter into their own-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

They have as their cause the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) manifested by one's own mind, and the cause of attachment to the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpitasvabhāva*) through continuous delusion. These various unrealities are like illusions;
these various attachments are unattainable."
Habitual tendencies and attachments are unreal, like a phantom. The three paths encompass the nine realms; hence it is said that there are "various attachments.
Yet these three paths are originally the three virtues. Sentient beings, deluded by them, wander through the three paths. The Buddha taught this Dharma [to reveal their true nature].
It causes one to realize that self-nature is fundamentally empty; thus, the delusory becomes the real, and both the real and the delusory are extinguished. Hence it is said:
"unattainable.

The commentary states: "The Dharma relies on the Buddha" means that the Dharma is the Dharmakāya (the Dharma-body), while the Buddha upon whom it relies is the Sambhogakāya (the Reward-body) in its functional aspect.
This means that the entire body [of reality] gives rise to its function, thereby teaching all dharmas; these dharmas are precisely the Mahāyāna dharma.

Regarding the phrase "entering into self-characteristics and common characteristics," it refers to sentient beings who are deluded regarding their original nature and enter into the grasping of self-characteristics and common characteristics.

These are afflictions manifested by one's own mind, termed the cause of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). Through the continuous succession of afflictions and false conceptualization, they create various [karmic actions].

The binding of karma is called the cause of clinging. Because one undergoes all manner of false birth and death through the binding of afflictions and karma, it is said to be unreal, like an illusion.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, by clinging to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the characteristics of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) arise. Mahāmati, it is like a craftsman...
Just as a magician relies upon grass, wood, tiles, and stones to produce various illusions,
manifesting the diverse forms and colors of all sentient beings and giving rise to various false conceptions— yet those false conceptions possess no reality whatsoever.
(Various illusions are produced based on grasses, trees, and so forth; this is a metaphor for the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
"Various forms" and so forth refer to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Those various delusions are like the illusory appearances created by a magician;
therefore, it is said that they lack any reality).
The commentary states: Because the characteristics of the imagined nature arise by depending upon the dependent nature, it is further illustrated through a simile.
Thus, Mahāmati, based upon the dependent nature, the imagined nature arises; it is the manifold seeds of the mind consisting of various conceptualizations.
The characteristic of the imagined nature arises from the habit-energies of clinging to the characteristics of various phenomena and activities.
Mahāmati, this is called the teaching of the Dharma by the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha.
(Above, the illusory nature of phenomena was used as a metaphor for various deluded thoughts; this now correlates with the preceding metaphor.
The commentary states: Regarding "various deluded thoughts" and so forth, because there is mind, there are perceptions; because there are perceptions, there are volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).

Where there is practice, there is activity; nothing is other than conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). This is precisely the characteristic of the three aforementioned paths; they differ only in their expansion and contraction.
Mahāmati, the Dharma-Buddha is that which is free from the self-nature of the mind, the realm of objects perceived by the noble ones through self-realization, established and bestowed [upon others].

[This is] the act [of realization]. (The Dharma-body is ultimate; what is there that it does not transcend? Yet, why specifically mention the "mind"? It is because the mind is the root of all phenomena.
If the mind does not perish, then all phenomena arise. Now, when one speaks of transcending appearances, then all phenomena are quiescent. Quiescence...)
"Characteristics" refers to what is called the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

The commentary states: "The Dharma-Buddha" refers to the Dharma-body of cultivated virtue. To say that one is "separated from the characteristics of the self-nature of the mind" means to be separated from deluded thoughts.

Since it is said to be "separated from characteristics," how could the names and characteristics of the Dharma-body be established on their own? Therefore, it is called "self-awakening" (*svasaṃvedana*).
This is the establishment and application of the objective sphere of the Noble Ones; that is to say, designating the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) as the Dharmakāya.
This is the name of the nameless and the characteristic of the characteristicless.
Mahāmati, as for the transformation Buddha (nirmāṇa-buddha), he teaches generosity, morality, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, as well as mind and wisdom.

He establishes the analysis and observation that transcends the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, and is free from the characteristics of consciousness and the views of non-form held by outsiders.

(Xing said to Jianzi: "Concentration and wisdom: the yin is like concentration, and the yang is like wisdom. Those who are biased toward either wisdom or concentration will all fail to see the Buddha-nature.
The commentary states: The "Transformation Buddha" is the Response Body (nirmāṇakāya) Buddha. He preaches the Dharma of the Three Vehicles to deliver all sentient beings.

To speak of the six perfections is the Dharma of the Bodhisattva. To transcend the five aggregates, the eighteen elements, and the twelve bases, as well as to resolve the characteristics of consciousness and discrimination, is the Dharma of the Two Vehicles.
To observe and establish [these] refers to the two kinds of awakening mentioned in the subsequent text;
this is the Dharma for the Bodhisattva’s self-cultivation and transformation of others. To transcend the views of non-Buddhists is to depart from the two extremes of nihilism and eternalism.

It is seen. As for those who see the formless: they reckon the formless concentrations (*ārūpya-samādhi*) to be the concentration of nirvāṇa, which is the cessation of sensation, perception, and mind.

Mahāmati, what is the characteristic of the attachment to the self-nature of the false imagination of natures as held by the śrāvakas? It refers to the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), blue, yellow, and so forth.
The red, white, solid, moist, warm, and moving—these self-characteristics and common characteristics are not produced by an agent; this has been excellently explained by the former Victors.

Having seen these, one gives rise to conceptualizations of intrinsic nature regarding them. A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should understand and abandon these, entering into the characteristic of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) and extinguishing the views regarding the characteristic of the selflessness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*).
By gradually establishing the continuity of the various stages (*bhūmi*), this is called [the realization of] all... [omitted].
The characteristic of attachment to the imagined nature of the Śrāvaka-nature.
(This section explains the Śrāvakas who cling to characteristics. The commentary states:
Regarding the statement that the matter of the four great elements is "not produced by action," it means it is not produced through artificial creation; yet, with respect to...
Attachment arises from the self-characteristics and common characteristics of the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas).
Previously, the Victorious One—the Buddha—skillfully proclaimed that those śrāvakas who cling to his teachings cannot realize that intrinsic nature is fundamentally empty.
Seeing the various marks within those objective realms, they give rise to conceptualizations of intrinsic nature. Those who are bodhisattvas should recognize this fault and abandon it accordingly.

Regarding the phrase "entering the characteristics of the selflessness of phenomena": this refers to departing from the view of the selflessness of persons and entering the characteristics of the selflessness of phenomena.
By entering the characteristics of the selflessness of phenomena, one gradually enters the various stages (*bhūmi*). This is called the concluding summary.
The supplementary note states: First, the nature of false conceptualization is explained. This refers to the four great elements and their forms, each possessing its own inherent nature.
For example, earth has solidity as its nature; water has moisture; fire has heat; and wind has motion. These are all inherent natures.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying:

“World-Honored One, regarding the realm of the self-realized noble path and the realm of the ultimate truth (paramārtha) spoken of by the World-Honored One as being eternal and inconceivable—World-Honored One, is this not the same as the ‘eternal and inconceivable cause’ taught by the non-Buddhists?
The Buddha told Mahāmati: “My ultimate truth is eternal and inconceivable...”

Consideration: It possesses characteristics because it is established through the characteristics of the cause of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), and because it attains the characteristic of self-realization apart from existence and non-existence.

It possesses causes because it is the cause for the wisdom of the ultimate truth; this is because it is apart from existence and non-existence. For example, it is like unconditioned space, nirvāṇa, and cessation.
This permanence and inconceivability are attained through the self-realized wisdom of all Tathāgatas.
