Because it is thus, one should train in this permanence and inconceivability attained through the noble wisdom of self-realization.
(This statement refutes the errors of non-Buddhists and reveals the correctness of the True Path. The primary truth (*paramārtha*) is precisely the Middle Way and the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Taking this as its cause constitutes the eternal cause; taking this as its characteristic constitutes the eternal characteristic.
Regarding the Tathāgatas who transcend the words of existence and non-existence, the Buddha said: "It is not only my teaching that is thus; all Buddhas..."
That which is realized is eternally inconceivable and there is nothing that is not so. Therefore, it is admonished that Bodhisattvas should practice and study this.

The commentary states: To say it is "free from nature" means it is not existent; to say it is "free from non-nature" means it is not non-existent. Being neither existent nor non-existent precisely reveals the Middle Way.
Because the Middle Way is free from all relativity, it is eternal; because it is eternal, it is wondrous; and because it is wondrous, it is inconceivable. This...

Therefore, the Tathāgata is ultimately eternal and inconceivable. Unlike those non-Buddhists who lack a cause characterized by intrinsic nature (*sva-lakṣaṇa*), [the Tathāgata] is said to possess both a cause and characteristics.
As for the statement "like unconditioned space and so forth": space is eternal because it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*);
nirvāṇa is eternal because it is the cessation of impermanence. This eternity and inconceivability thus differ from those of the outsiders.
The *Mārgavivāda-śāstra* [differs] from this of its own accord.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the eternal and inconceivable of the non-Buddhists is not eternal by virtue of the power of the characteristics of its own causal nature;

rather, it is because its nature is impermanent and its characteristics are diverse. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the eternal and inconceivable of the various non-Buddhists pertains to that which resembles a created nature.
It is not of the nature [of permanence]. Having perceived impermanence, one deliberates and reckons it as permanent.
(This refutes the non-eternal nature of the non-Buddhists; thus he challenges their lack of result, because their cause is not a true cause.)
[The text] repeatedly refutes this.
The commentary states: "To speak of causes characterized by difference means it is not the characteristic of my own self-cause.

That which they call 'permanent' is not a permanence established by the power of the true reality of the correct cause produced by itself; rather, it is a permanence that consists in regarding the impermanent as permanent."

How could this manifest the fruit of eternal nature? Furthermore, regarding the "eternal and inconceivable" as conceived by the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), they claim that all phenomena produced in the world exist and then cease to exist;
these are entirely impermanent. They assert that "nature" and "non-nature" are simply existence and non-existence.
Having formed such a view, they falsely calculate a self (ātman) and take it to be eternal and inconceivable; therefore, it is called "thought."
"Mahāmati, they calculate [things] as eternal.

Mahāmati, I too, having perceived through such causes and conditions that the nature of what is produced is neither existence nor non-existence, and having realized impermanence, speak of that eternity which is without cause, as it is the realm of the noble ones' self-realization.
Mahāmati, if the marks of the causes of the various non-Buddhists were to establish eternity..."

It is inconceivable. Because its self-characteristic is neither existence nor non-existence, it is like a rabbit’s horn. This eternal inconceivability is merely a conceptualization of verbal expression;
such is the fault of the various non-Buddhists. Why is this so? It is because their conceptualizations of verbal expression are like a rabbit’s horn;
they do not pertain to the actual nature of their own causes and characteristics.

(This statement means that ordinary beings fall into the three views of arising, abiding, and ceasing, as well as existence and non-existence; therefore, they distance themselves from the Way day by day.

(Regarding the section beginning with "The various heterodox practitioners," there are four points that summarize their errors: first, the conceptualization of verbal expression; second, the non-appropriation of the characteristics of their own causes;
third, the failure to realize the characteristics through self-awakening; and fourth, the calculation and reckoning of permanence. Therefore, it is said: "There are such [errors].")
(An error). The commentary states:

"Furthermore, it says 'I too, by such causes and conditions' means that the Tathāgata also perceives that nature as impermanent, yet he cultivates the perception of permanence to manifest the realm of the noble self-realization; only thereafter does one come to know its impermanence."

Therefore, it is said that they are eternal and without cause. Furthermore, if one were to establish them as eternal and inconceivable through the false causes and false characteristics of non-Buddhist outsiders, such causes and intrinsic natures would exist only as mere verbal designations and lack any real meaning;
thus, it is said that they are equivalent to the horns of a rabbit.

Mahāmati, my "eternal" and "inconceivable" are due to the realization of the self-characteristic through personal awakening; they are eternal because they are free from the nature of being produced, whether as existence or non-existence.

Mahāmati, it is not that external things—whether existent or non-existent—are impermanent, while one conceptually calculates them to be eternal, or that the inconceivable eternity is merely a conceptual calculation of the impermanence of external existents and non-existents.
For they do not understand that the eternal and the inconceivable have their own internal cause.
...the characteristic [of such views]. They are far removed from the characteristic of the realm of self-realized noble wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna-gocara*).

They should not speak [of it]. (This refutes four points of external calculation: first, refuting the calculation that conceives of permanence; second, refuting the failure to know the characteristic of the self-cause of permanence and the inconceivable;
third, refuting being far removed from the characteristic attained by the Buddha; fourth, "they should not speak" refutes their mere...)
There is a discourse [on this]. The commentary states:
"The 'self is eternal and inconceivable,' etc., means that the attainment of the self is inconceivable, taking self-realization as its causal characteristic (*nimitta*).
It is not like the heterodox views which hold that what exists becomes non-existent, making it impermanent; rather, it is through the deliberation of the *puruṣa* (the divine self)."
Regarding the calculation of permanence: "Furthermore, as for external natures, etc."—this again refutes the calculations of outsiders, which likewise possess four meanings.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the great assembly fears the suffering of the delusive discrimination of birth-and-death and seeks nirvāṇa;

yet they do not know the distinction between birth-and-death and nirvāṇa, nor that all natures are merely the non-nature of delusive discrimination. [This leads to] the cessation of future sense faculties and their objects.

They conceive the notion of *nirvāṇa*, yet this is not the transformation of the *ālayavijñāna* through the noble wisdom of self-realization. Therefore, the foolish and ignorant speak of three vehicles;

they speak of the "measure of mind" (*cittamātra*) as tending toward non-existence. For this reason, Mahāmati, they do not understand that the realms of all Tathāgatas in the past, future, and present are the manifestations of their own minds.
Clinging instead to external realms manifested by the mind, they remain perpetually in the wheel of birth and death.
[He] turned [the discourse]. (Xing said, "To preach the Mahayana Dharma to those of the Hinayana vehicle causes their minds to become deranged, deluded, and full of doubt;
it is what is called 'attempting to contain the great ocean within the footprint of an ox. If one preaches the Hinayana Dharma to those of the Mahayana vehicle, this is like using filth..."
The food is placed in precious vessels; those ordinary fools speak of three vehicles, which are the very roots that cause one to fall into the cycle of craving and rebirth—yet the bird knows nirvāṇa.

The commentary states: Those of the Hīnayāna fear birth and death and long for nirvāṇa, yet they do not know that the distinction between birth-and-death and nirvāṇa is entirely a product of false imagination and possesses no real nature.

With this eye of Hīnayāna wisdom, they perceive the cessation of future faculties and sense-objects and take this to be nirvāṇa; how could this truly be what is reached by the noble wisdom of self-awakening?

This realm is also not the nirvana manifested by the *ālayavijñāna*. When it is said that ordinary, deluded beings speak of three vehicles, they mean that birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is itself nirvana.
The Dharma of the Mahāyāna is not known to them; for their sake, the emptiness of the Small Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) is taught as nirvana.
That the measure of the mind (*cittamātra*) is non-existent is itself true emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Furthermore, they do not know the [Buddhas of] the three periods of time...
The Buddha’s wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa* manifests from within one's own mind; it does not exist elsewhere.
Through false conceptualization that phenomena exist outside the mind, one gives rise to delusions and creates karma, thereby revolving through birth and death.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are five types of immediate lineage (*gotra*). What are the five?

They are: the immediate lineage of the Śrāvaka vehicle, the immediate lineage of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, the immediate lineage of the Tathāgata vehicle, the indeterminate lineage, and the distinct lineage.
"Śrāvakas who cling to signs are no different from outsiders; though they wish to transcend the triple world, they are unable to do so.
The commentary states: "When considering their spiritual lineage (*gotra*), there is originally no distinction.
Due to beginningless habitual conditioning, these may be internal or external, great or small, fixed or unfixed. This is why this sutra clarifies that there are five types of spiritual lineage."
How is one to know the lineage of the śrāvaka-vehicle that is immediate?

If, upon hearing the teaching on the attainment of the knowledge of the specific and general characteristics of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, all the pores of one’s body bristle with joy and delight, and one delights in cultivating the wisdom of characteristics (*lakṣaṇajñāna*) rather than cultivating the signs of awakening through dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), this is called the immediate lineage of the śrāvaka-vehicle. The śrāvaka of the immediate lineage attains vision at the eighth stage.

On this stage, the afflictions that arise are severed, yet the latent tendencies (*vāsanā*) of those afflictions are not yet severed. One has not transcended the inconceivable death of transformation (*nirvikalpa-pariṇāmi-cyuti*), but one has transcended the death of fragmentation (*bheda-cyuti*).
One makes the true lion’s roar: "Birth has been exhausted; the holy life has been established; there is no further existence.
Thus, one knows reality as it is through the cultivation of the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*), until finally attaining the realization of parinirvāṇa.
(Śrāvakas possess a sense of weariness toward suffering that is so acute they are in haste to realize the fruit; therefore, the Four Truths are further taught.

When one knows suffering, abandons its origin, aspires for cessation, and cultivates the path, the body and mind become joyful and serene. Although the aggregates, elements, and sense bases differ in their modes of classification—whether expanded or condensed—they are, in essence, the Truth of Suffering.
"Knowledge of characteristics" refers to the knowledge of the general characteristics of the Four Truths).

The commentary states: The faculties of the śrāvakas are dull; they delight in cultivating this wisdom, yet do not cultivate the signs of awakening through dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
"Dependent" refers to the twelve links of dependent origination, which are what the pratyekabuddhas cultivate to achieve awakening, whereas the śrāvakas do not delight in such cultivation.
Through the *anantarya-samādhi*, the śrāvaka perceives the eighth stage of the pratyekabuddha and severs the manifest [afflictions].

Regarding the practice of seeing through afflictions of thought (*saṃyojana*) and deliberation (*kleśa*): as long as ignorance (*avidyā*) and distinct delusions have not been severed, what are called "habitual afflictions" (*vāsanā-kleśa*) are precisely this ignorance.

For this reason, one is unable to transcend birth and death within the *parināmika-saṃsāra* (transformation-death); yet, one is able to transcend the ocean-like *viparyāsa-jāti-maraṇa* (segmented birth and death).
The "Lion’s Roar" refers to fearless preaching; it means that upon reaching the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), one declares, "I am born [no more]."

"It has been exhausted" means that the accumulation of suffering has been severed. "The holy life has been established" means that one will not undergo further existence. "The path has been cultivated" means that cessation has been realized.
These are all true and not false; therefore, it is said that they are known as they truly are. One cultivates the selflessness of persons until attaining the awakening of nirvana;
this refers to emptying the grasping at a person and thereby realizing the proof of true emptiness.
Mahāmati, as for those of the lineage of the uninterrupted Pratyekabuddhayāna:
if they hear it said that there is an uninterrupted [realization] through individual conditions, their hair stands on end and they weep with flowing tears.

Upon hearing it said that they do not associate with others' conditions and remain unattached to all things, and that they possess various bodies and various supernatural powers—manifesting various transformations whether in union or separation—their minds enter into accordance with this when it is taught. If they know...
Having identified that one belongs to the lineage of uninterrupted succession for the Pratyekabuddhayāna, [the teacher] accordingly teaches them the Pratyekabuddhayāna;
this is called the characteristic of the lineage of uninterrupted succession for the Pratyekabuddhayāna.

(As for the Pratyekabuddha: having received the teachings from a Buddha, they contemplate the twelve links of dependent origination and awaken to the principle of the True Dharma; thus they are called Pratyekabuddhas.
They are also called Solitary Realizers because they appear in worlds where no Buddha exists and attain awakening through their own contemplation of conditions.)

The commentary states: "Each individually contemplates the immediate" means that upon hearing the teaching on the cyclic causality of the twelve links of dependent origination, one awakens to non-arising.
This accords with one's aspiration; moved by a convergence of compassion and emotion, one comes to the point of shedding tears.

Regarding the phrase "words do not approach one another," etc., it refers to delighting in solitary, sublime tranquility, practicing the conduct of seclusion, and being unable to cling to any signs whatsoever.
At times, he may explain for them the transformations of the supernormal powers of the body—such as manifesting many bodies from one, or merging many bodies into one.

Hearing such an explanation, their minds find entry [into the truth]. The Bodhisattva, knowing that they possess the lineage of a Pratyekabuddha, should then preach this Dharma of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle for them.
Mahāmati, there are four types of the lineage of uninterrupted continuity for that Tathāgata-vehicle: namely, the lineage of uninterrupted continuity of the dharma of intrinsic nature;
the lineage of uninterrupted continuity of the dharma apart from intrinsic nature; the lineage of uninterrupted continuity of the noble self-realized wisdom;
and the lineage of uninterrupted continuity of the excellence of external realms.
"The lineage of the Tathāgata is uninterrupted" means that its nature is perfectly interfused and unobstructed.
The commentary states: Regarding the "four kinds," first is the dharma of self-nature, which is the intrinsically pure mind of the Tathāgatagarbha.
Second is the dharma apart from self-nature, meaning this nature is free from attachment to a self-nature. Third is the attainment of the noble self-awakening... [text continues]

This is the Tathāgata’s ultimate awakened wisdom. Fourth is the excellence of the external lands, which refers to the various excellences of the Tathāgata’s adornment of the lands through his compassionate vows and his gathering of sentient beings.
Mahāmati, as for those of indeterminate lineage, this means that when the three types [of lineage] are taught, they enter according to what is taught and are established according to that.

Mahāmati, this refers to the initial stage of cultivation; that is, the establishment of lineage is made for the purpose of transcending and entering the stage of non-existence (*nirabhilāpya-bhūmi*).

As for their own inner storehouse consciousness (*svasaṃvittigotra*), once the habitual tendencies of their own afflictions are purified, they perceive the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*).
The Śrāvaka who dwells in the bliss of samādhi shall attain the most supreme body of a Tathāgata.
(The realm of the Tathāgata can only be entered through meditative concentration; as long as one has not severed the sensory dusts, one will ultimately remain subject to delusion.

Regarding the phrase "his own self-awakened store" (*svasaṃvidita-garbha*), the Tang translation states: "If the Śrāvaka dwelling in the bliss of samādhi is able to realize and know that which he himself relies upon..."
Consciousness perceives the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), purifies the habitual tendencies of afflictions (*kleśavāsanā*), and will ultimately attain the body of a Tathāgata.

The consciousness upon which it itself depends is precisely the eighth consciousness, the *svasaṃvittigotra* (the self-awakening treasury). The "habitual tendencies of afflictions" refers to ignorance (*avidyā*).

The commentary states: Regarding those of indeterminate lineage (*aniyata-gotra*), when they hear the teachings on the three vehicles of the Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, and Tathāgata, they give rise to faith and understanding accordingly and practice in accordance with them.
Because their nature can shift as they enter the Great Vehicle from the Small, they are said to be "indeterminate.
Those who have first cultivated the ground are persons of the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuklavidarśana-bhūmi*); for them, the teaching of the indeterminate lineage is expounded so that they may...
He transcends and enters the stage of non-existence (*akiṃcanya-bhūmi*). This stage is precisely the seventh stage, the Stage of Having Accomplished What Was to Be Done (*kṛtāvī-bhūmi*).
To establish it thus is to speak thus.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva skillfully contemplates the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*). What are the three natures? They are as follows:
The imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).
Mahāmati, the imagined nature arises from signs (*nimitta*). Mahāmati said: "World-Honored One, how does the imagined nature arise from signs? The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"In the dependent nature, there are the characteristics of things, the characteristics of signs, and the characteristics of activities. Through the manifestation of these characteristics of things and signs, there are two kinds of attachment to the imagined nature."
This is established by the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha. It refers to the characteristic of attachment to names and signs, and the characteristic of attachment to objective entities.
Regarding the characteristic of attachment to names and signs: it refers to attachment to internal and external phenomena. Regarding the characteristic of attachment to objective entities:

it refers to attachment to the specific and general characteristics of those very same internal and external phenomena. These are called the two kinds of characteristics of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
That which arises based upon and conditioned by [factors] is called dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
(This, moreover, subsumes five dharmas into three natures. (In the verse:

[This refers to] what is called "dharmas produced by causes and conditions" in the *Gaṅjīng* (The Scripture on the [Dharma-]Gate). The commentary states:
To say that the nature of false conceptualization arises from characteristics means it precisely arises from the mutual production of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
"Dependent origination" refers to the arising of phenomenal characteristics from causes and conditions; once these phenomenal characteristics manifest, two kinds of clinging arise.
"Attachment. Regarding "the characteristic of characteristics," this refers to the manifold nature of phenomenal characteristics.

"The characteristic of attachment to names and characteristics" refers to the conceptual attachment to names and characteristics within the internal and external phenomena of the sense organs and their objects; this is the characteristic of attachment to phenomenal characteristics.

"If based upon" (yi) and "conditioned by" (yuan) refer to that which arises; this correctly elucidates the dependent origination of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Here, "based upon" (*yi*) signifies the cause (*hetu*).
What is the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*)? It refers to that which is free from the conceptual constructions of names, characteristics, and the characteristics of things;

it is that which is attained by noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*), as well as the sphere of activity traversed by the noble wisdom of self-realization (*pratyātma-āryajñāna-gocara*). This is called the perfected nature, the Tathāgatagarbha-mind.
"Attainment" means achievement. Regarding the statement "to be free from the signs of names, the signs of things, and delusive signs":

this refers to the Buddhas and sages who, in contemplating phenomena produced by causes and conditions, realize that they are simultaneously empty, provisional, and the Middle Way; thus, being free from all delusive thoughts, they achieve correct wisdom and suchness.
The commentary states: That which is attained through noble wisdom is correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*). Self-awakened noble wisdom is suchness (*tathatā*).
When these two dharmas are unified into a single self-nature, this constitutes the *tathāgatagarbha*-mind.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva skillfully contemplates the two kinds of selflessness (*anātman*). What are the two kinds of selflessness?

They are the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*). What is the selflessness of persons? It refers to being free from the notions of "self" and "mine.

It is the arising of consciousness through the grasping and attachment to the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*), which are mere collections produced by ignorance, karma, and craving, such as the eye and forms. First.

For a provisional designation is not provisional in itself; it exists in dependence upon actual dharmas. If one analyzes the provisional, one must necessarily include its actual basis.

Therefore, it is said that the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases (*skandha-dhātv-āyatana*) are the collection [of these]. Ignorance is affliction (*kleśa*); this means that actual dharmas arise from affliction.
"Born from afflictions, karma, and craving; eyes, forms, and so forth" refers to the various consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, which grasp at objects such as forms.

Manifesting like a flowing river, like a seed, like a lamp, like the wind, and like clouds; perishing moment by moment in succession; restless like a monkey;

The various forms and colors of bodies arise through illusion, spells, or mechanical devices. To understand these characteristics thoroughly is called the wisdom of the non-self of persons (pudgala-nairātmya-jñāna).
(This explains that there is no self in persons. (The Tang translation says: "It is like a corpse moving by the power of incantations, or like a wooden man moving because of a mechanism.

This is a metaphor for the illusory body. Just as a magical illusion can cause a mechanical device to move, so too can the spirit cause an image to arise.

It is agitated. All phenomena are likewise; they are devoid of the unreal marks of self- and common-characteristics.

(This elucidates the non-selfhood of phenomena. (The Tang translation says: "There is no agent. Since there is no agent, there are [in reality] no phenomena that are acted upon;

...Indeed! Therefore it is said: "The self-nature is detached. (Note:

The phrase "such as the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases" serves as an analogy for the aforementioned contemplation of the non-self of persons (*pudgalanairātmya-vipaśyanā*), which is to be detached from the notions of "self" and "what belongs to the self" (*ātma-ātmīya*)).
It is merely due to the accumulation of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth, entwined by karma and craving, that they arise in mutual dependence.

The view of slander. One does not slander the True Dharma. At that time, the World-Honored One further said:

This is based upon dependent origination, just as the imagined nature exists within the realm of dependent origination. It is, for example, like a multitude of..."
Like a wish-fulfilling jewel of form, they universally manifest all buddha-fields and the great assemblies of all Tathāgatas, and within them all, they listen to and receive the Buddha-dharma.

(One establishes the view of eternalism and slanders the view of annihilationism; by departing from these two views, one attains the True Dharma of Bodhi.

The commentary states: "As with deluded thoughts, etc. This means that while Bodhisattvas provide teachings according to the capacities of beings, it is also like the deluded thoughts of ordinary people arising from conditions.

That which is taught is like an illusion, like a dream, like a reflection in a mirror, and like the moon in water;
it is far removed from arising and ceasing, as well as from annihilation and permanence, and does not abide in the stages of the two vehicles.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again requested of the Buddha, saying:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One will explain for us the emptiness, non-arising, non-duality, and the characteristic of being devoid of self-nature of all phenomena.

Having awakened to this emptiness, non-arising, non-duality, and the characteristic of being devoid of self-nature, we and the other assemblies of Bodhisattvas shall quickly abandon the false conceptualizations of existence and non-existence."
[They] attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "As for 'emptiness of emptiness' (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*), it refers to the locus of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Mahāmati, for those who are attached to the imagined nature, [the Tathāgata] speaks of emptiness, non-arising, non-duality, and the characteristic of being devoid of intrinsic nature.

Mahāmati, in that realm, seven kinds of emptiness are taught: namely, the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of things (*svabhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*), and the emptiness of conditioned activity (*saṃskāra-śūnyatā*)."
The emptiness of non-activity; the emptiness of all phenomena being beyond verbal expression; the great emptiness of the ultimate reality and noble wisdom; and mutual emptiness.
(Mahāmati, having realized that all phenomena are unborn and undifferentiated, and being free from both intrinsic nature and characteristics, he requests instruction on the noble path;

therefore, I answer him point by point. As for "emptiness of emptiness," it refers to the emptiness of that which is already empty. It is the emptiness of what has been emptied once again. It is the emptiness of the further emptiness.
The contemplation that is able to empty is the subject; the locus of the self-nature of false conceptualization is the object that is emptied.

Because ordinary beings cling to this as being the self-nature of false conceptualization, the Tathāgata teaches emptiness, non-arising, and non-duality—the Dharma that is free from both nature and characteristics.
What is the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*)? It refers to the fact that all natures are empty of both specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).

This is because, when one contemplates them as mutually accumulated, they are found to lack the nature of specific and general characteristics through conceptual differentiation; since they lack an intrinsic nature whether individually, collectively, or both, their characteristics do not abide.
Therefore, it is said that all natures are empty of characteristics. This is called the emptiness of characteristics.
(This explains the emptiness of characteristics. [It means that all phenomena originally lack the four natures of self, other, both, or neither.

The commentary states: "Accumulating through successive succession" refers to the mutual dependence and correspondence of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*).

"Discerning the absence of intrinsic nature" means that when analyzed and investigated, all things lack self-nature; since even the absence of nature is non-existent, it is said that "characteristics do not arise.

Regarding "the nature of self, other, and both being non-existent," this is a further explanation of the preceding meaning. "Self" refers to arising from itself; "other" [refers to arising from another].
"From another" refers to arising from another. "Together" refers to arising from both. "Non-existent" refers to arising without cause; arising without cause is precisely arising apart [from causes].
"Characteristics do not abide" means that characteristics themselves do not abide.
What is the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*)? It means that the intrinsic nature of itself does not arise;
this is called the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena. Therefore, it is called the emptiness of intrinsic nature.

(This explains emptiness of intrinsic nature. (Regarding the fact that "emptiness" was mentioned previously and "emptiness of nature" is stated here again: the former involved an analytical investigation that entered into emptiness;

thus, both nature and characteristics are included as nature, and it is explained in terms of nature.)

The commentary states: Regarding "emptiness of intrinsic nature" (svabhāva-śūnyatā), it means that when one contemplates all phenomena as they arise in the present moment, they lack the nature of arising from themselves;
this is called emptiness of intrinsic nature.

What is the emptiness of formations (*saṃskāra-śūnyatā*)? It refers to the fact that the aggregates (*skandha*) are devoid of a self (*ātman*) and what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*). They arise through causes, conditioned factors, actions, and skillful means;

this is called the emptiness of formations. (This explains the emptiness of formations. [Regarding the statement "the aggregates are devoid of a self and what belongs to a self" in the context of the emptiness of formations: the aggregates are what belong to a self; their nature is fundamentally...
"Detachment from grasping. This means that the self is established based on the aggregates (*skandha*), and conditioned activities (*saṃskāra*) arise from the self;

thus it is said. The commentary states: "Caused by what belongs to the self" means caused by that which is mine (*mama*). That is to say, one gives rise to karmic activity because of what is mine, and through the conjunction of skillful means, false attachment arises.
When one investigates according to the nature of reality, none of these can be found; this is called the emptiness of conditioned activities (*saṃskāra-śūnyatā*).

Mahāmati, this very emptiness of practice (*caryā-śūnyatā*), which is the dependent origination of successive conditions and lacks intrinsic nature, is called the emptiness of non-practice (*acaryā-śūnyatā*).
(This explains the emptiness of non-practice.)
The commentary states: Regarding "emptiness of non-action," it does not mean abandoning the actions previously performed;

rather, it is the thorough realization that the various aggregates (skandhas) arise in succession through mutual dependence and possess no inherent nature (svabhāva). This is to practice non-action, which constitutes the emptiness of non-action.
What is the emptiness of all phenomena being beyond verbal expression? It means that because the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is inexpressible, all phenomena are beyond verbal expression;
this is called the emptiness of all phenomena being beyond verbal expression. What is the great emptiness of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) and noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) of all phenomena?

It means that upon attaining the noble wisdom of self-realization, all views and the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are empty; this is called [the emptiness of the ultimate reality and noble wisdom of all phenomena].
All phenomena are the great emptiness of the ultimate meaning of noble wisdom.
(Regarding "the emptiness of all phenomena being beyond verbal expression": this means that for all phenomena, their falsely imagined nature is realized through self-awakening;

how could it admit of verbal expression? This is the emptiness beyond verbal expression. As for the noble wisdom of self-awakening, it is fundamentally not something that can be made empty, yet it is able to...)
It empties that view of habitual tendencies. Since the object is already empty, the subject that empties it is also empty; [this is] ultimate emptiness.
The commentary states: The preceding section explains the emptiness of verbal expression, while the subsequent section explains the emptiness of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*).
What is mutual emptiness (*itaretara-śūnyatā*)? It refers to the emptiness of something in relation to that which is absent from it; this is called mutual emptiness.
Mahāmati, for example, in the house of Mṛgāramātṛ there are no elephants, horses, oxen, or sheep, yet it is not that there is no community of bhikṣus.

Thus one speaks of its being empty [of those things], but it is not that the house is empty of the very nature of a house, nor is it that the bhikṣus are empty of the very nature of bhikṣus. Nor is it that there are no elephants or horses in other places. This is called...

The specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena: that [characteristic] does not exist within that [phenomenon]. This is called "emptiness of this and that" (*itaretara-śūnyatā*). These are the seven kinds of emptiness.
As for the emptiness of this and that, it is the coarsest form of emptiness; you should distance yourself from it.
(Regarding the example of Mṛgāra and others: "Mṛgāra" is a personal name.
His mother, the laywoman Viśākhā, deeply revered the Triple Gem and constructed a vihāra to provide a dwelling for bhikṣus; therein, she did not keep elephants, horses, or the like.
(The initial character "that" [彼] refers to non-Buddhists. While they lack that [the self], they cannot lack this [the aggregates]. Furthermore, it speaks of the seven kinds of emptiness.)

[Included within the preceding context]. Furthermore, that which is called "emptiness of this and that" (*itaretara-śūnyatā*) is the coarsest form; it is the false conceptualization of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

Therefore, those who train in the precepts should distance themselves from it deeply. The commentary states: "Emptiness of this and that" refers precisely to the emptiness conceptualized by the non-Buddhists. In contrast to this [true emptiness], it is merely...
It is empty of that, but not empty of this; therefore it is said, "it is empty of that which is absent therein. For example, as stated below regarding the son of a deer (*mṛgapati*):
when one says "that house is empty," it means it is empty only of elephants and horses, not that the mounds and the multitude [of other things] are also empty.

Yet one cannot empty the nature of these two. Even if one were to consider this place where many elephants and horses are present as empty, other places would not be empty.

This is called "all phenomena" (*sarvadharma*), a concluding term used for refutation.
“Mahāmati, [dharmas] do not arise from themselves, yet they are not non-arising—except for those abiding in samādhi.

The commentary states: "Not non-arising" means that it is not the case that there is absolute non-arising.
According to principle, there is no arising and nothing that does not arise, with the exception of those who abide in samādhi. This refers to those who have ascended to the first stage (*bhūmi*).
By attaining the first dwelling, one shatters the darkness of non-manifestation; this is true non-arising.
Being devoid of intrinsic nature is itself non-arising. Devoid of intrinsic nature, there is the momentary succession and flow of continuity, as well as the manifestation of diversity.
All natures are devoid of intrinsic nature; therefore, all natures are devoid of intrinsic nature.
(This is the answer to the question regarding the absence of intrinsic nature.

Because they exist as distinct characteristics arising from causes, they are called non-dual. Just as it is with nirvāṇa and saṃsāra, so it is with all phenomena. This is...
Therefore, one should practice and study emptiness, which is non-arising, non-dual, and free from the characteristics of intrinsic nature.
(This answers the question regarding non-duality. These two are non-dual yet dual, and dual yet non-dual.

If one does not understand this and claims there are distinct characteristics or causes, then each would possess its own intrinsic nature; therefore, it is said that they are non-dual in order to unify them.
Once these two are understood to be non-existent, then there is no phenomenon that is not likewise so. Therefore, it is necessary to provide a concluding statement. The commentary states:
First, by means of phenomena, the two characteristics are demonstrated—the characteristics of cold and heat, long and short, black and white.
Their mutual dependence is manifest; they cannot but be non-dual. Furthermore, the statement "all phenomena are non-dual" is a summary. This is because...
The principle is one. It integrates those diverse phenomena so that all dharmas are non-dual.

As for the statement "not apart from nirvāṇa, etc.," it means that birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are fundamentally equal: there is no birth-and-death existing separately outside of nirvāṇa, nor is there a nirvāṇa existing separately outside of birth-and-death;
that [birth-and-death] is itself the external.
Chapter Two: The Heart of All Buddha-Speech.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the World-Honored One has declared in the sūtras that the Tathāgatagarbha is pure by nature;
it possesses the thirty-two marks and enters into the bodies of all sentient beings."
Just as a precious gem of great value may be wrapped in a soiled garment, the Tathāgata-garbha is likewise eternally abiding and unchanging;
yet it is enveloped by the soiled garments of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, and defiled by the dust of afflictions—the unreal conceptualizations of greed, hatred, and delusion.
"This is what all Buddhas have proclaimed. World-Honored One, why do you speak of a *tathāgatagarbha* in the same way that the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) speak of a self (*ātman*)?
World-Honored One, the non-Buddhists also speak of a permanent agent that is devoid of qualities (*guṇa*), omnipresent, and indestructible;
World-Honored One, they claim that there is a self. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "My teaching of the *tathāgatagarbha* is not the same as that of the non-Buddhists."

"Mahāmati, regarding the 'self' that has been taught: there are times when it is described through such terms as emptiness, signlessness, wishlessness, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), nirvāṇa, being devoid of intrinsic nature, non-arising, non-ceasing, primordial quiescence, and natural nirvāṇa.
Having spoken of the Tathāgatagarbha in this way, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas do so in order to eliminate the fear of selflessness in foolish people."
Because it is a phrase [of the teaching], I have taught the gate of the Tathāgatagarbha as being free from false conceptualization and devoid of any objective realm.
Mahāmati, future and present Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should not form attachments based on the view of a self.
It is just as a potter, from a single lump of clay, through the skillful means of human effort, water, wood, a wheel, and a string, fashions various vessels; the Tathāgata is also like this.

Regarding the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), which is free from all marks of conceptual construction (*vikalpa-lakṣaṇa*), [the Buddha] employs various forms of wisdom and skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) to speak either of the *tathāgatagarbha* or of selflessness (*anātman*).
For these reasons, he speaks of the *tathāgatagarbha*. This is not the same as the "self" (*ātman*) propounded by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*);
this is what is called speaking of the *tathāgatagarbha*. It is taught in order to attract and lead those non-Buddhists who cling to the notion of a self. Thus it is said.

The Tathāgatagarbha causes one to abandon the false conceptualization of an unreal self and enter the sphere of the three gates of liberation, so that one may swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. For this reason, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha—
Thus is the Tathāgatagarbha described. Were it otherwise, it would be identical to the views of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
Therefore, Mahāmati, in order to avoid the views of the non-Buddhists, one should rely upon the Tathāgatagarbha as being without self (anātman).
Regarding the thirty-two marks of a Tathāgata: First, the soles of the feet are level and full, like the bottom of a casket;

though the ground be uneven, wherever the feet tread, it is touched with evenness and ease. Second, beneath the soles of the feet are the patterns of thousand-spoked wheels, with all their rims and hubs perfectly complete.
Third, both hands and feet are soft and supple, like *tūla* cotton. Fourth, the two feet... [one]...
1. Each finger is like that of a king of geese. 2. The webbed fingers and toes are interlaced, their patterns as exquisite as fine embroidery. 3.
The five fingers and toes of the hands and feet are perfectly rounded, slender, long, and lovely. 4. The heels are broad, long, and well-rounded, in perfect proportion to the arches of the feet.
5. The arches of the feet are high and full, in perfect proportion to the heels. 6. The two calves are gradually tapered and rounded, like those of a deer king. 7. The two [calves]...
10. His arms stand level when extended, reaching his knees, like the trunk of an elephant king. 11. His male organs are retracted and concealed within a sheath, as in a thoroughbred horse.
12. A single hair grows from each pore; they are deep blue-black and curl gracefully. 13. The hairs of his head all point upward; they curl to the right in a graceful spiral.
14. His skin is fine, thin, smooth, and supple; dust and water do not adhere to it. 15. His skin is golden in color.
15. His complexion is radiant and adorned with various jewels. 16. The two soles of his feet, the two palms of his hands, the front of his neck, and both shoulders—these seven places are full.
17. His nape is perfectly rounded and exquisite. 18. His upper arms and armpits are entirely well-filled. 19.
His deportment is majestic, full, upright, and straight. 20. His physical form is tall, broad, dignified, and handsome; his bodily proportions are symmetrical and perfect.
21. His chest and upper body are as broad as those of the *nyagrodha* tree; his majestic presence is vast, like that of a lion king. 22.
His constant radiance extends one fathom in every direction. 23.
His forty teeth are even and level, clean and closely set with deep roots, and whiter than white jade or snow. 24. His four canine teeth are brilliant white and sharp. 25. Constantly...
25. He obtains the supreme taste among all tastes. 26. His tongue is thin, pure, broad, and long, able to cover the face up to the ears and the hairline.
27. His Brahma-voice is harmonious and elegant; regardless of the number of listeners, it reaches everyone equally. 28.
His eyelashes are like those of a bull king, deep blue and perfectly even. 29. His eyes are deep blue and brilliant.
The joints between his fingers and toes are encircled by red lines, clear and distinct; his thirty-two facial marks are like the full moon.
His eyebrows are pure and refined like the bow of Śakra; between his thirty-one eyebrows is the white tuft mark (*ūrṇā-kośa*), as soft as silk and whiter than jade or snow.
Thirty-second, the *uṣṇīṣa* on the crown of the head is lofty, prominent, and perfectly round, like a celestial canopy.

The commentary states: "I say that the Tathāgatagarbha is originally devoid of the characteristics of a self; however, in order to reveal the true and destroy the false, I speak of both 'self' and 'non-self.
This is not the same as the falsely imagined self of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). As for the terms 'emptiness,' 'signlessness,' and 'wishlessness'..."

These are the three emptinesses. Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*). Signlessness (*animitta*) is the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*). Wishlessness (*apraṇihita*) is the emptiness of both nature and characteristics;

it is that which has nothing to be wished for. It is like the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); it is the true suchness-limit (*tathatā-bhūtakoṭi*). Regarding "dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*): "dharma" means a rule or norm.
"Nature" (prakṛti) means that which is unchanging. As for the "Dharmakāya," it takes the dharmatā as its teacher and model, and thus takes the dharmatā itself as its body.

"Nirvāṇa" means extinction or liberation. It is sometimes described as being free from self-nature, sometimes as neither arising nor ceasing, sometimes as primordial stillness, and sometimes as natural nirvāṇa.
All such phrases are alternative names for the Tathāgatagarbha.
However, the Tathāgata expounds the meaning of the *tathāgatagarbha* through various names in order to cause sentient beings to abandon the notion of a self.

This is solely because their capacities and inclinations differ. For those who fear hearing the term "selflessness," he speaks of a realm that is free from deluded thought and devoid of anything existing.

To be free from delusion is itself to be without a self; this constitutes the gateway of the *tathāgatagarbha*. A "gateway" is that which enables passage; it is intended for the sake of the multitude...
Birth enters through this gate; therefore, the precepts state that one should not harbor attachments. To illustrate this, an analogy is provided below to conclude and clarify the point:
A lump of clay is a single entity, yet by the skillful means of a potter’s craftsmanship, it becomes various vessels.
Likewise, the dharma of non-self is also a single reality; originally it has no fixed name, but it is explained through the skillful means of wisdom.

There are various names, such as those previously mentioned: emptiness, signlessness, up to nirvāṇa, and so forth. Therefore, it is concluded that some speak of the *tathāgatagarbha* while others speak of selflessness (*anātman*).
Although the names differ, the meaning is one and the same. This is because the *tathāgatagarbha* is taught to attract and guide non-Buddhists who cling to a self;
its purpose is fundamentally to cause them to abandon such clinging, enter the three gates of liberation, and achieve perfect enlightenment.
How could this be the same as the view of a self (ātman) held by non-Buddhists? As for the three liberations, they are:
liberation through intrinsic purity, liberation through perfect purity, and liberation through the purity of skillful means.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, observing future sentient beings, again requested of the World-Honored One:
"I only pray that you will explain for them the uninterrupted practice and the great skillful means of those who practice, such as the Bodhisattvas-Mahāsattvas.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "By accomplishing four dharmas, one attains the great skillful means of the practitioner. What are the four? They are: being skilled in..."

Discerning that which appears as one's own mind, observing that external natures have neither existence nor non-existence, and being free from views of arising, abiding, and ceasing, one attains the sublime bliss of the noble wisdom of self-realization.
This is called the great skillful means of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who, having accomplished four dharmas, becomes a practitioner.

(If the fruit is not present, the causal practice cannot be accomplished; if the practice is not based on skillful means, one cannot progress. Therefore, this is brought forth in response to the question. The commentary states:

To say that accomplishing these four dharmas constitutes the great skillful means (*upāya*) means that while there are many doors to skillful means, these four dharmas represent the greatest among them;
thus, they differ from other forms of skillful means. Nevertheless, these four do not go beyond cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
The nature of cause and effect refers to the entirety of nature giving rise to cultivation, proceeding from cause to fruit.

What is meant by "skillfully discerning that which is manifested as one's own mind"? It means observing that the three realms are merely the extent of the mind, thereby abandoning the notions of "I" and "mine.
They are without fluctuation, free from coming and going, and are variously [manifested] within the three realms due to being perfumed by the habitual tendencies of beginningless falsehood.

The bondage of form and formations, established through body and wealth, appears as one enters into false conceptualization; this is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s skillful discernment of what is manifested from one's own mind.

(This explains the discernment of what is manifested from one's own mind. [Regarding the mention of "form and formations" alone for the five aggregates: it is a brief enumeration of the five aggregates.
(2). The commentary states:

"Regarding the statement that one contemplates the three realms as being merely the extent of the mind: the three realms arise from deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*), and deluded conceptualization does not transcend one's own mind.
'Extent' (*pramāṇa*) refers to boundaries. When one realizes that there are no phenomena outside the mind, then [the person...]"
Since the Dharma is free from both types of grasping, how could there be any movement or the characteristics of coming and going?
It is merely due to the perfuming of beginningless false conceptualization that there are the various five aggregates (pañca-skandha) binding one within the three realms.

Because of the body composed of the five aggregates, there is the establishment of material resources and wealth. All such phenomena manifest solely through the false conceptualization of one's own mind. If...
Knowing that all things are originally empty and quiescent, how could there be arising and ceasing? This is what is meant by skillful discernment.

What is meant by skillfully observing that external natures are non-natures? It refers to all natures—such as mirages and dreams—which have their causes in beginningless, false, and deluded habitual tendencies.
By observing the self-nature of all natures, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva thus skillfully observes external [natures].
"Nature and non-nature. This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s skillful contemplation of the external nature and non-nature (this explains the meaning of "external nature and non-nature").
[The former was the contemplation of the internal mind; this is the cultivation of external contemplation. These two contemplations—]
Cultivation should be performed according to what is appropriate; it is not necessarily the case that all methods must be employed together).

The commentary states: Regarding the phrase "the nature of external things is non-nature," this means one realizes that the nature of external phenomena does not arise from the four natures—self, other, both, or causeless.
This refers to the nature of such things as mirages and dreams. All these phenomena [arise] from beginningless time...
With false habitual tendencies as their cause, all things are unreal, like a mirage or a dream; this is what is meant by skillfully contemplating that external natures have no intrinsic existence.
How does one skillfully abandon views of arising, abiding, and ceasing? It means that all natures—whether self-nature, other-nature, or both—are like illusions and dreams.

Birth occurs according to the limits of one's own mind; therefore, one perceives that external natures are neither existent nor non-existent. One perceives that consciousness does not arise and that conditions do not accumulate.
One perceives that what arises from the conditions of false discrimination cannot be found among any phenomena, whether internal or external to the three realms.

One perceives that views regarding the arising of things apart from self-nature are entirely extinguished. Knowing the self-nature of all phenomena to be like illusions and so forth, one attains the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). One attains...

Having attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one is free from views of arising, abiding, and ceasing. This is called the bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s skillful discernment that is free from views of arising, abiding, and ceasing.

(This explains the meaning of being free from views of arising, abiding, and ceasing. [Being free from views of arising, abiding, and ceasing means, for example, like a dream; this restates what was previously mentioned.]
This is what is observed. "Seeing that consciousness does not arise from below" (the correct demonstration of being free from views).
The commentary states: Because of the preceding observation, one sees that the internal consciousness of the mind does not give rise to external conditions, and sensory objects do not accumulate.
When each and every thing is investigated, its intrinsic nature cannot be found; therefore, it is said to be "unborn.

Yet, though unborn, it arises through the conditions of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), giving rise to all phenomena within and without the triple world. Because they share a single, uniform principle, none of them can be apprehended;
thus, they are devoid of self-nature (*svabhāva*). Since they are devoid of nature, both dependent origination and views are entirely quiescent. In this way, one realizes and knows all [phenomena].
Dharmas are like illusions; this is precisely the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Since there is no arising, there is no cessation.
Therefore, there is nothing that the body—which is characterized by arising, abiding, and ceasing—is not free from.
How does one attain the sublime bliss of the noble wisdom of self-awakening? It means attaining the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas and dwelling in the eighth stage of a bodhisattva.

On this ground, one attains liberation from mind, thought, mentation, the five dharmas, the three natures, and the two forms of selflessness; one attains the body born of mental mastery (*manomayakāya*).

(This explains the accomplishment of the sublime bliss of the noble wisdom of self-realization. (Regarding this noble wisdom of self-realization, it refers to the attainment of the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*);
this is the initial manifestation of the destruction of non-existence.)
The commentary states: Regarding the phrase "delighting in the good," having attained non-arising (anutpāda), one takes this as joy.

Furthermore, concerning the statement "dwelling in the eighth bodhisattva stage," this refers to the eighth stage of the Shared Teaching (tongjiao). Upon reaching this stage, the bodhisattva receives the empowerment of transformation.
One first realizes the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). It is impossible to provide an explanation of this through other teachings.

Since one has already realized non-arising by being detached from mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-mano-vijñāna*), what dharma could there be to detach from? Thus, it is a detachment that is not detachment. One who attains the body of wondrous mind-born mastery (*manomaya-kāya*) possesses the very basis for the arising of function;
yet, having even abandoned the mind, one attains the function of the wondrous mind.
“World-Honored One, by what causes and conditions does the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) arise? “Mahāmati, as for the mind-made body:
it is called ‘mind-made’ because its movement is swift and unimpeded, like the flight of the mind. It is like the mind moving through stone walls without obstruction;

even across immeasurable *yojanas* in distant lands, it remembers and does not forget what was previously seen. The flow of one’s own mind continues without interruption, and within the body there is no [obstruction].”
"Obstructed arising. Mahāmati, such is the mind-made body (manomaya-kāya). The mind-made bodies of Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas arise simultaneously;

adorned with the marks of the noble lineage, they possess the power of the illusory samādhi and mastery over supernormal powers (abhijñā), arising all at once just like the mind-made body that is without obstruction.
They manifest according to the spheres of their original vows as they are remembered, in order to bring them to fulfillment."

Regarding sentient beings, they attain the sublime bliss of the noble wisdom of self-awakening (which, being unobstructed and unhindered, leads one into the realm of Bodhi). As for the "mind-made body" (*manomaya-kāya*) and so forth, "mind" has three meanings.
These are taken as metaphors: first, swiftness; second, unimpededness; and third, universal arrival.
This refers to the fact that when a Bodhisattva attains the *māyopama-samādhi* (illusion-like samādhi) and manifests a body to gather in his father, these three meanings are likewise present.

The commentary states: For ordinary beings, the mind may reach a place while the body cannot; it is only for sages and those who have attained supernatural powers that both body and mind reach together.
What is called the sovereign supernormal power of the illusion-like samādhi refers to the intention capable of producing [such manifestations].
The "body of the noble lineage adorned with wondrous marks" refers to the body that is born.
"Simultaneously born, as if produced by mental power" merges the dharma and the metaphor. "Bringing sentient beings to fulfillment" means causing them likewise to attain wholesome bliss.

At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again requested of the World-Honored One: "I pray that you will explain the characteristics of the causal conditions (*pratyaya-hetu*) of all phenomena.

By awakening to the characteristics of causal conditions, I and the other Bodhisattvas may leave behind the false views of the existence and non-existence of all natures, and be free from the deluded views of gradual or simultaneous arising. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Those causes are of six kinds."

The types [of causes] are as follows: the cause of future existence (*bhaviṣyat-hetu*), the cause of continuity (*saṃtati-hetu*), the cause of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-hetu*), the cause of activity (*kāraka-hetu*), the cause of manifestation (*pradarśana-hetu*), and the cause of dependence (*apekṣā-hetu*).
Regarding the cause of future existence: once the causal activity has been performed, internal and external phenomena arise. Regarding the cause of continuity:

once the objective support (*ālambana*) has been established, internal and external phenomena arise, such as the seeds of the aggregates (*skandha-bīja*). Regarding the cause of characteristics: it produces uninterrupted characteristics that arise in succession. Regarding the cause of activity: it performs the function of predominance (*adhipatya*).

The matter is like that of a wheel-turning monarch (*cakravartin*). To demonstrate the cause: once the phenomena of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) have arisen, their characteristics manifest as the agent and the action, just as a lamp illuminates forms and so forth.
Regarding dependence on causes: at the time of cessation, the continuity is severed and the non-conceptual nature arises.
(Regarding "having causes": this refers to the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), which consists of the phenomena produced by the sense faculties and their objects. Regarding "causes of continuity":

this refers to the conditions that draw upon the sense faculties and their objects to form wholesome or unwholesome karma, thereby producing the seeds for future rebirth; thus, the fruit itself becomes a cause. Regarding "causes of manifestation":
this refers to the manifestation of uninterrupted wholesome or unwholesome karma, wherein cause and effect continue in an unbroken succession. This is the active cause.)
This refers to designating that which functions as a cause upon a cause as "augmentation. To reveal the cause means that all things of deluded thought must have a cause for their arising;
the relationship between the agent and the object of action is as clearly visible as a lamp illuminating an object. Regarding dependence on causes:
this means that when deluded thought ceases, it again arises, and when it arises, it again ceases. If the continuity of these thoughts is severed, then the delusion...
The nature of perception arises by relying on the false as its counterpart to the non-false; this constitutes the "conditioned cause" (*pratītya-hetu*).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "All things are entirely without arising, Nor do they perish through causes and conditions.

Within that [reality] of arising and perishing, One gives rise to the conceptualization of causes and conditions. It is not that cessation is blocked and then rebirth occurs, But rather a continuous succession."
The arising of causes and conditions exists solely to sever the delusive imaginings of the ignorant and foolish regarding the conditions of existence and non-existence.
These dharmas of dependent origination are entirely without birth; they revolve through being deluded by habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). From this, the three realms of existence manifest.

In reality, there is no birth of conditions, nor is there any cessation. One should contemplate all conditioned phenomena as being like flowers in the sky, abandoning both the grasper and the grasped.
The vision of delusion is neither that which has already arisen nor that which is yet to arise; furthermore, it is without causes or conditions. All things are non-existent;
these are all merely conventional designations.
(This verse was spoken in response to a question concerning the gradual principles of the Great Causal Dharma. (As...)

"Like flowers in the sky" means that sentient beings give rise to views of arising and ceasing within the true principle of *tathatā* (suchness), just as one with diseased eyes perceives flowers [where none exist].
The commentary states: It is said that all phenomena are neither produced gradually nor instantaneously; since they are said to be "unproduced," how could they possibly exist?
Is it extinguished? It is merely that, due to fundamental delusion, one gives rise to the notion of arising and ceasing.

Therefore, when it is said that there is no arising or ceasing, this does not mean that the dependent origination of arising and ceasing does not actually exist; rather, such a statement is made to sever the false conceptualizations of the ignorant and foolish.

If one investigates its fundamental nature, what is born and what is extinguished? It is merely that, through beginningless habitual delusions, one wanders in confusion, and thus there arise the birth and extinction of the three realms.
"The three existences" (trai-bhava) refers precisely to the three realms. As for "that which grasps" and "that which is grasped," these refer to the grasper and the grasped.

If, regarding these sense organs, objects, and spheres of experience, one does not perceive characteristics such as existence, non-existence, or delusive confusion, then one has already [attained realization].
Birth is indeed the non-existence of all that is born; it is merely a conventional expression through names and words.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for us the *Sūtra on the Mind of the Characteristics of Verbal Conceptualization*. World-Honored One, if I and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas thoroughly understand these words..."

The *Sūtra on the Exposition of the Characteristics of the Mind of Discursive Thought* enables one to penetrate the two kinds of meanings—namely, speech and that which is expressed by speech—and swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
By means of these two modes of speech and that which is expressed, one purifies all sentient beings.

The Buddha told Mahāmati: "There are four kinds of characteristics of discursive thought regarding speech: namely, speech concerning signs (*nimitta*), speech concerning dreams (*svapna*), [speech concerning delusions], and speech concerning the past."
Regarding discursive speech based on false conceptualization and attachment: there is the speech of beginningless false conceptualization, and the speech of signs.
The speech of signs arises from attachment to the forms of one's own false conceptualizations. The speech of dreams arises from recollecting previously experienced objects;

it arises from the absence of intrinsic nature in objects once one has awakened. The speech of following past false conceptualization and attachment arises from the actions performed by former enemies.

Recollection arises from beginningless false conceptualization and verbal expression; it arises from the habitual tendencies of one's own seeds due to the fault of beginningless attachment to falsehoods.
These are called the four kinds of characteristics of false conceptualization regarding verbal expression.
In ultimate reality, when one is free from the characteristics of verbal expression, even those characteristics themselves cannot be apprehended; how then could there be these four?

When the Tathāgata speaks of these four, he uses words to dispel words; even while teaching the mind of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), one should remain free from attachment—how much more so regarding these four categories.
All these are said to be the deluded imaginings (*vikalpa*) of sentient beings. Regarding "discourse based on signs" (*nimitta-vyavahāra*):

this refers to the arising of the discrimination of specific and general characteristics from the forms and signs of deluded imagination manifested from one's own mind. Regarding "discourse based on dreams" (*svapna-vyavahāra*):

this refers to the occurrence of discourse when one recalls experienced objects that manifest within a dream; yet once awake, no real object exists, and thus it is said to be without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

Furthermore, "discourse based on the attachment to erroneous conceptualization" refers to the recollection at various times of past karmic enmity—such as when someone once harmed me—and the resulting speech born of resentment and conceptual thought.

"Discourse based on beginningless erroneous conceptualization" refers to that which arises from the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of beginningless frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*) and false clinging.
If one can distance oneself from these four kinds of discourse based on erroneous conceptualization, then...
This reveals the wondrous principle of the single reality.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "All natures lack intrinsic nature, And likewise lack verbal expression.
The profound meaning of emptiness within emptiness Is not understood by the foolish. The self-nature of all natures Is beyond verbal expression."
Dharmas are like shadows. This is what I have taught as the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) for the sons of those who possess the noble wisdom of self-realization.
That "all natures lack intrinsic nature" means they are free from the marks of mental objects; that "they are also beyond verbal expression" means they are free from the marks of verbal expression.
The commentary states: Since it transcends both speech and thought, this is the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).

Fools are ignorant of this and thus fall into the various realms of existence (*bhava*). Regarding "the self-nature of all natures" and so forth—meaning that all phenomena possess a self-nature—this entails verbal expression;
yet all such things are unreal, like shadows. Only the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) realized by noble wisdom is what I have taught.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for us that which is free from being one or different,
both or neither, existent or non-existent, neither existent nor non-existent, permanent or impermanent—

that which is not traversed by any externalists, but is the domain of the noble wisdom of self-realization, which transcends the imagined nature of individual and common characteristics, and enters into the supreme reality."

The meaning of this is as follows: the characteristics of the successive stages (*bhūmi*) that progressively advance toward higher and higher purity; the characteristic of entering the stage of the Tathāgata;

the unmanifested original vow; and all phenomena—which are like the realm of a multicolored *maṇi* jewel, possessing boundless characteristics and activities, and appearing as the various divisions within the manifestations of one’s own mind—may I and other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas be free from [these].
By thus perceiving the self-nature and the specific and general characteristics of such false imaginings, one will swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*,
causing all sentient beings to be fully endowed with and completely filled with every form of peace and happiness.
(Regarding the fourfold propositions from identity and difference up to impermanence, there are three sets. First, the fourfold proposition of identity and difference:

taken together, they are "identity," "difference," "both different and not different," and "neither different nor not different. "Both" refers to both different and not different; "not both" refers to neither different nor not different.
Regarding the fourfold proposition of existence and non-existence: "existence," "non-existence," "both existent and non-existent," and "neither existent nor..."
There is none. Regarding the fourfold set of "permanent," "impermanent," "both permanent and impermanent," and "neither permanent nor impermanent":
the scriptural text is abbreviated and does not list them in full.
The commentary states: Each of the first four phrases represents a specific tenet; all non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) sit squarely upon these views.
As for those who "do not practice," they are unable to transcend them. Only through noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) can one transcend the four extremes (*catuṣkoṭi*);

thus, one does not perceive the existence of either self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) or common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). In this way, one may ascend to the ground of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-tattva*), gradually traversing the various stages (*bhūmi*) until reaching Buddhahood.

Regarding the stage where one who has not yet developed their original vow [enters]: once one's own practice is perfected, one further enters all Buddha-fields by means of that original vow to transform all sentient beings.
This is like the manifestations of a wish-fulfilling jewel; there is nothing that is not fully revealed. Regarding "those who practice infinite marks":
"marks" refers to the characteristics of the stages, and "practice" refers to the conduct being cultivated. Although these are infinite, they are all merely...
The various differentiated characteristics of all phenomena are manifested by the mind; "parts" refers precisely to these differentiations.
From "I and those below" onwards, it concludes by requesting that the practices for fulfilling the vows of oneself and others be perfected.

The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Ignorant and deluded ordinary people, not understanding the measure of the mind (cittamātra), grasp at internal and external natures. Relying on [the concepts of] identity, difference, both, or neither;

existence, non-existence, or neither existence nor non-existence; permanence, or impermanence—driven by the causes of their own inherent nature and habitual tendencies—they become attached through false conceptualization."

(Second is the habitual cause of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-vāsanā-hetu*). It arises through being perfumed by past habits. Below, there are twelve similes concerning false conceptualizations and deluded views;

each has its respective *dharma* [the principle], *dṛṣṭānta* [the simile], and *upanaya* [the application]. There are differences and similarities among them, which should be identified according to the specific text).

The commentary states: Generally speaking, there are two types of discourse regarding the Dharma. First, not knowing that [the world] is the manifestation of one's own mind, one perceives external phenomena within the five aggregates and internal [consciousness].

One calculates the nature of the internal and external; regarding common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), one gives rise to the view of identity; regarding specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), one gives rise to the view of difference;
based on these two intervals, one gives rise to the view of both; and apart from these two intervals, one gives rise to the view of neither. There are...
"Impermanent, impermanent"—all things are thus.
It is like a herd of deer, driven by thirst, who see a springtime mirage and perceive it as water; deluded and frantic, they rush toward it, unaware that it is not water.
In this same way, foolish people are perfumed by beginningless false conceptualizations and burned by the three poisons.

The mind delights in the objective realm of forms and perceives their arising, abiding, and ceasing. It grasps at internal and external natures, falling into the conceptualizations of oneness or difference, both or neither, existence or non-existence, being or non-being, and permanence or impermanence; thus it is ensnared by false views.

(Once fallen into the obstacle of karma, one enters the realms of suffering). (Just as a deer pursued by [a mirage] does not know that the flames are not water, the foolish person who delights in desire does not know that pleasure is the cause of suffering.
To speak of "the perfuming of false conceptualization" is precisely the meaning of the habitual cause of self-nature.
The grasping of internal and external natures, etc., refers exactly to the arising of views).

It is like a city of the gandharvas: those who are foolish and ignorant conceive the notion of a city; through the habitual tendencies of beginningless time, the appearance of signs manifests due to their clinging.
That city neither exists nor does not exist. In the same way, the heterodox teachers [conceive their views] through the clinging to the false habitual tendencies of beginningless time.

Based on views of identity and difference, bothness and not-bothness, existence and non-existence, and neither-existence-nor-non-existence, as well as the views of permanence and impermanence, one is unable to understand that these are merely the manifestations of one’s own mind.
(This illustrates how non-Buddhists fail to realize that all is the manifestation of one’s own mind, giving rise to views of identity and difference. (The City of Gandharvas...)
There are no cities or seeds; it is only people of little wisdom who, perfumed by false habituation, conceive the notion of cities.

For example, Mahāmati, suppose a person dreams of men, women, elephants, horses, chariots, infantry, cities, towns, gardens, groves, mountains, rivers, bathing pools, and various other adornments, and enters into them.
Upon waking, they recall these things. Mahāmati, what do you think? Is this so?
"O Great Wisdom, would a man who does not let go of the memory of a dream he previously had be considered wise? In the same way, ordinary people are bitten by evil views;
they do not understand through their wisdom that external objects are of the nature of being manifestations of one's own mind, like a dream.
They rely on views of oneness and difference, bothness and neitherness, existence and non-existence, and the views of permanence and impermanence."
(The objects seen in a dream are fundamentally not real things, yet one continues to recollect them without letting go; what is this if not delusion?
This serves as a metaphor for the false calculations of non-Buddhists, who fail to understand that all is mind-only and thus give rise to various views.)
For example, a fire-wheel is not a wheel, yet the foolish perceive it as a wheel; it is not so for the wise.

In this same way, the evil views and aspirations of the non-Buddhists—based on notions of identity, difference, both, neither, existence, non-existence, neither-existence-nor-non-existence, permanence, and impermanence—give rise to the notion that all natures are produced.
(This metaphor illustrates how those of external paths take objects with a distorted mind, perceiving what does not exist as existing, and giving rise to various views.
