Only upon reaching the ultimate fruit can [afflictions] be completely severed. To realize and penetrate in this manner is called the awakening and knowledge of a Buddha.
Although the two vehicles are minor, if they can turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle and awaken as the Buddha does, they are simply Buddhas;
therefore, they are also called Buddhas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati again requested of the World-Honored One:

"I pray that you will explain for me the characteristics of existence and non-existence regarding all phenomena, so that I and other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas may depart from the characteristics of existence and non-existence and swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "In this world, there are two kinds of dependence, namely, dependence on existence..."
Furthermore, regarding the nature of non-falling and the absence of intrinsic nature: one who desires to see [reality] does not depart from the characteristic of detachment.

(The ultimate principle is quiescent and transcendent; it is neither existent nor non-existent. Sentient beings are deluded by this and fall into the two extremes, unable to return to their original state.)
Therefore, Mahāmati raised questions on behalf of the assembly. The Buddha first answered in accordance with the questions, and subsequently subtly explained their meaning. The commentary states:

"Relying on two kinds [of views]" refers to worldly sentient beings who, relying on the objects of existence and non-existence, give rise to the views of existence and non-existence, falling into the extremes of being and non-being;

this is precisely the view of existence and non-existence. "Desiring to see" means to take pleasure in and become attached to these views. It is not... [the rest of the sentence is incomplete in the source].
Regarding the dharma of renunciation (*niḥsaraṇa*): because one falsely claims it to be renunciation, it is said that "one does not depart from the characteristic of departure.
Mahāmati, what is meant by the world depending on existence? It means that the world arises from causes and conditions;
it is not that it exists without [causes], nor does it arise from non-existence. Mahāmati, those who speak in such a manner are asserting that the world is without cause. Mahāmati!

What is meant by "the world relies on non-existence"? It means that after one has experienced the nature of greed, anger, and delusion, one subsequently engages in false conceptualization and attachment regarding whether the nature of greed, anger, and delusion exists or does not exist.
Mahāmati, if one does not grasp at the existence of a nature, then the characteristics of that nature are quiescent;
therefore, the Tathāgatas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas do not grasp at the nature of greed, anger, and delusion as being either existent or non-existent.
(This is the response to Mahāmati’s question regarding the characteristics of existence and non-existence, and to whom those characteristics of existence and non-existence belong.

(The section beginning with "Depending on existence" below explains the characteristic of existence; the section beginning with "Depending on non-existence" below explains the characteristic of non-existence.)

The commentary states: What is meant by "relying on existence"? It refers to the view that there truly exist causes and conditions for the world, from which all phenomena arise, rather than arising from what is not truly existent.
To say they "truly arise from existence" means that the productive causes and conditions are real; this is said because they conceive of non-existence as being existence.
Furthermore, it is stated that those who speak in such a manner are the causeless heretics (*tīrthika*).

This is a treatise. What is meant by "relying on non-existence"? It means that after first accepting the nature of the three poisons, one subsequently falsely discriminates that their nature is not a nature;
this "non-nature" is then falsely discriminated as being non-existent. If one did not falsely accept the three poisons as having a nature, [this error would not arise].
Thus, there is nothing to be grasped. When there is no grasping, the nature and characteristics are primordially quiescent. This is like the Buddha’s One Vehicle:
by not grasping the nature of the three poisons, one departs from the views of existence and non-existence.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, we pray that you will explain the characteristics of unreal imagination (*abhūta-parikalpa*).
How does unreal imagination arise? What kind of phenomena are called unreal imagination?
Within what kind of phenomena does unreal imagination occur? The Buddha told Mahāmati: "There are various meanings and various unreal imaginings. One calculates..."

Attachment gives rise to false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), Mahāmati. Through attachment to the grasped and the grasper, one fails to understand that all is a manifestation of one's own mind (*svacittadṛśyamātra*).

Falling into the views of existence and non-existence, one increases the views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), giving rise to the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of perception. By clinging to various external objects, the false conceptualizations of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta-vikalpa*) arise, leading to attachment to "self" and "what belongs to self."
(Mahāmati’s questions were threefold: first, he asked how delusive discrimination arises; second, he asked what dharma is called delusive discrimination;
and third, he asked from what cause delusive discrimination originates. Therefore, the Buddha answered them in detail.)
The commentary states: Regarding the meaning of "various" (*vividha*): all external phenomena possess various characteristics and meanings, yet these are entirely false and illusory.
Because they give rise to deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*), it is said that "various unreal deluded thoughts and attachments arise.

Next, the answer regarding "attachment to the grasped and the grasper" (*grāhya-grāhaka-abhiniveśa*) means attachment to the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*), failing to realize that these are merely manifestations of one's own mind, as well as [attachment to]...
Falling outside of the mind, one lapses into views of existence and non-existence; based upon these, the various views of the externalists increase.

All are phenomena of false imagination (*vikalpa*). To know those phenomena is to know why they are false. Later, when it speaks of "the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of false imagination," this refers precisely to what was mentioned above as the basis [of those views].

Furthermore, it says: "That which arises from the mental attachment (*abhiniveśa*) of the mind and its mental factors (*caitta*) through the false imagination of 'self' and 'what belongs to self' (*ātma-ātmīya*)."
That is to say, the two selves of person and phenomena are their locus. Once one knows that their source is not real, delusion is immediately extinguished.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "If various meanings and various unreal conceptualizations give rise to the attachment of conceptualization..."

Attached to the grasped and the grasper, they do not understand that these are merely manifestations of their own minds. Falling into the views of existence and non-existence, they increase the views of the non-Buddhists.

Through the attachment to various external objects arising from the habitual tendencies of false imagination, there arises the false imagination of the mind and mental factors, along with attachment to "I" and "mine.
If one thus falls into the characteristics of existence and non-existence regarding these various external objects, one must abandon both being and non-being, as well as all views.

The characteristic [of the object] is thus; the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is also like this. It is free from the characteristics of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), sense organs (*indriya*), parts (*avayava*), analogies (*dṛṣṭānta*), and reasons (*hetu*).

Why is it that in one place, false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) regarding unreal objects arises through attachment to various natures, whereas in another place, conceptualization does not arise regarding the characteristics of the ultimate truth?
Is this not a discourse on fallacious reasoning (*hetuvāda*), which speaks of one thing arising and another not arising?
Mahāmati asked: "If it is as you say, then regarding the various external objects, one would fall into the characteristics of existence and non-existence;

yet these [objects] are also by nature free from existence and non-existence, and free from the characteristics of all views. Furthermore, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is also free from the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) associated with the sense faculties, as well as from the characteristics of propositions, reasons, and examples.
Since the various external objects and the ultimate truth are thus no different, for what reason do you speak of 'various' [objects]?"

[One] gives rise to discrimination regarding conventional meaning (*saṃvṛti*), but does not give rise to discrimination regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Is it not the case, then, that what the Blessed One has said contradicts reason—namely, that there is both arising and non-arising?

The Buddha told Mahāmati: "It is not that false imagination (*parikalpita*) arises in one way and does not arise in another. Why is this? Because [the notion of] existence and non-existence is a false imagination."
Because thought does not arise, external appearances—whether existent or non-existent—are seen as the mere manifestation of one’s own mind; thus, false discrimination does not arise.

Mahāmati, I say that for other ignorant people, various signs of their own mental false discriminations appear before them, and through attachment to the nature and characteristics of these various false discriminations, activity arises.
How can ignorant people become free from the views of attachment to "I" and "mine," and how can they be freed from [the cycle of] action?

Having transcended the faults of causal conditions and awakened to the fact that [the world] is merely the measure of one’s own mind of delusive thought (*svavikalpa-cittamātra*), there occurs a transformation of body and mind.
One ultimately attains clear understanding of all stages (*bhūmi*) and the realm of the Tathāgata’s self-realization.

Being free from the delusive thoughts of views regarding the five dharmas, the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), and the categories of phenomena (*vastu*), for this reason I say that delusive thought arises from attachment to various unreal objects. By knowing the reality as it truly is, one attains liberation.
Liberation from the various delusive imaginings of one’s own mind.
(This was stated in response to Mahāmati’s question, [showing that] it is not a false discrimination.
(This section explains that fools are unable to realize [the truth]; how, then, can they attain liberation and bring their delusive imaginings to rest?)

The commentary states: As for why conceptualization arises or does not arise, it means that when one realizes that the external phenomena perceived through the delusion of existence and non-existence are devoid of intrinsic nature, and understands that they are merely manifestations of the mind, such conceptualization does not arise. It is not that there is some separate ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
Rather, it is simply because foolish people do not understand that these are manifestations of their own minds that they perceive the activities of conditioned phenomena as existing externally.

Previously, within that [state], one merely gives rise to various conceptualizations and false imaginings; there is no separate conventional reality (saṃvṛti-satya). Subsequently, the Buddha further reflected:
"How can these deluded fools, remaining in confusion, be able to abandon the two selves of persons and phenomena, as well as the faults of the causal conditions of agent and action?
He further reflected: "How can they awaken to the fact that all false imaginings are merely the measure of their own minds? And so forth.
One attains the transformation of body and mind, ultimately realizing and clearly understanding the stage of all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*).

Reaching the realm of the Tathāgata’s self-realization, one leaves behind the five dharmas and the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). Seeing that phenomena are merely conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), one sees that names and marks (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*) are themselves conceptual construction. Seeing them as conceptual construction, they are seen as such.
Having formed this thought, I therefore say that false conceptualization arises from various kinds of deluded attachments.
One who knows the meaning as it truly is—that is, one who can thus understand the meaning as it truly is—attains liberation.
This is to still all deluded thoughts.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "Various causes and conditions give rise to this world;
Deluded thoughts cling to the four extremes, Yet they do not know the penetration I have attained. The world does not arise through birth, nor does it..."

It is not non-arising; it does not arise from existence or non-existence, nor is it other than existence and non-existence. How can the various causes and conditions be the deluded imaginings of the ignorant?
It is neither existent nor non-existent, nor is it both existent and non-existent. By observing the world in this way, the mind is transformed and attains selflessness.
All natures are unarisen because they arise from conditions; all that is produced by conditions is merely a product.
It does not arise from itself. A thing does not produce itself, because there would be the fault of two things existing, or because there would be the fault of no two things existing.
No intrinsic nature can be apprehended.
(This verse summarizes the aforementioned causes and conditions. (Whatever phenomena are produced, if they have a cause, they must necessarily...)

[The term] "fruit" [is used here]. Just as the causal karma produces the fruit of birth and death, if one traces its cause back to its origin and finds that it is not produced, how could the fruit itself produce a fruit?
(Commentary states: All causes and conditions—that is, all worldly phenomena—without exception arise from causes and conditions.)

As for those who give rise to false conceptualization: they cling to views of the four extremes, such as existence and non-existence, regarding the nature of dependent origination, and thus fail to understand the principle realized by the Tathāgata.
Regarding the passage "the world is not existent," it refers to being free from the four extremes of inherent nature;

that is to say, all phenomena are fundamentally devoid of the four natures. Furthermore, it states that causes, conditions, and so forth—this continues to address the previous error, asserting that all...
The Dharma is fundamentally empty. Why do deluded beings give rise to false conceptualizations within it?

Not only is there no grasping at the nature of the four propositions of existence and non-existence, but there is also no grasping at the characteristics of the four propositions of neither existence nor non-existence. This is fully explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* regarding the two kinds of emptiness:

the emptiness of nature (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*). If one can observe in this way, one will transform those two attachments to nature and characteristics and attain the [Dharmakāya].
The Dharma is the wisdom of the two kinds of selflessness. However, its nature is truly non-arising; it exists only by virtue of conditions.

Since all these phenomena arise from conditions, they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Furthermore, regarding the statement that "a phenomenon does not produce itself," "phenomenon" refers here to the effect.

If a fruit were to arise spontaneously without a cause, there would be the fault of these two [contradictory] states. Thus, one naturally transcends the clinging to the nature of existence and non-existence;
therefore, it is said that no nature can be apprehended.
When observing all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), they are free from the grasper and the grasped; this mindless measure of mind (*cittamātra*) is what I call "mind-only" (*cittamātra*).
"Measurement (pramāṇa) is the locus of self-nature; it is free from both conditions and nature. Its nature is ultimately wondrously pure; I call this the 'measure of mind' (cittamātra).
(This follows the preceding discussion on awakening to the measure of the deluded mind, revealing the realm of the Tathāgata. Regarding the mention of 'conditions and nature':
'conditions' refers to the subjective perceiver, and 'nature' refers to the objective phenomena perceived.)"

The commentary states: These eight lines briefly summarize the "measure of mind" (*cittamātra*). If one does not realize that all phenomena are merely mind, then there will be objective realms of perception.

When these are examined with correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*), they are found to be separate from the perceiving mind. Since the perceived object is thus separated from the perceiver and the perceived, the non-conceptualizing mind remains;
this is what is meant by "merely mind. Therefore, it is said: "I declare this to be the measure of mind."

Although one may realize that all phenomena are mind-only, one still maintains attachment to their inherent nature; thus, one is unable to forget the thought of a perceiving subject when facing objects.
One must directly transcend both objects and their inherent nature before this can be considered the ultimate measure of the Tathāgatagarbha-mind.
The self is a conventional designation; it has no substantial reality. The aggregates are likewise designated as "aggregates," yet they too lack substantial reality.

There are four kinds of equality: equality of characteristics, equality of causal nature, equality of arising, and thirdly, equality of selflessness; fourthly, equality of cultivation and the cultivator.
(The "self" of conventional truth refers to the grasping at a person; the "aggregates" of the aggregates refer to the grasping at phenomena). The commentary states:
Regarding the two graspings of self and phenomena, if one seeks them through their specific and general characteristics, no real entity can be found. Thus, all phenomena are equal.
Characteristics must have causes, and the nature of the cause is equal to the nature of the effect. Because both cause and effect are fully present, [phenomena] exist.
The self is, in fact, equal to non-self. One who can thoroughly understand non-self practices that which is conditioned as being equal to non-practice.
When the habitual tendencies of false conceptualization revolve, various states of mind arise, and objects manifest externally; this is the conventional measure of the mind.
External appearances are not real; the mind perceives them in various ways. The construction of bodies and possessions—I declare these to be the measure of mind (cittamātra).
[Free from all doubts and not clinging to the view of emptiness, one cannot be deluded by non-Buddhists.]
The commentary states: Regarding "delusive thoughts" and so forth, due to the perfuming of beginningless delusive thoughts, various forms of mind-consciousness arise in succession.
Once the deluded mind has been produced, one perceives external objects; this is the conventional measure of mind (*citta-mātra*). However, external objects fundamentally do not exist;
they are perceived as various appearances because the mind grasps them. These very appearances—such as the five sense-objects—are what establish the body and its possessions.
That which is called the wealth of the five bodies of consciousness is precisely the measure of the mind of false discrimination.
Free from all views, and free from both the perceiving thought and the perceived object, where there is neither attainment nor arising—this I call the measure of the mind.
Neither existence nor non-existence; existence and non-existence are both transcended. That which is called the liberation of the mind—I declare this to be the Mind-only (cittamātra).
Suchness, the limit of emptiness, nirvāṇa, and the dharma-realm, as well as the various types of mind-made bodies—I declare these to be the Mind-only.

(By departing from the preceding names, marks, and conceptualizations, one reaches right gnosis; through the ultimate *tathatā* and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), one abides within the *dharmadhātu* of nirvāṇa.
Thus, one is able to manifest various kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomayakāya*) to deliver sentient beings.
This is the Tathāgata’s first-principle mind, which is the measure of the mind.)

The commentary states: The first four lines mean that by abandoning the views of the two selves—person and phenomena—and by abandoning both the subject of cognition and the object of cognition, there is neither attainment nor arising;
this is the mental measure (*citta-mātra*) of right wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*).

The middle four lines mean that by abandoning the attachment to the nature of existence and non-existence, as well as the mind that abandons them, this is likewise the mental measure of right wisdom, which is neither a nature nor non-nature.
There is. That which is not non-nature is not non-existence; nature and non-nature are existence and non-existence. Regarding the latter four phrases:

"Suchness" (tathatā) is identical to "True Suchness" (bhūtatathatā); "the limit of emptiness" (śūnyatākoṭi) is identical to "the reality-limit" (bhūtakoṭi); "nirvāṇa" is identical to "ultimate great nirvāṇa";
and "dharma-realm" (dharmadhātu) is identical to "the Buddha-dharma-realm. These are all one essence with different names.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has taught, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should be skilled in words and meanings.
What is meant by a bodhisattva being skilled in words and meanings? What are words? What are meanings? The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"When one contemplates words and meanings, they are neither different nor not different. When one contemplates meanings and words, it is likewise."
Thus it is. If words were different from their meanings, one would not discern meaning by means of words; rather, one would enter into the meaning through the words, just as a lamp illuminates forms.

(Words are the expressive verbal teachings themselves, while meaning is the principle expressed. This means that by thoroughly understanding the expressive [words], one immediately attains the expressed.)
"Explanation: [This refers to] well-understanding that which is explained (i.e., realizing the signifier).
The commentary states: Speaking in terms of the Mahāyāna, although there is that which speaks and that which is spoken, the signifier and the signified are non-dual;
therefore, it is said they are neither different nor not different. Although the meaning transcends words, there is no way to discern the meaning without words; thus, one must rely on them."

To speak so as to enter into the meaning is like a lamp illuminating forms. For example, it is like a person holding a lamp to illuminate an object, thereby knowing that this object is such and exists in such a place.
That which is called the nature of words being devoid of self-nature is itself liberation;
this is what is meant by "excellent speech and excellent meaning."

Mahāmati, regarding non-arising, non-ceasing, intrinsic nature, nirvāṇa, the three vehicles, the one vehicle, the mind, and self-nature—if one becomes attached to the meanings of these as they are expressed through words, one falls into the views of superimposition and denial.
This is a false conceptualization that constructs something different from what is actually established;

it is like various manifestations of false conceptualization that appear like illusions. Just as with various illusions, foolish ordinary beings construct false conceptualizations of them as being different, whereas the noble ones do not.
"Worthy one.
(This section speaks of the fault of conceptual attachment to words. The commentary states:
"To establish difference based on difference through false discrimination" means that one gives rise to [discrimination] by establishing distinctions based on verbal expressions.
It is the attachment to false conceptualization, like seeing a magical illusion and reckoning it to be real; this is the vision of the foolish, not that of the noble ones.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are three kinds of knowledge: namely, knowing arising and ceasing, knowing specific and general characteristics, and knowing the non-arising and non-ceasing.
Cessation. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the characteristic of non-obstruction is wisdom (*jñāna*); the various obstructed characteristics of objects are consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Mahāmati, the characteristic of skillful means arising from the conjunction of the three factors is consciousness; the characteristic of the self-nature of skillful means devoid of objects is wisdom.

Mahāmati, the characteristic of attainment is consciousness; the characteristic of non-attainment is wisdom. Because one’s own realization of the realm of noble wisdom neither emerges nor enters, it is like [space].
The moon in the water.
(To know arising and ceasing is the knowledge of all things (*sarvajñatā*). To know specific and general characteristics is the knowledge of the paths and their varieties (*mārgajñatā*).
To know non-arising and non-ceasing is the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).)

The commentary states: There is but a single Buddha-wisdom, yet it possesses three functions, which are termed the "three wisdoms. It is further said that the characteristic of non-obstruction is wisdom;
this means that within the aforementioned three wisdoms, they are unified and merged within a single mind, free from the characteristics of defilement and obstruction—this is wisdom.

Conversely, that which is otherwise is called consciousness (*vijñāna*). It is also said that the "three things are equal"; these three things refer to the objects (*viṣaya*), the sense organs (*indriya*), and...
The self [is such that] when these three factors come together and correspond, this consciousness arises.

Because it does not know its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*), if one were to know this nature, then the numinous awareness of a single thought-moment would not depend on arising; therefore, it is said: "The expedient means of non-action, the intrinsic nature and characteristics, is wisdom.

Furthermore, it is said: "To obtain characteristics and yet not obtain characteristics is wisdom, while [merely obtaining] characteristics is consciousness. Here, "characteristics" refers to the intrinsic nature and characteristics (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*).
Their characteristics are essentially one and the same, yet there is a distinction between being detached from them and not being detached; hence the terms "attained" and "not attained.
That which is "self-attained" refers to the realm of the Tathāgata’s own realized noble wisdom, which cannot be described by names or forms;
thus it is said that it neither emerges nor enters, like the moon reflected in water.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses: "The accumulation of karma constitutes consciousness; non-accumulation constitutes wisdom (*jñāna*).
By observing all phenomena and penetrating their non-existence, one attains the power of mastery;
this is what is called insight (*prajñā*). Binding to objects constitutes the mind (*citta*); the arising of conceptualization constitutes wisdom. Regarding non-existence and the supreme, insight..."
From this, it arises.
(One does not fall into inert emptiness nor cling to heterodox views; maintaining only the single mind, which is profoundly still and constantly illuminating, the light of wisdom is born.)

The commentary states: "To 'gather' means to collect; to 'assemble' means to summon together. By means of the sense faculties confronting their objects, grasping and attachment arise, giving rise to wholesome and unwholesome karma and summoning the cycle of birth and death;

this is what is called consciousness (*vijñāna*). Observing in this way that phenomena born of causes and conditions are empty in their very essence, one attains liberation and mastery—this is called the supreme wisdom (*uttara-uttara-jñāna*). Here, *hui* (wisdom) is synonymous with *zhi* (knowledge). Outside of the mind, there is nothing."
When one does not realize that objects are merely mind and is instead driven by those objects, this is called bondage. "Mind" here refers to consciousness (*vijñāna*).
To awaken to this deluded mind is wisdom.
Mind, mentation, and consciousness—far removed from conceptualization and perception—one attains the state of non-conceptual dharma. Such a one is a Son of the Buddha, not a Śrāvaka.
Through the supreme progress of tranquil patience, the Tathāgata’s pure wisdom arises within the excellent ultimate truth; all that is practiced is utterly transcended.

(The first phrase refers to consciousness (*vijñāna*). The second phrase refers to wisdom (*jñāna*). The third phrase refers to the transformation of consciousness into wisdom. The fourth phrase refers to the beginning of wisdom.
The fifth phrase refers to the Tathāgata’s wisdom of the patience of cessation (*śānti-akṣānti-jñāna*), which is the culmination of wisdom.)
The commentary states: Pure wisdom arises from the most excellent ultimate truth (*paramārtha*); therefore, it is entirely free from the spheres of activity [of conceptualization].
I possess three kinds of wisdom that reveal the reality of the noble ones (*ārya*). Within those perceptions and reflections, they fully comprehend all natures.
It is not associated with the two vehicles; wisdom is detached from all that exists. Clinging to intrinsic nature arises from the śrāvakas;
transcending all mental measures, the Tathāgata’s wisdom is pure.
(Third, the arising of the objects of knowledge. Because these are what the Tathāgata has revealed, all phenomena—the objects of knowledge that arise and perish—are collectively and entirely real.
This is what is meant by "the two wisdoms are one mind.")
The commentary states: "Regarding 'contemplating that' and so forth, the previous two types of wisdom are reiterated here to manifest the progressively superior wisdom.
This means that ordinary beings undergo various births and deaths due to their deluded conceptualizations; the Two Vehicles are the opposite of this, and thus [their wisdom] is not in accord."
To be free from all that exists, yet still to cling to intrinsic nature, is merely the wisdom of the two vehicles.
If the Tathāgata’s ultimate wisdom is pure, it transcends all mental objects.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are nine kinds of theories of transformation among the non-Buddhists, from which the views of transformation among the non-Buddhists arise.

They are: transformation of form and place, transformation of characteristics, transformation of cause, transformation of accomplishment, transformation of view, transformation of nature, transformation of the clarity of conditions, transformation of the clarity of what is produced, and transformation of things. Mahāmati, these are called the nine kinds of transformation.
Manifestation through transformation. Based on this, all non-Buddhists give rise to theories of existence and non-existence, and of birth and transformation.

What is meant by "transformation of form and location"? It refers to the visible change in form and location; for example, when gold is transformed into various vessels, diverse forms and locations become manifest, yet the nature of the gold does not change.
The transformation of all natures is likewise. Or there are non-Buddhists who assert as follows:
These are false imaginings, even up to the false imagining of the transformation of things; for they are neither identical nor different from false imaginings.

(This refers to the ninefold theory of transformation falsely conceptualized by these non-Buddhists—namely, that which is formed through causes such as shape—which does not transcend the dharmas of the four great elements and the five [sciences].
Because they perceive the distinct characteristics of arising and ceasing, they conceive of transformation. However, according to the True Teaching:)

It is said that [all things] arise through conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*); it is said they are like illusions; it is said they are manifestations of one's own mind; external natures have no inherent existence; they are neither changing nor unchanging, and so forth.
Yet, these have never been definitively declared as being either heterodox or orthodox, or as gain or loss—this is how they are distinguished.

The commentary states: "Form" (*rūpa*) refers to the physical body. "Characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing. "Cause" (*hetu*) refers to the cause that produces. "Accomplishment" (*siddhi*) refers to the fruit that is accomplished.
"Appearance" (*darśana*) refers to shifting according to objects. "Nature" (*svabhāva*) refers to that which is born again and again without changing.

"Conditions" (*pratyaya*) refers to transformation and cessation due to causes and conditions. "Action" (*kriyā*) refers to conditioned activity that is not permanent. "Phenomenon" (*vastu*) refers to conditioned dharmas. These constitute the nine.

Regarding the statement that "arising from causes" refers to existence or non-existence: this means either the non-existence of what previously existed, or the existence of what was previously non-existent;

these are all modes of transformation (*pariṇāma*) and do not transcend existence and non-existence. The following section provides an analysis and explanation. As for "transformation of form and location": [text continues].
This refers to the locations of the four great elements, the sense organs, and physical forms.

One perceives these forms changing according to time and thus speaks of "transformation," yet one does not realize that their nature has never changed. It is like gold being fashioned into various vessels;
although the vessels have diverse differences, the nature of the gold remains unchanged. Furthermore, when it is said that "the transformation of all natures is likewise," this "nature" is—
This is the Dharma. To say that although all phenomena undergo transformation, their nature does not change, is likewise so.

Or, when there are non-Buddhists and others, one refutes them by stating that they are neither identical nor different; this means that regarding what is not identical [to the ultimate], those [non-Buddhists]— [...are thus refuted.]
Mahāmati spoke again to the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the Blessed One has taught, one imagines various natures through various imaginings;
yet those intrinsic natures do not exist, for they are merely the nature of imagination itself.

If it is only the nature of imagination and there is no mutual dependence between nature and intrinsic nature, would this not entail the fault of asserting that both affliction and purification are without intrinsic nature? [End of excerpt]
Because the self-nature of dharmas is a false conceptualization and lacks intrinsic reality.
(This explains the intent behind the Tathāgata’s teaching on various conceptualizations, posed as a question.
Commentary: "Those various" refers precisely to those various conceptualizations. However, all dharmas fundamentally lack any real nature.
"It is merely a false fabrication. Yet Mahāmati still harbors doubt, thinking:

"If this is merely the nature of false imagination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and not that phenomena possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then regarding this 'intrinsic nature' and its counterpart 'lack of intrinsic nature,' is it not the case, as the World-Honored One has taught, that all defiled and pure phenomena are devoid of any real nature?
Mahāmati’s intention is based on the fact that all phenomena lack...
Regarding intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*): it is difficult to establish that there is an intrinsic nature in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "So it is, so it is; it is just as you have said. Mahāmati, it is not as the intrinsic nature of things is imagined by foolish people to be real.
This imagined intrinsic nature does not possess the characteristics of an existing intrinsic nature."
(That is to say, all phenomena lack intrinsic nature; this is a false conceptualization.

To have an intrinsic nature would be incorrect. The commentary states: "Not as with the foolish" means that it is not like those ordinary worldlings who take the false conceptualization of an inherent nature to be real.
Furthermore, it says: "This false conceptualization of an inherent nature, etc. refers merely to a deluded attachment.
"There is no nature or characteristic, Mahāmati.
Just as there is a self-nature for noble wisdom—known by the noble ones, seen by the noble ones, and perceived by the noble eye of wisdom—in this way one knows that self-nature.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "If it is so that the noble ones, by means of their noble knowledge, noble vision, and noble eye of wisdom [perceive it], then it is not..."
The divine eye is not the fleshly eye; such is the knowledge of the nature of self-nature. It is not like the deluded imagination of foolish people.
World-Honored One, how do foolish people abandon this deluded imagination? Because they do not realize the reality of the noble nature.
World-Honored One, that [nature] is neither inverted nor non-inverted. Why is this? Because they do not realize the reality of the nature of the noble reality, and they do not see its transcendence.
Because they possess the characteristics of existence and non-existence.
(The previous statement that "intrinsic nature is not a nature" refers to the phenomenal aspect; this present statement that "there is the intrinsic nature of existence" reveals the principle.)

However, this reality as it truly is (yathābhūta) is not, by its very nature, the Buddha’s wisdom; even the Buddha-eye cannot perceive it. Therefore, it is said: "It is known by the noble ones (ārya) and seen by the noble ones.
The commentary states: Since the Buddha had thus revealed the realm of his own realization, Mahāmati immediately attained realization of this principle. Furthermore—
He said: "If it is indeed as the noble ones know and see—rather than as the knowledge and vision of ordinary beings—it is therefore said to be neither the divine eye nor the fleshly eye.
Thereupon, he again raised a doubt and questioned him: "Since ordinary fools cannot awaken to the reality of the noble ones' own nature, how can they be free from deluded thoughts?
How can one clarify this principle based on what is seen by the noble and the ordinary?"
They are not the same. Therefore, it is said that "those [phenomena] are neither inverted nor non-inverted.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that "ordinary beings do not perceive the nature of the sacred reality," this means that ordinary beings are not non-inverted.

Regarding the statement that "sages are not inverted because they do not see anything apart from the marks of existence and non-existence," this is because there is nothing that is not true as seen by the eyes of a sage; they do not see a single dharma [that exists apart from such reality].
This is because it is to be relinquished.

The Buddha told Mahāmati: "It is not that I teach emptiness as the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Nor do I fall into the view of existence by teaching the reality of the self-nature of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*).
Rather, it is for the sake of causing sentient beings to abandon phrases that provoke terror. Since beginningless time, sentient beings have been attached to..."
"Mahāmati, there are those who, through attachment to the characteristics of the self-nature of things and to the reality of noble wisdom, preach the doctrine of emptiness based on views.
Mahāmati, I do not speak of the characteristics of the self-nature of things. Rather, Mahāmati, I abide in the emptiness of reality as it is personally realized;

I am free from the views of the characteristics of delusive confusion, and free from the views of the existence or non-existence of things manifested by one's own mind. I am sealed by the seal of reality of the three gates of liberation regarding the nature [of things]."
One abides in self-awakened observation through the attainment of intrinsic nature, free from views regarding the characteristics of existence and non-existence (neither emptiness nor non-emptiness;
neither form nor non-form; neither non-being nor being; neither being nor non-being). From beginning to end, one remains in darkness.
(They are ultimately deluded). (Ordinary beings hear of emptiness and give rise to fear; hearing of existence, they develop attachment.
Therefore, the self-nature of noble wisdom is taught to guide them).

The commentary states: The reality of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) is certainly neither existent nor non-existent. Yet, for those who are attached to existence, the teaching of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is expounded as an antidote.
Thus we know that the teachings of emptiness and existence are both for the sake of sentient beings; never has it been said that there exists a truly real dharma. Therefore, it is said:
"I do not speak of the characteristics of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*). This indicates the dharma of self-realization (*pratyātma-vedya*), saying: "But I have attained suchness (*tathatā*)."
The reality of emptiness is the primordial, ultimate, and wondrous emptiness. It does not fall into the delusions of false inversions, but always abides in the Middle Way.

Therefore, although there are various views regarding the existence or non-existence of what is manifested by one's own mind, one immediately attains the three gates of liberation and acquires the seal of suchness.
One perceives the self-nature of phenomena, realizes the realm of the sages, and becomes free from all attachments to existence and non-existence.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should not establish the thesis that "all dharmas are unarisen. Why is this?
Because it would imply that all natures are non-natures, and because it involves the characteristic of being produced from causes;
thus, the thesis that "all dharmas are unarisen" would be undermined. As for that thesis that "all dharmas are unarisen," its very thesis is undermined.
Because that thesis arises in dependence [on something else], and because that thesis does not enter into all phenomena (*sarvadharma*), it fails to establish the non-arising of characteristics.
Thus, for one who establishes the thesis that all phenomena are unarisen, that very statement is undermined. Mahāmati, there is no such thing as a "thesis of non-arising.
That thesis enters into all natures (*bhāva*); therein, neither existence nor non-existence can be apprehended. Mahāmati, if that thesis...
Non-arising. One establishes the thesis that all natures are non-arising; thus, that thesis is undermined because the characteristics of existence and non-existence do not arise.
One should not establish a thesis, because the five-membered syllogism contains many faults, because its successive reasons have different characteristics, and because it is something produced.
One should not establish the members of the thesis, namely that "all dharmas are non-arising," and likewise that "all dharmas are empty."
In this way, all phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). One should not establish a thesis (*pakṣa*).
(Since it has been stated that both conceptual construction and noble wisdom are empty, there is nothing that is not simultaneously negated; they share the same sense of being "arisen.
Furthermore, fearing that a bodhisattva might establish this as a thesis and thereby confuse it with externalist views, he speaks thus to refute it. (The first thesis has nine parts.)

There are [the following] fallacies: contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), contradiction with authoritative scripture (*āgama*), contradiction with worldly consensus (*loka*), contradiction with inference (*anumāna*), contradiction with one's own words (*svavacana*), and those that are established by agreement (*siddhasādhana*).

Furthermore, there are fallacies regarding the subject (*dharmin*): the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) being unestablished, the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) being unestablished, and both the qualifier and the qualificand being unestablished.

Next, there are fourteen fallacies regarding the reason (*hetu*, specifically its first characteristic, *pakṣadharmatva*). Regarding the first characteristic, "being a property of the subject," there are four types of non-establishment (*asiddha*).

It is said: there are the fallacies of non-establishment for one of the two parties (*anyatarāsiddha*), non-establishment of the locus (*āśrayāsiddha*), non-establishment for both (*ubhayāsiddha*), and non-establishment due to doubt (*saṃdigdhāsiddha*).

The latter two types share ten common faults. There are also cases where the direction [of the reason] is indeterminate: namely, the case where the similar instances (*sapakṣa*) are entirely indeterminate, and the case where the dissimilar instances (*vipakṣa*) are entirely indeterminate.

The indeterminate [reason] that functions partially in both [similar and dissimilar instances], the common indeterminate, the non-common indeterminate, and the indeterminate due to contradiction with the certain—these are the four types of contradictory reasons. They are:

contradiction regarding the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the property (*dharma*), contradiction regarding the specific qualification (*viśeṣa*) of the property, contradiction regarding the specific characteristic of the subject (*dharmin*), and contradiction regarding the specific qualification of the subject.
Regarding the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), there are five fallacies; regarding the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), there are five fallacies. [These apply to] the similar instance.

Regarding the internal [fallacies], it says: the probandum is unestablished, the probans is unestablished, both are unestablished; there is no application (*yukti*) or inverted application (*viparyaya-yukti*); and regarding the dissimilar example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*), it says:
the probans is not contradicted, the reason (*hetu*) is not contradicted, both are not contradicted; there is no separation (*aviyoga*) or inverted separation (*viparyaya-viyoga*).
Together, these constitute thirty-three fallacies.

The commentary states: Since all dharmas are non-arising, both speech and conceptualization are utterly severed. Having already transcended verbal expression, how could one falsely establish a thesis (*pakṣa*)?

This is like those non-Buddhists who, while establishing the thesis of "non-arising," instead produce karma through their very activity. Therefore, it is said that one should not establish such a thesis.
As for the passage beginning "Why is this so?": it refers to the thesis that "all natures are non-natures. The intended meaning is that [this] is the thesis of the thesis.

It has a thesis. If you take the position that all natures are themselves non-natures, where does the meaning of your thesis reside? Generally speaking, the term "non-arising" must be established in dependence upon "arising.

Since there is a mutual dependency, then by negating arising, you negate non-arising itself; this destroys the very meaning of non-arising. Thus, it is the first reason why your thesis should not be established.
Furthermore, your thesis of non-arising must necessarily be included within all phenomena. To say "not... [is to fall into the same category].

Regarding the meaning of "arising": it pervades all phenomena within the entire world. As for the statement that "the unchanging characteristic does not arise," this means that all phenomena are fundamentally non-arising from the outset;
how could they depend upon being established? Therefore, it is said that such a position would be undermined.

This is the second point regarding why one should not establish a thesis. Regarding the statement that "existence and non-existence do not arise": previously, non-existence was taken as non-arising; now, however—
Furthermore, one turns [the analysis] to conclude that both existence and non-existence are unarisen. To say "entering all natures" (sarvabhāva): "nature" (*bhāva*) refers to dharmas.
This means that neither existence nor non-existence arises, and this also pervades all dharmas, as they are all devoid of the characteristics of existence and non-existence.

Even if one further turns [the analysis] to conclude that the nature and characteristics of existence and non-existence are both unobtainable, this too is the meaning of non-arising. Thus, one should not establish a thesis; three.
Furthermore, regarding the "fivefold discussion of many fallacies," this refers to the three fallacies concerning the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

Regarding "successive differences in the characteristics of the reason," this means that their shifting calculations result in different characteristics for the reason, leading to the fallacy of [the reason] being conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and produced (*kṛtaka*). This constitutes the fourth point of why a thesis should not be established.
Furthermore, it is said: "All phenomena are non-arisen"; it is also said: "They are empty"; and it is also said: "They lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*)."
If each of these three were to establish its own thesis, there would be many theses; thus, it is improper to establish a thesis in five ways.
Mahāmati, nevertheless, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva speaks of all phenomena as being like illusions and dreams, because they possess the characteristics of appearing and not appearing.
One should explain that all phenomena have the nature of illusions and dreams, except for the case of providing phrases to remove the fear of fools.
Mahāmati, fools fall into the views of existence and non-existence; do not cause them to become terrified and thereby abandon the Mahāyāna.
(Thus having refuted the error of establishing a formal thesis, this further clarifies its correctness to instruct [the reader]).

The commentary states: "All phenomena are like illusions or dreams; they possess the characteristics of appearing and not appearing. 'Appearing and not appearing' means they are not substantially real.

Furthermore, it is for the sake of causing sentient beings to abandon the faults of seeing, hearing, sensing, and cognizing. It also says: "It shall be explained," meaning that [the thesis] is excluded.

Regarding "for the sake of the foolish": it is because the foolish fall into the views of existence and non-existence; they do not speak of things as being like illusions or dreams, and thus cannot abandon those two views.
Furthermore, fearing that those of inferior capacity might hear that things are neither existent nor non-existent and thereby give rise to fear—refusing to accept the Mahāyāna—the precept states:
"Do not cause them to be terrified and to distance themselves from the Mahāyāna. The intent is to...
The Bodhisattva teaches the Dharma according to the capacities of sentient beings.

At that time, Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, if the various phrases, expressions, causes, and analogies used by non-Buddhists in their worldly treatises lack any self-attained realization and are merely attachments to their own affairs, then why does the World-Honored One also speak of worldly treatises for the sake of various [beings]?"
"Are the various assemblies of devas, humans, and asuras gathered from other regions not also extensively expounding immeasurable varieties of phrases and expressions?
Are they not also [engaged in] their own realizations? Do they not also fall within the category of the wisdom and discourse of all non-Buddhists? The Buddha told Mahāmati:
I recall once, while staying in a certain place, a world-theorizing brahmin came to where I was.
Without first seeking my leave for an opportunity to speak, he asked me: "Gautama, is everything created?
Is everything uncreated? Is everything eternal? Is everything impermanent? Is everything born? Is everything unborn? Is everything one?"
Is it all different? Is it all simultaneous? Is it all not simultaneous? Do all things manifest through various types of sensation?
Are all things indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)? Are all things determinate (*vyākṛta*)? Does a self exist? Does a self not exist?
Does this world exist? Does this world not exist? Does another world exist? Does another world not exist? Is there liberation? Is there no liberation?
Is it liberation? Are all things momentary? Are all things non-momentary? Is it space? Is it analytical cessation?
Is it nirvāṇa? O Gautama, is it created? Is it uncreated? Is there an intermediate state (antarābhava)? Or is there no intermediate state? O Mahāmati!
I then replied: "Brahmin, such statements as these are all merely worldly discourse (*lokāyata*); they are not what I teach. These are your worldly theories.
I teach only that the various evils—the causes of the three realms of existence (*tribhava*)—arise from the habitual tendencies of beginningless false discrimination.
Failing to realize that these are but manifestations of one's own mind, one gives rise to deluded thoughts and clings to external objects, just like [the perceptions of] an external world."
Regarding the Dharma of the Path: "The arising of the cognition of the meaning of my various faculties occurs through the conjunction of three factors.

I do not say this, O Brahmin. I do not speak of causality, nor do I speak of causelessness. I speak only of the dependent origination established by the nature of the grasped and the grasper, which arises from false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
This cannot be realized by you or others who have fallen into the grasping of the continuity of the self (*ātman*). Mahāmati, nirvāṇa, space, and cessation are not existent things.
There are three kinds; there are simply three numbers.

(The term "Brahmin" [婆羅門] means "Pure Lineage" in the language of China, also called "Pure Conduct. Their ancestors were born from the mouth of Brahmā-deva, and thus they derive from the Brahman caste.
(This demonstrates that the True Teaching does not go beyond the three paths: the path of beginningless habitual tendencies and afflictions.)

Furthermore, the various kinds of evil are the paths of karma; they are also the paths of suffering. As for "causes," this refers to afflictions and evil karma, which serve as the causes for the path of suffering.
This arises because one is unable to realize that all phenomena are manifestations of mind alone, and thus [clings] to those external phenomena.

Yet they give rise to false conceptualization and clinging to objects; this is a teaching that includes both causes and conditions, which is not something known by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Furthermore, it says:
"As for the dharma of the non-Buddhists," [the text] again cites their calculations to refute their assertions.

Regarding the statement, "Cognition arises from the conjunction of the three—the self, the faculties, and their objects"—this means that cognition arises through the harmonious union of the three conditions: the self, the faculties, and the objects. "Cognition" (*jñāna*) is precisely consciousness (*vijñāna*). Therefore...
I say that I do not speak of causes, nor do I speak of causelessness; rather, based solely upon the deluded mind, I speak of dependent origination through the grasping subject and the grasped object.
This cannot be fathomed by you or other non-Buddhists who cling to self-grasping and fail to sever it.
As for what is called nirvāṇa, space, and cessation—these three unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛta-dharma)—though they are enumerated as three, in reality they do not exist as three.
Chapter Four: The Heart of All Buddha-Speech.
Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, regarding the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha: is he a creator? Is he a non-creator?
Is he an effect? Is he a cause? Is he a characteristic? Is he that which is characterized? Is he speech? Or is he that which is spoken?”
"Is it the awakener? Is it awakening? Or is it that which is awakened to? Regarding such phrases, are they different or not different?
(Nirvāṇa is the dharma to be realized; the Tathāgata is the person who realizes it.
Having grasped the meaning of nirvāṇa, Mahāmati now asks about the Tathāgata.)
The commentary states: The three titles of the Tathāgata, Arhat, and Samyaksaṃbuddha correspond to the three virtues. "Tathāgata" is the Dharmakāya, which is the Middle Truth (madhyama-satya).
"Arhat" is liberation (vimukti), which is the Conventional Truth (saṃvṛti-satya). "Samyaksaṃbuddha" is Prajñā, which is the Ultimate Truth (paramārtha-satya).
Although there are ten general titles, these three are asked about because they are the essentials. "Making" (zuo) carries the meaning of cultivation, practice, and creative formation.

Regarding these terms: "cause" refers to the causal factor; "matter" (*vastu*) refers to the result; "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to bodily marks; "speech" (*vyavahāra*) refers to verbal expression; and "cognition" (*buddhi*) refers to conscious awareness.
This asks whether, with respect to these words and phrases, the Tathāgata is different from them or not different.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha is not caused by such terms and phrases.
Why is this? Because both positions entail faults. Mahāmati, if the Tathāgata were a conditioned thing (*bhāva*), he would be either produced or impermanent;
thus, all conditioned things would be the Tathāgata, which neither I nor the other Buddhas accept. If [he is] not..."
Regarding that which is produced: because nothing is obtained, skillful means are empty, being like a rabbit’s horn or the son of a barren woman;
for they do not exist. Mahāmati, if there were no object and no cause, it would be neither existent nor non-existent.
That which is neither existent nor non-existent transcends the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). These four propositions are worldly discourse. That which transcends the four propositions—
Thus, it does not fall into the four propositions. Because it does not fall into the four propositions, it is that which is grasped by the wise.
The meaning of the phrases of all Tathāgatas is also like this; the wise should know this.
(This answer explains the meaning of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, and the Samyaksaṃbuddha. It is neither an entity nor a cause; it is neither non-action nor non-non-action.
Regarding the statement that both [positions] entail faults: this does not merely mean that entities and causes are not effects. One should rather say "Tathā-āgata" [Come-as-such].

If it were merely an entity or a cause, one would fall into the fault of being something produced through action. If it were simply not a cause, that too would indeed entail the fault of being as described.)
"If there is a cause for an event, one falls into [the error of] non-existence.
The commentary states: "To say that the Tathāgata is such an event, etc., means that if the Tathāgata necessarily required causes and effects and so forth, he would be impermanent.
If he were impermanent, then all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) should likewise be the Tathāgata."
Come now. However, neither I nor the Buddhas wish to be the same as those [who hold such views].

If things were not produced through causes and so forth—this refers back to the previous refutation of the claim that there is no causal basis for phenomena—then if nothing were produced, nothing could be attained;
thus, wisdom and skillful means would all be rendered in vain, becoming like the horns of a rabbit or the son of a barren woman. Furthermore, it is said that there is neither phenomenon nor cause.
This means that since the Dharma-body is not a product of conditioned activity, it is free from the faults of existence and non-existence.

Being free from the faults of existence and non-existence, it transcends the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). These four propositions consist of: identity and difference; both and neither; existence and non-existence;
and being neither existent nor non-existent; as well as permanence and impermanence, and so forth. Not falling into these four propositions constitutes the meaning of the Tathāgata’s statement.
It is that which is grasped by the wise.
In this way, the Tathāgata’s liberation is neither different nor not different [from it]. Thus, the Tathāgata is designated by the name "liberation."

If the Tathāgata were different from liberation, he would be constituted by material characteristics (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*). Because he would be constituted by material characteristics, he would be impermanent.
If he were not different, then when a practitioner attains the mark, there should be no conceptual differentiation; yet practitioners perceive conceptual differentiation.
Therefore, he is neither different nor non-different.
(This refers to the Dharmakāya Tathāgata in relation to liberation.
The commentary states: That which the Tathāgata has thoroughly revealed is because one realizes that karma itself is liberation.
As for this Tathāgata being neither different from nor not different from liberation: if one were to say they are different, then liberation would [necessarily] possess form and color.

The characteristic is impermanent. If it were not different [from the dharma], then the practitioner who accords with liberation would have no distinction between cause and effect, or between person and dharma;
yet, there exists the discrimination of subject and object. Therefore, it is concluded that they are neither different nor non-different.

In this way, wisdom (*jñāna*) and its radiance (*jyotis*) are neither different nor not different. Mahāmati, that wisdom and its radiance are neither different nor not different means they are neither eternal nor impermanent;
neither an agent nor an object of action; neither conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) nor unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); neither the perceiver nor the perceived;

neither a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) nor that which is characterized (*lakṣya*); neither the aggregates (*skandha*) nor distinct from the aggregates; neither speech (*abhilāpa*) nor that which is spoken. Not...

It is neither one nor different; it is neither simultaneous nor non-simultaneous. Because it is neither one, nor different, nor simultaneous, nor non-simultaneous, it is entirely free from all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
(This refers to *prajñā* in relation to the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Wisdom is *prajñā*; "blazing" (*jvālā*) refers to the cognitive obscuration. This means that...)
If they were different, then wisdom would be separate from the obstruction; if they were not different, how could the obstruction be wisdom?
To say that they are neither different nor not different is merely an abbreviated expression.

The commentary states: That *prajñā* and the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are neither different nor not different means that they are neither one with nor distinct from the *dharmakāya* and liberation.
Therefore, it concludes by generalizing this principle, saying: "Neither permanent nor impermanent," and so forth;

these do not go beyond [the truth] that does not manifest the path of benevolence through two extremes, does not manifest the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*) through subject and object, and does not manifest through the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
To forget words, it is therefore further said that one is "beyond all measures" (*pramāṇa*).
"Measures" refers to numbers. To be beyond all measures means there is no verbal expression. Where there is no verbal expression, there is no arising. Where there is no arising, there is no ceasing.

Where there is no ceasing, there is quiescent extinction (*śānti*). Quiescent extinction is the nirvāṇa of self-nature (*svabhāva-nirvāṇa*). The nirvāṇa of self-nature is without phenomena and without causes.
When there is no object and no cause, there is no objective support (*ālambana*). When there is no objective support, one transcends all falsehood.
To transcend all falsehood is to be the Tathāgata. The Tathāgata is the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Mahāmati, this is what is called the Samyaksaṃbuddha. Mahāmati, the Samyaksaṃbuddha is free from all sense-faculties and all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
(Now, to be free from all verbal measures is simply the unborn, quiescent, and intrinsically nirvanic nature itself.
Having manifested this original nature, the text concludes its core teaching by stating: "Without affairs, without causes," and so forth; it is solely the universal body, standing utterly solitary.)
Because he does not perceive any phenomena as objects of attachment, he transcends all falsehood; thus he is named Tathāgata-Samyaksaṃbuddha.
The repetition of the title is due to the distinction between seeing, knowing, and awakening; therefore, these two names are joined together.
At that time, Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has taught, the sūtras uphold the doctrine of non-arising and non-ceasing;
yet it is also said that 'non-arising and non-ceasing' is another name for the Tathāgata.

World-Honored One, is it because of the absence of intrinsic nature that you speak of non-arising and non-ceasing, or is it indeed another name for the Tathāgata? The Buddha told Mahāmati: "I have taught all..."
“Dharmas are neither born nor extinguished; the categories of existence and non-existence do not appear.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “If all dharmas are unborn, then the apprehension of dharmas cannot be found, because all dharmas are unborn.
If there are dharmas within names, I pray that you will explain this for me. The Buddha told Mahāmati, “I say that the Tathāgata is not without nature, nor is he not [without nature].”
"Arising is non-extinction. Because it encompasses all dharmas and does not depend on conditions, it is neither arising nor extinction. Nor is it without conditions... and so forth.
(In the sutras, the terms "non-arising and non-extinction" appear most frequently; however, the intended meaning they convey varies. Therefore, Mahāmati [said]...)
(Question). The commentary states:
"The Sūtra encompasses that which is neither born nor extinguished. To "encompass" means to include its underlying principle within it.
Furthermore, it says that this is another name for the Tathāgata. Mahāmati, however, considers "neither born nor extinguished" to be the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
[The interlocutor asks: "What is the meaning? Why do you say these are synonyms? Is it that even the Tathāgata lacks intrinsic nature? The Buddha answers:
"Because 'neither arising nor ceasing' is the departure from existence and non-existence, it is said that the categories of existence and non-existence do not appear.
This single answer addresses two inquiries. Mahāmati further asks: "If 'not appearing' means 'non-arising,' and if all dharmas are non-arising, how can this be..."
The Tathāgata has various names. If these are merely different names, could there not also be the meaning of "non-arising" within those names?
Therefore, he asks again. The answer is: "It is not that they lack intrinsic nature. This means that the Tathāgata is not a non-existent thing;
nor does he grasp at non-arising and non-ceasing as a conceptual entity; nor does he speak of non-arising and non-ceasing in dependence upon the conditions of arising and ceasing.
As for the statement that "speech is not without meaning," this is the response given later.
Thus, Mahāmati, in this Sahā world, I have three hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya* names.
Fools hear all these names and each speaks of my name, yet they do not understand that these are the various epithets of me, the Tathāgata.
Mahāmati, there are sentient beings who know me as the Tathāgata; some know me as the Omniscient One (Sarvajña); some know me as the Buddha; some know me as the Savior of the World;
some know me as the Self-Awakened One; some know me as the Guide; some know me as the Universal Guide; and some know me as the One... [text continues].
Among all guides, there are those who know the Victorious One (Jina), those who know Kapila, those who know the Limit of Reality (Bhūtakoṭi),
those who know the Moon, those who know the Sun, those who know the Lord (Īśvara), those who know the Unborn, those who know the Undying, those who know Emptiness (Śūnyatā),
those who know Suchness (Tathatā), those who know the Truths (Satya), and those who know the Ultimate Reality (Bhūtakoṭi). There are...
Those who know the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), those who know nirvāṇa, those who know the eternal,
those who know equality, those who know non-duality, those who know signlessness, those who know liberation, those who know the path,
and those who know the mind-born— Mahāmati, these three hundred thousand names of the asaṃkhyeya kalpas neither increase nor decrease. This and...
All other worlds know me; I am like the moon in water, neither emerging nor entering.
(This enumerates the various names and titles of the Tathāgata. In worlds such as Sahā, there are twenty-three distinct names in total.
It begins by stating that fools hear them all and each speaks of my name, implying that each name possesses its own specific meaning. And...
If one does not understand that these are different names for me, the Tathāgata, then one will not know that their essence is one, rooted in neither arising nor ceasing.
It continues, saying: "Such as these three *asaṃkhyeya* hundreds of thousands of names. *Asaṃkhyeya* here means "innumerable time.
These are merely the traces of the Tathāgata’s manifestations after attaining the fruit; it is said that these hundreds of thousands of names neither increase nor decrease.
Regarding "diminution": it is because when one name is cited, it subsumes the names of all dharmas; thus, they do not increase with many, nor do they diminish with one person.
In this world or in other realms, all are like the name of the Buddha. As for the statement that "it is like the moon in the water, neither emerging nor entering":

the moon is a metaphor for the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body), and the water is a metaphor for the minds of sentient beings. When the minds of sentient beings are pure, the Tathāgata responds accordingly, just as the moon appears in the water.
However, while the moon is in the sky, its reflection appears in the water; the moon does not descend, hence it is said that it does not enter.
Nor does it leave the water, hence it is said that it does not emerge.
At that time, Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, there is nothing extraordinary about manifesting non-arising and non-extinction. Why is this?

All external paths also claim their causes are neither born nor extinguished. World-Honored One, you too have spoken of space, cessation not through deliberation, and the realm of nirvana as being neither born nor extinguished.
World-Honored One, the external paths speak of a cause that gives rise to all things..."
“Worldly existence: The World-Honored One has also taught that the various worlds arise conditioned by ignorance, craving, karma, and false discrimination;
these are merely differences in names for those causes and conditions. The causes and conditions of external objects are likewise.

Thus, there is no distinction between the World-Honored One’s discourse and that of the non-Buddhists regarding the nine entities—such as atoms, pradhāna, Īśvara, and Puruṣa—which are neither produced nor [ceased].”
"Extinction. The World-Honored One also teaches that all natures are neither produced nor extinguished, and that existence and non-existence cannot be apprehended.

The heterodox teachers also say that the four great elements do not perish, their self-nature is neither produced nor extinguished, and that the four great elements are eternally the four great elements, even as they circulate through the various realms of existence without abandoning their self-nature.
What the World-Honored One says is likewise so. Therefore, I say there is no [extinction]."
It is truly extraordinary. We pray that the World-Honored One will explain the reasons for this distinction and why it is superior to all other heterodox paths.
If there were no such distinction, then all heterodox teachers would not be Buddhas, since they too do not arise and do not perish.
Yet, as previously stated, it is impossible for many Buddhas to appear in a single world-system. One...
"There would have to be many Buddhas in the world, because there is no distinction [between them].

(This question consists of four parts: first, it raises an objection based on the causes of birth taught by non-Buddhists, contrasting them with the three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) taught by the Buddha.
Space is the unconditioned phenomenon of space; cessation not through deliberation is the unconditioned phenomenon of non-analytical cessation.)

Nirvāṇa is precisely the unconditioned state of analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). Second, they raise objections based on the causes of arising, challenging the Buddha’s teaching on the dependent origination of the twelve links.
Third, they raise objections based on the arising of atoms and the like, challenging the Buddha’s teaching that all natures are neither produced nor extinguished.
Regarding the nine entities: first, time; second, space; third, emptiness; fourth, atoms; fifth, the four great elements; sixth, the six [objects].
"Brahmā, the seven victorious and sublime heavens, and the eight honored ones have declared that the four great elements are difficult to master. These are all the teachings of non-Buddhists;
they are identical to what the Buddha has taught."
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "When I speak of non-arising and non-ceasing, it is not the same as the non-arising and non-ceasing of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
Why is this? Those non-Buddhists maintain that there is a self-nature (svabhāva) which attains the characteristic of non-arising and non-ceasing.

I do not fall into such categories of existence or non-existence. Mahāmati, my [teaching] is free from the categories of existence and non-existence, and free from arising and ceasing; it is neither a nature nor a lack of nature."
Just as various illusions and dreams appear, they are therefore not non-existent in nature. Why are they non-existent in nature?
It is because form lacks the characteristic of self-nature, appearing or not appearing through being grasped or not grasped. For this reason, all natures are neither existent nor non-existent;

rather, when one realizes that which is the manifestation of one’s own mind, conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) does not arise. One then dwells in peace and happiness, and worldly affairs are forever stilled.
(Although the non-Buddhists speak of non-arising and non-extinction, this is merely a conceptual discrimination that serves as the cause of birth and death.
When the Buddha speaks of non-arising and non-extinction, this is the true principle of the Middle Way; it is the meaning of non-arising).
The commentary states: The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) speak of "intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva*) and so forth; that is to say, they claim that the nature of things possesses an intrinsic nature.

For example, they assert that because the four great elements (*mahābhūta*)—characterized by solidity, moisture, heat, and motion—are eternal, their natures are neither destroyed nor dried up. Thus, they take this to be the mark of being unarisen and unchanging.
However, this is merely a result of their arduous and deluded conceptualization; although they speak of non-arising and non-ceasing, [they nonetheless maintain that] it truly exists.
Arising and ceasing; falling into existence and non-existence. The Buddha said, "I do not hold such a view.

What I teach is neither arising nor ceasing, free from existence and non-existence, arising and ceasing, as well as neither existence nor non-existence. It is like the appearance of forms in a dream or an illusion: they manifest, so it is not non-existence;
yet their essential nature cannot be apprehended, so it is not existence. To speak of form as being devoid of self-nature and characterized by grasping is like a dream."
The illusory marks of form are fundamentally not real; they appear due to the deluded conceptualizations of fools, yet in reality they do not appear.
The deluded mind grasps them, though in truth they cannot be grasped. Therefore, know that all dharmas are neither existent nor non-existent.
If one can awaken to the realization that all dharmas are but mind—that there is no object external to the mind—then deluded conceptualization will naturally cease, and one will abide in nirvāṇa.
"...is bliss. It is the eternal cessation of the affairs of birth and death.

Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, all non-Buddhists give rise to the false discrimination of impermanence. World-Honored One, you also say that 'all conditioned phenomena are impermanent;
they are dharmas subject to arising and ceasing. What is the meaning of this? Is it erroneous or is it correct?"
"How many kinds of impermanence are there?
(The previous statement that 'neither arising nor ceasing' constitutes the meaning of true permanence has not yet distinguished between the heterodox and the orthodox;
therefore, I ask again.)"

The commentary states: Regarding the names "permanent" and "impermanent," there is no difference from the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). If one does not determine right and wrong by means of the meaning [of these terms], how can the intent of this question be distinguished?
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "All non-Buddhists have seven kinds of impermanence; these do not belong to my Dharma. What are they?"
7. Regarding that, some say that having performed [an action] and then abandoning it is called impermanence; some say that the destruction of shape and location is called impermanence;
some say that form itself is impermanent; and some say that the interval during which form undergoes transformation is called impermanence.

It disintegrates spontaneously and without interval; just as the transformation of milk into curd cannot be perceived during the intermediate stage, so too impermanence destroys all natures and causes them to transform.
Some say that nature itself is impermanent; some say that both nature and non-nature are impermanent;
others say that the non-arising of all phenomena is impermanence. This enters into all phenomena.
