(Although there are seven names, they all ultimately do not transcend the two characters "form-nature" (*rūpa-dharmatā*). The seven kinds of impermanence are all externalist calculations;

their meanings will be explained below. Regarding "the impermanence of the transformation of form": this refers to the transformation of the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) produced by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), namely birth, subsistence, change, and cessation, as well as the immediate self-disintegration and so forth.
"The continuity is uninterrupted" means that it is able to cause [the continuum] to undergo transformation.)
Nevertheless, they return to extinction. Just as with the transformation of milk into curd, although it is invisible, it occurs within the nature of phenomena;
thus, all phenomena naturally undergo change and decay.
Mahāmati, as for impermanence in terms of existence and non-existence, it refers to the destruction of the specific characteristics of the four great elements and their derivatives;
the self-nature of the four great elements is unattainable and does not arise.
(Regarding "nature and lack of nature": this refers to the nature of the four great elements, all of which lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Since both the primary creators and their derivative forms all undergo transformation and decay, they are called impermanent.)
The commentary states: Regarding the intrinsic nature of the four great elements, it means that the intrinsic nature of the primary elements is fundamentally unarisen.
Since they do not even exist as unarisen, how could there be arising or ceasing? How, then, can one speak of impermanence?
That which is "non-arising impermanence" is not the impermanence of destruction. All phenomena, whether existent or non-existent, do not arise;
even when analyzed down to the subtlest atom, they cannot be perceived. This meaning of non-arising is not arising; this is called the characteristic of non-arising impermanence.
If one does not awaken to this, one falls into the view of all external paths that holds impermanence to be arising.
(As non-Buddhists do not comprehend the principle of non-arising, although they speak of non-arising, it is in reality arising;
therefore, he rebukes them, saying that arising is impermanent.)
The commentary states: "That which is non-eternal" refers to all characteristics of existence and non-existence, whether eternal or non-eternal.
As for the fundamental nature of dharmas, they are originally unarisen; even when analyzed down to the subtlest atom (*paramāṇu*), nothing whatsoever is perceived.
For this reason, it is said that there is no non-arising. This is the characteristic of the non-arising impermanence taught by the Tathāgata. If one does not understand this...
This meaning would then fall into the non-Buddhist (tīrthika) conception of the impermanence of arising.
Mahāmati, as for the impermanence of intrinsic nature, it is a conceptual construction of one’s own mind, not the true nature of permanence or impermanence. Why is this so?
This means that the self-nature of impermanence is indestructible. Mahāmati, this is the matter of the impermanence of all things being both existent and non-existent.
Apart from impermanence, there is nothing else capable of rendering the nature of all phenomena non-existent, such as a staff, a tile, or a stone might destroy various objects.
(The essence that is true, eternal, and indestructible—how could it be fully understood by ordinary beings?
The commentary states: Among all phenomena in the world, those that undergo destruction do so because they are impermanent. Impermanence pervades all phenomena;
just as a staff, a tile, or a stone can destroy other objects while their own substance remains undestroyed.

It is observed that each is not different; this nature is impermanent. There is no distinction between the agent and the acted-upon, such that one could say, "this is impermanence" and "this is the thing.
If there were no difference between the agent and the acted-upon, all natures would be eternal and devoid of causal nature. Mahāmati!
The fact that all natures are without nature has a cause; this is not something known by the ignorant and foolish.

(Regarding the phrase "all natures" below: it means that the destruction of all phenomena also truly has a cause, but this meaning is subtle and hidden, such that it cannot be understood by the ignorant and foolish.)
The commentary states: This means that all phenomena perceived before one’s eyes are no different from impermanence. How could there be a nature that differs from the thing itself?
Therefore, it is known that impermanence is the thing, and the thing is impermanence. Since this subject and object are not distinct, they ought to be of the nature of permanence.
Regarding "having no cause for its nature": this means that impermanence has no cause for the destruction of phenomena.
It does not arise from causes that are dissimilar. If it were to arise [from such], then all natures would be entirely impermanent; this would be a case of dissimilarity.

There would be no distinction between the agent and the acted-upon, yet a distinction is clearly perceived. If nature were impermanent, it would fall into the characteristic of being a causal agent of action.
If it were to fall [into that state], then all natures would not be ultimate, as all natures would fall into the characteristic of being causal agents of action.

If that were so, then that which is itself impermanent would have to be non-impermanent; because impermanence is non-impermanent, all natures would not be impermanent and would instead have to be permanent.
(This refutes the error of the non-Buddhists. [“All natures” refers here to all phenomena (*dharma*).]
The commentary states: "That which is not produced from a dissimilar cause" means that if the impermanent were without a cause, then there would be no production of distinct phenomena.
If such production did occur, then all phenomena would arise simultaneously with it, and all would be equally impermanent;
how then could there be distinct phenomena? Thus, by this examination, it is certain that impermanence must have a cause, contrary to what they [the opponents] imagine.
In that case, these phenomena and those phenomena, as agent and object, would have no distinction; yet we clearly perceive their distinct differences.

How can one falsely imagine that distinct phenomena arise without a cause? If you claim that their nature is impermanent and so forth, then by definition "nature" must ultimately be unconditioned (*akṛtaka*);
what is unconditioned is eternal. Since you say it is impermanent, you fall into the position of [admitting] existence.

To claim that all phenomena are not ultimately real is to take this as a cause, whereby one falls into the nature and characteristics of a causal agent and loses the meaning of their essential nature (*dharmatā*).
To say that "because the self is impermanent, [phenomena] should be impermanent" means that if the nature of the creator were impermanent, [then so would the created].

All phenomena produced through causes and conditions should likewise be impermanent. If their intrinsic nature is already impermanent, then those produced phenomena that are impermanent by nature should, conversely, be permanent.

If the nature [of things] were to enter into all natures as something permanent, it would necessarily fall within the three periods of time. That past form is coextensive with destruction; future form does not arise because form does not arise [in the future].
Present form is coextensive with the characteristic of destruction. Form is a specific accumulation of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

The self-nature (*svabhāva*) of the four great elements and the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) is indestructible, because it is free from being either different or non-different. [Thus it is said by] all the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
All four great elements are indestructible. All four great elements and their derived forms within the three realms of existence are subject to arising and ceasing among all that is knowable.
Apart from the four great elements and their derived forms, what nature could all non-Buddhists contemplate as impermanent?
For the four great elements are unarisen, and their intrinsic nature and characteristics are indestructible.
(The nature of the four great elements remains constant as it is. How could one conceive of them as impermanent? The commentary states:
If the nature of impermanence were pervasive throughout all phenomena, then it would belong to the transformations of the three periods of time:
past form has already perished; future [form] has not yet arisen; and present form is simultaneously perishing. Form is thus merely a differentiation of the four great elements.
Regarding form (*rūpa*), the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) that constitute it and the derivative form (*upādāya-rūpa*) they produce are such that their nature is indestructible.

Apart from these, all non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) claim that the essential nature of the four great elements is indestructible. However, within the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*), both the primary and derivative elements are characterized by arising, abiding, and ceasing.
How could there be any other nature of impermanence (*anityatā*) that exists separately and yet gives rise to material things?
Is it extinguished?

Regarding those who depart from the beginningless impermanence: it is not that there are others apart from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), for the four great elements each possess distinct characteristics and individual natures;
thus, no differentiation can be found. Since they lack differentiation, these things do not undergo further creation. Through these two skillful means, they are not produced.
One should know that this is impermanent.
(The second [type of] expedient means refers to the expedient means of creating through similarity and difference.

The commentary states: "That which is created at the beginning and then immediately abandoned is impermanent; this is not a fault of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) acting upon one another, for the primary elements are distinct from one another."
Therefore, it is not produced by its own characteristics, because there is no difference [between them]; nor is it produced collectively, because they are disjoined.
One should know that this is the impermanence of non-initial-creation.

Regarding the impermanence of the destruction of form and location: Mahāmati, this refers to the fact that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derivatives do not perish, nor do they perish when encountering their respective objects.

Mahāmati, as for "objects," even when analyzed down to the level of atoms (*paramāṇu*), they are seen to perish upon examination. As for the four great elements and the matter derived from them, when one perceives differences in form and location—such as length and shortness—they cannot be apprehended.

It is not that the four great elements themselves perish; rather, it is the manifestation of the destruction of form and location within the four great elements that falls under the category of numerical reckoning.
Treatise:
(Although their false conceptions [of it] are impermanent, the self-nature of the four great elements is indestructible).
Commentary: The non-Buddhists reckon that these primary and derivative elements are ultimately indestructible; "ultimate" (zhì) means reaching the limit, and "limit" (jí) means exhaustion.
This means that even when analyzing the process of creation down to the subtlest atoms, they still cannot be destroyed.

One merely observes the forms of destruction and decay, such as length and shortness; yet, the essential substance of the primary and derived matter remains indestructible. This, however, is merely conventional terminology.
Therefore, it is said that they fall into the Sāṃkhya school.
Regarding the statement "form is itself impermanent," this means that form is identical to impermanence; thus, it is the spatial configuration that is impermanent, not the four great elements.
If the four great elements were impermanent, they would not be conventional designations; if conventional designations lacked intrinsic nature, one would fall into the worldly doctrine (Lokāyata).
[The worldly doctrine] perceives all natures as existing through verbal expression, yet fails to see the manifestation of their own-characteristics.
(Furthermore, the statement that "conventional discourse is without intrinsic nature" summarizes the preceding error. Worldly discourse refers to the Lokāyata view of those non-Buddhist outsiders;
because they falsely perceive all phenomena as being merely conventional discourse and lacking any characteristic of intrinsic nature.)
The commentary states: "Form is impermanent" means that this refers specifically to the impermanence of shape and location, not to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

This means it does not refer to the nature of the four great elements themselves. If [one were to claim] that even the great elements are impermanent, there would be contradiction and fallacy regarding conventional discourse.
Contradiction implies they are not conventional; fallacy implies they deviate from the ultimate truth. Thus, one loses ground both ways; such views are all incorrect doctrines.

Regarding transformational impermanence: this refers to the manifestation of a different state of form (*rūpa*) that is not the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). It is like gold being fashioned into an ornament;

the ornament manifests through transformation, yet the nature of the gold is not destroyed. It is simply that the configuration of the ornament is destroyed. The same applies to the transformation of other natures and so forth.
(This refers to the fact that while a vessel is fashioned from gold, the nature of the gold itself does not change).

The commentary states: "The appearance of different forms manifests the nature [of impermanence]. 'Universal form' refers to the form produced by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). Because the substance of form undergoes transformation, its impermanent nature is manifested;
thus, what is perceived as destruction pertains to the manifest form, not to the destruction of the four great elements themselves. It is like gold being fashioned [into various objects]."

It is complete; it possesses the nature of transformation and decay, yet the essence of gold remains unchanged. To say that while impermanent phenomena perish, their inherent nature does not perish, is likewise so.
Such are the various deluded views of the eternalism of non-Buddhists. When the four great elements are consumed by fire, their specific characteristics do not [perish].
"Regarding 'burning' and 'each being destroyed by its own characteristic': the four great elements and the derived matter should be abandoned.
(This collectively refutes the seven types of impermanence held by non-Buddhists; since they are not correct [manifestations], they are called 'delusive imaginings')."
The commentary states: Fire cannot burn the intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the great elements; it merely causes them to disperse individually.

If fire were able to burn that which constitutes the primary elements and their derivatives, then all would be annihilated. To claim that the four great elements do not perish is the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*);
to claim that the four great elements disperse is the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*). All manner of false conceptualizations do not transcend these two views.

Mahāmati spoke again to the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, we pray that you will explain for us the sequential continuity of the meditative attainments (*nirodha-samāpatti*) of all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.

If one is skilled in the characteristics of this sequential continuity of the meditative attainments of cessation, I and the other bodhisattvas shall never recklessly abandon the gateway to the bliss of the meditative attainment of cessation, nor fall into the external paths of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
This is called ignorance.
(Right reception is samādhi; it refers to the meditative absorption of cessation [nirodhasamāpatti]. This absorption is entered by all three vehicles, yet their stages and depths differ.
Knowing this, one will not abandon the Great Absorption of Cessation, nor will one fall into the Lesser Right Reception.)
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the sixth stage, as well as śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the seventh stage enter meditative absorption moment by moment, which is free from the characteristics of the self-nature of all phenomena;

this is not the case for śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, who fall into the meditative absorption of cessation where the grasped and the grasper—the marks of active conceptualization—are extinguished. Therefore, the seventh..."
The stage is not a meditative attainment (samāpatti) of mindfulness; it attains the non-differentiated characteristic of all phenomena.

It does not partially attain various characteristics or natures, but rather awakens to the correct meditative attainment regarding the wholesome and unwholesome characteristics and natures of all phenomena. Therefore, in the seventh stage, there is no meditative attainment of wholesome mindfulness.
"Mahāmati, for Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage, as well as for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, the conceptualizing marks of mind (citta), thought (manas), and consciousness (vijñāna) are extinguished.
(This answer contains four points. First, by contrasting the sixth and seventh stages to clarify their relative depth:

at the sixth stage, the three vehicles equally enter the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti). Since this stage is the shallowest, the absorption attained by the Bodhisattva does not yet differ from that of the two [vehicles].)"
[This refers to] the vehicle).

The commentary states: Regarding the phrase "the Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage enter into meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in every thought-moment," this means that in every thought-moment they enter and emerge from it without interval.

They enter into the meditative absorption that is free from all characteristics of intrinsic nature and self-nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*), because they do not grasp at any characteristics of the grasper or the grasped (*grāhaka-grāhya*).
This is different from the two vehicles falling into the awakening of conditioned activity (*saṃskāra*). "Awakening of conditioned activity" refers to conditioned formations (*saṃskṛta-saṃskāra*).

One must extinguish all marks (*nimitta*) before attaining meditative concentration (*samādhi*). For this reason, the seventh stage is called "not receiving correct reception" (*asamāpatti*), meaning it is not the correct reception attained through focused attention (*manasikāra*).
It is also said that one "attains the non-differentiated nature of all dharmas" and awakens to all [dharmas].

The characteristics of the dharma-nature are without differentiation. "Not partially attained" means that those of the two vehicles do not partially attain the various characteristics and natures within their meditative concentration.
Regarding "wholesome and unwholesome": this refers to the bodhisattva reaching the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), who does not yet abide even in the wholesome, much less in unwholesome thoughts.
This is called the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) without wholesome thought. Second, regarding the seventh and eighth stages...

The ground is distinguished by its diverse characteristics, which are precisely the characteristics of the conceptualization of mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna-vikalpa-lakṣaṇa*).

There are differences in height based on whether these have been extinguished or not; upon reaching the eighth ground, the conceptualizations of the three vehicles are entirely extinguished, which distinguishes it from the seventh ground.
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas from the first stage through the seventh stage contemplate the extent of the mind, mentation, and consciousness within the triple world.
They are free from the notions of "self" and "what belongs to self. Yet, due to their own false imaginings, they fall into the various marks of external natures.

Fools are gripped by the two aspects of their own minds—the grasper and the grasped—and are directed toward ignorance, lacking awakening, and being permeated by the habitual tendencies of false conditioning from beginningless faults and evils.
(This clarifies the three vehicles. The commentary states:
From the first stage (*bhūmi*) through the seventh stage, one contemplates that all phenomena of the triple world are merely mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*).

Although they share this common contemplation, there are differences regarding the cessation or non-cessation of deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*), as well as gains and losses. One attains [the realization of] being free from "self" (*ātman*) and "what belongs to self" (*ātmīya*), and so forth.

Furthermore, it is a failure to fall into the various characteristics of external natures. Regarding the "two kinds of one's own mind," this refers to non-Buddhists who fall into the extremes of existence and non-existence, falsely conceptualizing the grasper and the grasped;
they are entirely ignorant and lack awakening, being driven by the hands of beginningless habitual tendencies of faults and evils.
“Mahāmati, regarding the nirvāṇa of Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, śrāvakas, and pratyekabuddhas at the eighth stage: the Bodhisattva is sustained by the awakening of samādhi.
Therefore, due to the bliss of the gate of samādhi, they do not enter parinirvāṇa. If they were not so sustained, the stage of the Tathāgata would not be fulfilled;
for if they were to abandon all conditioned activities for the sake of sentient beings, the lineage of the Buddhas would surely be severed. Thus spoke the Buddhas.
The World-Honored One has revealed the inconceivable and immeasurable merits of the Tathāgata;
yet the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, being led by their attachment to the bliss found within the gates of samādhi, falsely conceive the notion of nirvāṇa.
(This clarifies the eighth stage [bhūmi]. Although the three vehicles share the same nirvāṇa, there is a distinction between abiding and not abiding therein).

The commentary states: It is said that because the bodhisattva is sustained by the empowerment of the Buddhas’ power of samādhi-awakening, they do not enter parinirvāṇa within the gateways of samādhi for the sake of transforming sentient beings.
If they were not so sustained, their meritorious practices could not reach fulfillment.
It is sufficient. To reach the stage of the Tathāgata while abandoning sentient beings and failing to transform and deliver them is also to sever the lineage of the Tathāgatas.
For this reason, the Buddhas preach inconceivable merits to encourage them toward ultimate realization.

As for those of the Two Vehicles, they discipline themselves and deliver themselves alone; they become attached to the bliss of samādhi and give rise to the notion that they have attained nirvāṇa, and it is for this reason that they fail.
Mahāmati, I have established the seven stages by skillfully cultivating the characteristics of mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*);

by skillfully cultivating the grasping of "self" and "mine," as well as the selflessness of persons and phenomena, and the characteristics of arising and ceasing, and of specific and general marks; and by skillfully [cultivating] the four kinds of unhindered power, the power of certainty, the gates of samādhi, and the sequential continuity of the stages, thereby entering the dharmas of the factors of enlightenment.
(Distinguishing categories, there are differences between the wholesome and unwholesome, and between that which is extinguished and that which is not.

The commentary states: Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage skillfully cultivate the characteristics of mind, intellect, and consciousness, thoroughly understanding that the nature of consciousness is fundamentally empty, thereby eliminating false conceptualizations.

Regarding "skillfully cultivating [the absence of] self and what belongs to self," this means understanding the two attachments of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi* and *dharma-dṛṣṭi*), and embracing the two [truths].

Regarding the nature of non-self: by not falling into the self-characteristics or common characteristics of arising and ceasing, and by following the unhindered eloquence of skillful means as well as the power of the samādhi of certainty, one attains the equilibrium of concentration and wisdom.
Thereby, one gradually enters the various stages (*bhūmi*) and acquires the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*).
At that time, Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "Regarding the arising and ceasing of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, there is no self therein.
Who is it that arises? Who is it that ceases? Fools rely upon this arising and ceasing; they do not awaken to the exhaustion of suffering and do not recognize nirvana."
(Regarding the dharmas of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, there is a distinction between delusion and liberation;
therefore, he asks again. The commentary states: The arising and ceasing of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases were discussed previously.

Yet Mahāmati requests further instruction because he intends to show that among the dharmas of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases there is both delusion and liberation. Through liberation, there is no self therein; who, then, undergoes arising and ceasing?
Because they are deluded, fools rely upon birth and death; they do not perceive the exhaustion of suffering and do not recognize *nirvāṇa*.
How, then, can it be said that they have transcended birth and death?
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "The Tathāgata-garbha is the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome; it is capable of universally producing all realms of existence."

Birth is like a performer manifesting various realms of existence while remaining devoid of "I" and "mine. Because one does not perceive this, birth occurs through the skillful means of the conjunction of three conditions.
Outsiders, failing to perceive this, falsely impute a creator; being perfumed by beginningless, false, and evil habitual tendencies, this is called the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness).
It gives rise to the ground where ignorance dwells and coexists with the seven consciousnesses, like the waves upon the ocean, its nature being constant.
Birth is uninterrupted; it is free from the fault of impermanence and free from the discourse of a self. Its intrinsic nature is stainless and ultimately pure.

(As in the following analogy: the dharmas produced according to conditions are fundamentally devoid of the two kinds of self, just as a performer, by means of incantations, manifests various forms—how could there be any clinging to a dual self? (The waves of the ocean, preceding and succeeding one another...)
"Chasing [the waves]—they are continuous and unceasing; only when the wind ceases will the waves stop. The commentary states:

In the response, it says that the *tathāgatagarbha* is the cause of both good and evil. "Tathāgata" refers to the *tathatā* (suchness) of the principle-nature, which is possessed within every present moment of thought;
this is termed the "garbha" (womb/storehouse). When the sense organs and objects give rise to a single moment of mind, [it follows...]
The conditions for defilement and purity: defilement is ignorance (*avidyā*). Following ignorance as a condition for defilement results in the birth-and-death of the nine realms.
Purity is teaching and practice. Following teaching and practice as a condition for purity results in the four kinds of cessation through the path (*mārga-nirodha*).

These four kinds are: arising-and-ceasing, non-arising, immeasurable, and unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*). Therefore, it is said that these are the causes of the wholesome and the unwholesome; a cause must inevitably produce its fruit.
What is called "all destinies and births" refers to the good and evil retributions within the ten realms.

What are called the "three conditions" are the sense organs (*indriya*), the objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). When the sense organs and objects combine, a single thought-moment of mind arises;

because of non-awakening (*abodha*), it pursues defiled conditions and, by creating only deluded karma, brings about birth and death within the nine realms. Because those externalists are not awakened, they falsely calculate and cling [to these].
Attached to conditioned activity, it is perfumed by beginningless evil habits and is termed the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness). It evolves to produce the seven consciousnesses;
this is the ground where ignorance dwells (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*), which refers to the very beginning of the arising of ignorance. From this root, the secondary branches of ignorance are produced;
therefore, it is metaphorically described as being like the body of ocean waves, constantly arising without interruption. This is defilement according to conditions, proceeding from the subtle.

This is the ultimate characteristic. If one can, in a single thought-moment, turn the light inward and accord with pure conditions, then one will be free from the fault of impermanence and the attachment to the two selves;
the self-nature will be pure, and what is called the Tathāgata of virtuous nature will be fully revealed.
The remaining consciousnesses arise and perish. Within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) and its associates, there are seven [consciousnesses] at every moment.

Due to unreal conceptualization (*abhūtaparikalpa*), they grasp at various objects, their diverse forms and locations, and falsely calculate them as names and characteristics (*nāmalakṣaṇa*). They do not realize that these forms and appearances are manifestations of their own minds;

they do not realize suffering or pleasure, and thus fail to reach liberation. Bound by the entanglements of names and characteristics, they crave existence and give rise to craving. If, due to suffering...

As they rely upon those objects of perception, the various faculties of sensation cease in succession and do not arise again; being unaware of pleasure or pain through the false imaginings of their own minds, they enter the fourth dhyāna, the meditative attainment of the cessation of sensation and perception.

(This statement means that all consciousnesses have arising and ceasing. "All consciousnesses" refers to the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), the manas-consciousness, and the five sensory consciousnesses;
these constitute the seven consciousnesses. It does not refer to the seventh consciousness of the two vehicles [śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas].
When the sense objects, faculties, and consciousnesses mutually cling to and become attached through grasping, by what means can one attain liberation?)

The commentary states: "Arising from the Buddha moment by moment, their arising is necessarily simultaneous. Regarding "unreal conceptualization and the like," this refers to the six consciousnesses grasping at objects.
"Various forms and locations" refers to the six sense-fields (*ṣaḍviṣaya*). Once the faculties and their objects have taken form, one pursues names and characteristics.
Because one does not understand that form and so forth are manifestations of one's own mind, one gives rise to feelings of suffering and pleasure, which in turn give rise to [further afflictions].

Death; there is no way to attain liberation. This is called being bound and entangled by names and signs (*nāma-nimitta*). From greed arises greed; cause and object-condition depend upon one another, and these are all what is termed the "characteristic of arising" (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*).
Below those various sensations (*vedanā*) is what is called the "characteristic of cessation" (*nirodha-lakṣaṇa*):

namely, that the faculties of sensation (*vedanendriya*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and so forth, do not arise in succession, leaving only the deluded conceptualizations of one's own mind which are unaware of suffering or pleasure. Thus it is said.

"Entering the cessation of sensation and perception" refers to the cessation of sensation, perception, and mind; that is, the attainment of the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), or the attainment of the fourth *dhyāna*.

Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, we pray that you will explain for us the ultimate characteristics of the five dharmas, the self-natures, consciousness, and the two kinds of selflessness, as they are sequentially continuous throughout all stages (*bhūmi*). Having analyzed these dharmas, one enters into all [stages]."
Regarding the Buddha-dharma: as for "entering all Buddha-dharmas," up to the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-awakened realization, the Buddha told Mahāmati:

"The five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness are the characteristics of the modes of conceptualization. These are: names, signs, false imagination, right knowledge, and suchness.
If a practitioner cultivates the practice to enter the noble mode of the Tathāgata’s self-awakened realization, they will be free from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism.
There is no peerless view; the dwelling in the meditative attainment of happiness in the present life manifests before one.

Mahāmati, it is because they do not realize that those five dharmas, the self-natures, consciousness, the two kinds of selflessness, and external objects are merely manifestations of one's own mind, that ordinary people engage in false conceptualization; this is not the case for the noble ones.
(Preceding Remarks: Although the five dharmas have been explained in detail, the reason why one enters the stage of the Tathāgata has not yet been distinguished;

therefore, he asks again. (Regarding the characteristics of the five dharmas, there is both delusion and awakening. When a practitioner enters [the path], these five dharmas are all characteristics of awakening;
conversely, when it is non-awakening, they are all characteristics of delusion. This is because dharmas have no intrinsic nature; delusion and awakening depend upon—)
...is a person. This is a general indication of the characteristics of how one enters [the path] and so forth (which will be detailed later).
Mahāmati, as for those characteristics: that which is illuminated by the visual consciousness is called "form" (*rūpa*);

that which is illuminated by the auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental consciousnesses is called "sound, odor, taste, touch, and phenomena" (*śabda-gandha-rasa-spraṣṭavya-dharma*). These are called "characteristics. Mahāmati, as for that "conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*), it is an establishment [of designations].

The various names manifest the various characteristics; in this way, they are not different [from them]. Names such as "elephant," "horse," "chariot," "infantry," "man," and "woman"—these are called false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
Mahāmati, as for right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*): those names and characteristics cannot be apprehended, being like passing guests;
the various consciousnesses do not arise, and they are neither annihilated nor eternal. They do not fall into the stages of any externalists, *śrāvakas*, or *pratyekabuddhas*.
(The six sense organs and the six sense objects together constitute the marks of form (*rūpa-nimitta*). To be free from all marks of form is not the realm of externalists.
As for "the names and marks being unattainable," it means that if one seeks true wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*), one should simply realize that names and marks are unreal, like passing travelers.

When the consciousness-mind does not arise, one is free from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism and does not fall into the realms of ordinary beings or the Lesser Vehicle; this is called right wisdom.
The commentary states: The two dharmas of name and form do not transcend the six consciousnesses. To grasp those six sense objects is what is meant by "name."
That which is grasped is the characteristic (*nimitta*). To manifest and establish various names and characteristics is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

Names such as "elephant" or "horse"—by means of these names, their characteristics are manifested. Once names and characteristics are established, this is called the discrimination of conceptual construction (*vikalpa-vikalpa*).

The three dharmas mentioned above all pertain to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). From "right knowledge" (*samyag-jñāna*) downward, one proceeds to the dharma of the noble ones (*ārya*) to explain the characteristics of awakening.
Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "As for the past Buddhas spoken of, they are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; so too are those of the future and the present."
It is likewise so. World-Honored One, do you accept it exactly as it was spoken, or is there further meaning?
We only pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately explain this for us.
"The Buddhas of the three periods of time are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; according to what is stated in the scriptures, the number of these Buddhas is often lost.
Is it that they receive [retribution] exactly as described? Or is there another meaning? Therefore, I humbly request clarification."
The commentary states: The Ganges is located within the borders of India; its sands are used merely as a metaphor for their great number.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Do not accept things according to how they are described. The measure of the Buddhas of the three periods of time is not like that of the sands of the Ganges.

Why is this? Because it transcends worldly perspective and cannot be illustrated by any analogy. This is because ordinary, ignorant people and non-Buddhist outsiders falsely imagine it to be eternal."

Nurturing evil views leads to an endless cycle of birth and death. Desiring to cause them to weary of and become detached from the wheel of saṃsāra so that they may apply themselves with diligence and excel, he says to them:
"The Buddhas are easy to encounter; they are not like the udumbara flower, which is difficult to see. Thus he causes them to cease their expedient seeking.
At other times, observing those who are to be transformed, he makes this statement: "A Buddha is difficult to encounter, like the udumbara flower."
The *udumbara* flower. The *udumbara* flower has never been seen, is not being seen now, and will not be seen; yet the Tathāgata is seen by the entire world.
It is not because he establishes his own realization that it is said, "The appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is like the *udumbara* flower.
Mahāmati, as for establishing one's own realization, it transcends worldly expectations and cannot be believed by those ordinary, foolish people. Establishing one's own...
The realm of noble wisdom is beyond analogy; the true Tathāgata transcends the characteristics perceived by the mind, intellect, and consciousness, and thus cannot be illustrated by comparison.
Mahāmati, nevertheless, when I speak of the Buddha being like the sands of the Ganges, there is no fault in this.
(If one says it is difficult, fear arises; if one says it is easy, negligence is provoked. Therefore, the Ganges is used as a metaphor.

The *utpala* is a flower that is yellowish-white in color. (These two metaphors—speaking of difficulty and ease—are both matters concerning the Buddha’s transformative activity (*nirmāṇa-karman*), not the realm of the Tathāgata’s self-realization.
Thus it is said: "One does not establish [the truth] through one's own communication. If we discuss self-realization, [it is beyond these].)
It is peerless in the world and beyond the reach of analogy; all ordinary and ignorant people are unable to believe and accept it, nor can it be known or seen by the mind and intellect.
Nevertheless, there are times when it is established for the sake of transforming others—what fault could there be in this?
The commentary states: The number of Buddhas exceeds the sands of the Ganges and surpasses the scope of what can be conceived by the minds of worldly beings;
therefore, they cannot be fully illustrated by any analogy. How could it be merely the sands of the Ganges? Generally, when analogies are established, their meanings are not uniform.
For instance, for those ordinary and ignorant beings who have not yet undergone transformation, birth and death are endless; thus, the Buddha speaks of the Buddhas as being easy to perceive.
It is not like the udumbara flower, which causes those who encounter it to give rise to thoughts of despondency and to cease their skillful means and vain seeking;
rather, by showing what is difficult to attain as easy to achieve, one encourages them to advance toward the Buddha-way.

Furthermore, for those who have already been transformed through special insight, one tells them that encountering a Buddha is as rare as the udumbara flower, causing them to admire and aspire toward the Way; thus, one urges them forward.
Furthermore, as for the statement that the *tánhuā* (rare flower) is difficult to encounter: it is already the case that we shall now see it;

for the Tathāgata is seen by all people in the world. Thus we know that those who say the Tathāgata is like the *tánhuā* merely intend to evoke in people the thought that he is truly difficult to meet.
It is like the sands of the Ganges, which are the intrinsic nature of earth. When the world is consumed at the end of a kalpa, all earth is burned;

yet that element of earth does not abandon its own nature because it arises simultaneously with the element of fire. Other foolish people conceive the notion that the earth is burning, but the earth is not actually burned, for fire is its cause.
In this same way, Mahāmati, the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is thus indestructible.
"This statement—that the nature of sand is indestructible—is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s dharmakāya being eternally abiding.

The commentary states: "Regarding the statement that this is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of earth, there is both the phenomenal aspect (*vastu*) and the noumenal aspect (*tattva*). In terms of the phenomenal aspect, they share the same quality of solidity."
Therefore, it appears as sand or stone. In principle, however, it is identical in its true nature to that which is hard, moist, warm, or moving.
Thus, when the kalpa ends and all is consumed by fire, the nature of earth remains as it was. This is because both earth and the fire-element are equally produced [from the same source].
Fools do not understand this; they merely see what they call "burning. As for the cause of fire: it is because earth lacks fire that it does not burn, whereas fire—[lacking earth]...
Because the earth does not continue [as a single entity], the earth cannot be burned. It is the same with the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body, which neither transmigrates nor changes.
Mahāmati, it is like the sands of the Ganges, which flow along with the water and are not without water. In this same way, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata...
All the teachings I have spoken flow toward Nirvana; therefore, they are said to be like the sands of the Ganges.
The Tathāgata does not follow the flow of the various realms of existence (*gati*), for that would imply destruction. Mahāmati, the original limit of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) is unknowable;
since it is unknowable, how can one speak of "going"? Mahāmati, "going" implies annihilation, yet the foolish do not understand this.
(To flow in accordance with the stream toward ultimate nirvana is to be truly, eternally, and correctly awakened. (The single word "sever" is most difficult to speak;
when one cuts off the roots of the dust and the obstacles of craving, one will know the original limit of birth and death.)
The commentary states: When the sands of the Ganges flow along with the current, the foolish see only the flowing sand and do not see the water;
yet when one observes with wisdom, it is not that there is no water. This is a metaphor for the Tathāgata’s teaching that all dharmas accord with *nirvāṇa*.
Just as there is that which accords with the current, there is no sense of "going. Therefore, it is said that the Tathāgata does not follow the currents of various goings. This refers to the dharmas.
Awakened understanding does not revolve according to appearances; therefore, it is not the same as "going" in the sense of flowing away.

This is because "going" carries the meaning of the destruction and cessation of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*). Regarding the "original limit of birth-and-death," this original limit of birth-and-death cannot be known.
Since it cannot be known, how can one speak of a "destination"? Mahāmati, the meaning of a destination is an object; ordinary fools do not know that a destination is simply "going."
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has taught that one attains perfect enlightenment by fulfilling the six pāramitās, what constitutes their traces?
Mahāmati, there are three kinds of distinctions regarding the pāramitās: namely, the mundane, the supramundane, and the supreme-supramundane.
Mahāmati, as for the mundane pāramitās, they involve grasping and attachment to ‘I’ and ‘mine,’ and the grasping [of objects].”
The two extremes: for the sake of the pleasures of various places of rebirth—namely, forms, sounds, scents, tastes, and tangibles—one fulfills the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).
The same applies to ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom. This also includes the supernatural powers of ordinary beings and birth in the Brahma heavens.
(From this shore one ascends to the other shore. Because it is based on the true permanence of each moment, there is no "act of crossing. Thus, Mahāmati asks.
The commentary states:

In response, he says that the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) are threefold. First, he asks about the six perfections, stating that they involve the grasping and conceptualization of "self" and "mine."
Regarding "attachment and so forth": this refers to the practice of ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). There are four faults therein:

first, by reckoning a self and what belongs to a self, they lack the intention to deliver sentient beings; second, by clinging to the two extremes, they are unable to reach the further shore of the Middle Way.

Second, if one seeks superior rewards, one cannot escape the cycle of birth and death. Third, if one delights in and clings to the six sense objects, it is not a gift given with the mark of non-abiding.

Fourth, even the attainment of the five supernatural powers by non-Buddhists, as well as their rebirth in the Brahma heavens, is achieved through the practice of the six perfections and the cultivation of untainted phenomena (*anāsrava*).

Mahāmati, as for the supramundane pāramitās: because śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas fall into the grasping of nirvāṇa, they practice the six pāramitās while delighting in their own personal nirvāṇic bliss.
(These two vehicles cultivate [the path] based on the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, practicing these six perfections).
The commentary states: "To speak of 'falling into the grasping of nirvana' means that they seek only their own deliverance and take pleasure in the bliss of true emptiness."
Therefore, it differs from what is practiced by bodhisattvas.

Regarding the "supreme worldly-transcending pāramitās": because one realizes that the objects of perception are merely the manifestations of one's own mind’s false conceptualization and that there is no duality within one's own mind, one does not give rise to false conceptualization.
One does not grasp at the various realms of existence as being real, nor does one falsely reckon upon the forms and appearances of one's own mind.
To bring peace and happiness to all sentient beings, one gives rise to the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) and initiates the most supreme skillful means.

That very non-arising of deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*) with respect to those objects is the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*); that same non-arising of deluded conceptualization is patience (*kṣānti*).

Knowing that which is grasped and that which grasps is the *kṣānti-pāramitā*. Diligently applying skillful means during the first, middle, and last watches of the night, practicing in accordance with skillful means so that false conceptualizations (*vikalpa*) do not arise, is the *vīrya-pāramitā*.

The total cessation of all false conceptualizations without falling into the grasping for the nirvāṇa of the śrāvakas is the *dhyāna-pāramitā*. The non-substantiality of the false conceptualizations of one's own mind is wisdom (*prajñā*).
Observing without falling into the two extremes, with the preceding body transformed into something superior and indestructible, one attains the noble path of self-awakening;

this is the *prajñāpāramitā* (the practice cultivated by the Bodhisattvas of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching). As for "receiving," it means that the six faculties receive the six sense objects within one's own mind.
Second: It is said that the cultivation of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) remedies stinginess and greed.

(Note: Since the Bodhisattva has realized that all phenomena are manifestations of mind alone—namely, practicing giving while not dwelling on form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental objects—the remedy and the object of remedy are non-dual. This non-duality...)
Because these two [factors] are absent, the three spheres (trimaṇḍala) are empty in essence. Therefore, it is said that not giving rise to deluded thoughts is the emptiness of the giver;
not grasping [the recipient] is the emptiness of the receiver; and not being attached to the marks of form is the emptiness of the object given.
When a Bodhisattva practices giving in this manner, it serves to bring benefit and happiness to all sentient beings; therefore, it is called the supreme skillful means (upāya). This is...

Regarding those conditions: it means that the mind which has well-cultivated the perfection of giving does not give rise to false conceptualization even toward conditions such as the observance of precepts;
rather, each and every precept is maintained in accordance with its true nature (*dharmatā*).
Maintaining the precepts in this way is neither maintaining them nor violating them. Practicing patience in this way is neither contravening nor conforming. Practicing diligence in this way...
Thus, what is there to exert or what is there to slacken? Practicing dhyāna in this way, there is neither fixed concentration nor distraction.
Practicing prajñā in this way, there is neither folly nor wisdom. Naturally, one does not adhere to the two extremes, nor does one depart from the two extremes;
resting securely in the Middle Way, one proceeds directly to the other shore. This is the conception of the supreme-to-supreme pāramitā. Within patience, it is said that "knowing" is its inclusion.

Regarding that which is subsumed: namely, the grasper and the grasped, both of which are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Among the [perfections], the term "expedient means" (*upāya*) occurs twice.

First, as a specific characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), it refers to the mastery of the sūtras and so forth. Second, as a general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), it refers to the inclusion of the other five perfections;

all must be practiced with diligence (*vīrya*). Regarding the statement in the section on meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) that one does not fall into the grasp of the śrāvakas: this refers to the śrāvakas.
Those whose concentration is excessive, as well as those who delight in and cling to nirvana, are not like this regarding the bodhisattva.

Thus, while it is said across the six perfections that false conceptualization does not arise, or that it is entirely extinguished, or that it has no inherent nature—despite these differences among the six perfections—[the underlying principle remains the same].
Yet, taking the departure from delusion as the foundation—if one can depart from delusion, what practice could not be accomplished?

That the previous body becomes increasingly superior and indestructible refers to the progressive advancement of the six perfections, culminating in the wisdom-body attained through *prajñā*, which is far superior to the preceding five and cannot be destroyed.
To attain the noble path of self-awakening is, moreover, the ultimate realization of *prajñā*.
